National news outlets increasingly report that Kansas is in play and that GOP nominee Roger “Doc” Marshall, infamous for suing hundreds of his own patients for payment and owning more stuff in Florida than in Kansas, is sweating bullets over the challenge from Democratic hopeful Adam Hamilton.
Hamilton has more in common with Bryan, the prairie populist who said God wants us to care for the poor, than with Democrat George McGill, a Wichita lawyer elected to his last U.S. Senate term in 1932.
Hamilton is a megachurch pastor from Leawood, and he’s saying some of the same things Bryan did, and getting national attention for it. During the senatorial debate Sept. 12 at the Kansas State Fair, Hamilton said he’s spent the last 38 years trying to teach people “what does it mean to be a decent human being, how are we meant to live our lives, to love God and to love our neighbor.”
Bryan is remembered today, if at all, as an antique from a bygone era.
But back in 1897, Bryan was adored by millions.
He was just 37 years old, an evangelical Christian, a famed orator, and a self-professed champion of the common man. The year before, he had been the Democratic nominee for president and come surprisingly close to defeating Republican William McKinley. McKinley won, but by a margin of just a few points in the popular vote.
Bryan eventually became a parody of himself, a politician with three failed attempts at the White House and the leader of a movement to keep public schools from teaching Darwin’s theory of evolution. Bryan, or at least a dramatic version of him, was held up to scorn in the 1955 Lawrence and Lee play “Inherit the Wind,” a fictionalized account of the Scopes Monkey Trial of 30 years before. The real Bryan had testified against the young high school teacher charged with teaching evolution and was skewered by famed defense attorney Clarence Darrow, who demanded to know when exactly the earth was created and where Cain found his wife.
I mentioned Bryan in this 2024 piece about some wackos in Topeka who wanted to make gold and silver legal tender. As a young congressman from Nebraska, Bryan had argued against high tariffs as a form of taxation on American consumers. He rose to fame when he delivered his “Cross of Gold” speech at the 1896 Democratic convention at Chicago. Although the politics are difficult to understand now, Bryan was arguing for “free silver” and against the gold standard because it favored wealth and empire over workers and agrarian interests.
“You come to us and tell us that the great cities are in favor of the gold standard,” Bryan said. “We reply that the great cities rest upon our broad and fertile prairies. Burn down your cities and leave our farms, and your cities will spring up again as if by magic; but destroy our farms and the grass will grow in the streets of every city in the country.”
Bryan, with his fiery oratory and rustic ways, became a hero of rural America at another time when economic depression and cultural strife had set working people on their heels.
“Bryan was the first leader of a major party to argue for permanently expanding the power of the federal government to serve the welfare of ordinary Americans from the working and middle classes,” writes historian Michael Kazin in his 2006 biography of Bryan. “With the backing of his followers, he preached that the national state should counter the overweening power of banks and industrial corporations by legalizing strikes, subsidizing farmers, taxing the rich, banning private campaign spending, and outlawing the ‘liquor trust’ (a monopoly on whiskey).”
More than any other politician, Kazin argues, Bryan transformed the Democratic party from Gilded Age insiders to FDR liberals. While the New Deal embraced much of what Bryan had proposed, it rejected the racism shared by nearly every white Democrat until the late 1930s — including Bryan. “Inherit the Wind,” though historically inaccurate, captured the white Protestant bigotry and mistrust of science that was a hallmark of a past age.
This is where any comparison between Hamilton and Bryan falters. Hamilton carries none of the generational sins that Bryan did, nor is he so obsessed with his own rhetoric that he might be lacking in substance. His political weaknesses may be in his handling of child sexual abuse incidents at a church camp in the mid-2000s and descriptions of him as a petty tyrant with high expectations by former employees, as reported in July by Kansas Reflector. Hamilton was not accused of abuse himself, and others praised his fast-paced, if taxing, leadership.
Hamilton is a fine and confident speaker and owned the stage at the state fair from the beginning (to be fair, Marshall was the target of much booing).
Adam Hamilton appears onstage during the Sept. 12, 2026, debate with U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
No, I’m drawing a parallel between the young and idealistic Bryan and the Democratic candidate we saw on the stage at Hutchinson.
Hamilton has seized the political imagination in a way that few Kansas Democrats have in what feels like ever. But in the Trump era “ever” can be measured in minutes and many voters may be driven to Hamilton out of a sense of increasing desperation about the state of the country. Although his megachurch credentials might be off-putting to some (I raise my hand here), his religious background provides a bridge for many undecided Kansans who find expressions of faith reassuring. It doesn’t hurt that he’s a Methodist, which is like the universal donor blood type of evangelical Christianity. The United Methodist Church, in 2024, also lifted a ban on LGBTQ+ clergy and same-sex marriages, a move that caused thousands of conservative congregations, mostly in the South, to leave the denomination.
The same thing happened to the Baptists in 1845, when they denounced slavery.
Hamilton’s megachurch, Resurrection, in the Kansas City suburb of Leawood, has 24,000 members and is one of the largest Methodist congregations in the world. Hamilton co-founded it as small church in a former funeral home in 1990.
Hamilton may be the counter to MAGA’s stranglehold on the faithful in the heartland, a well-spoken white pastor who loves Jesus and condemns the grift of Donald Trump. At the state fair debate, he was particularly hard on Trump’s promise of $5,000 bonuses if the GOP wins the midterms, saying that it was “exactly what’s wrong in Washington, D.C., right now” – and likely illegal. Marshall also said he disagreed with Trump on the bonuses, but was waiting for more information. Then, amid heckling, he quickly changed the subject to a chest-thumping defense of Kansas agriculture.
Hamilton has gotten attention not just for his numbers, but for a kind of moderate white bread charisma. Here is Bill McKibben writing about him in The New Yorker, making the point that what Hamilton says about loving one’s neighbor is a radical political notion in the era of Trump. The Atlantic also covered Hamilton, sending a writer to witness firsthand an August visit to a coffee shop at Emporia.
“Gravel City Roasters is a combination coffee shop and art gallery located directly across Emporia’s main drag from the county Democratic headquarters,” David von Drehle reported. “There is a Pride flag on the wall with REFUGEES WELCOME superimposed on its rainbow stripes. The chai, served in mismatched mugs, is excellent.”
Hamilton was at home at the coffee shop, according to Drehle, and Hamilton said he was one of the few Democratic politicians who could recite the Lord’s Prayer — and that it reminds us to make sure people have enough to eat.
What Hamilton offers is a kind of emotional glue that hasn’t been seen in the Democratic Party in at least a decade. It is a correction toward the middle. Before the arc of history can bend toward justice, there must first be a consensus of what is good — how to live a decent life — and then the people in agreement can work toward meaningful change by winning elections. In the past decade, people of conscience have been confronted by so many injustices that it has been easy to become paralyzed, not knowing which battle to fight first. What Hamilton is saying is that it’s all the same fight, and he speaks the language of the heartland.
“I hear God speak through the Bible,” Hamilton writes in his 2014 book on scripture. “Its words convict me, challenge me, and comfort me. And some of them disturb me. In this book, I’d like to share with you how I and many others have wrestled with the Bible and have come to make sense of its thorny passages while listening carefully for the One to whom all scripture bears witness.”
Hamilton hears something in the Bible I don’t, except for perhaps the “Song of Solomon.” But this is no matter. Hamilton writes not for me, but for the faithful. He is no fundamentalist, as he believes the earth is 4.5 billion years old, thinks Darwinian evolution doesn’t rule out the possibility of divine guidance and teaches that Bible verses condemning homosexuality shouldn’t be taken at face value.
At the state fair debate, Marshall said Hamilton was “too woke, he’s too weak, and he doesn’t stand for anything.”
But Marshall was shouting into a gathering wind. None of those hot buttons work anymore, and Hamilton’s gospel of compassion may appeal to voters beyond Kansas because of the way it’s framed. Others have said the same thing before, but pastor Hamilton tempers the message with a call to reject extremism.
Hamilton’s concept of personal decency, told through a personal struggle to understand scripture that is often indecently brutal, speaks to the conflict in the American soul.
After that 1897 train wreck, Bryan joined in the rescue to help carry the dead and wounded from the scene. As related in a newspaper account published the day after the accident, a badly maimed individual called out to Bryan.
“I went to hear you today,” the man said. “I am dying now and want to shake your hand and say God bless you. If possible, Mr. Bryan, can you get me a drink of water?”
Bryan, according to newspaper story, which seems so fantastically Biblical as to be untrue, went to a burning mail car and returned with water for the dying man. (Wasn’t the water hot? Never mind, that’s not the point.)
At that moment, 129 years ago this month, Bryan so held the trust and the promise of rural America that a newspaper anecdote anointed him a political prophet.
Hamilton carries a similar cup of spiritual and political water.
Or maybe it’s chai.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The Vernon grumble over rumble/mumble
description: There has been some grumbling in Vernon about rumble strips. But is there a quieter way to save lives?
text:
Why would anyone oppose road safety?  Well, perhaps, when the solution can be heard from your bedroom.
State Route 527 in Vernon (known locally as West Street), which carries 7000+ cars a day, has a blemished record for traffic accidents:  90 crashes in a recent three-year period. Too often cars veer over the centerline of the highway, off the road or into oncoming traffic.



The proposed solution by the Connecticut Department of Transportation is “rumble strips.”
You’ve probably seen, felt or heard them in your own driving… when the road makes a low rumbling sound as you drive across the centerline.  The sensations are designed to alert you, usually in time to correct your path and avoid danger.
CDOT told the Hartford Courant that “hundreds of miles of centerline rumble strips have been installed across Connecticut, and CTDOT has received very few noise complaints. They remain a low-cost improvement with a significant safety benefit for the traveling public.”
Vernon’s mayor Dan Champagne says he’s all for public safety but not if it comes with noise.  
In a posting on Facebook he writes: “When cars and trucks drive on these rumble strips they make a lot of noise and neighbors are going to hear them around the clock.  Cars and trucks travel West Street at all hours of the day and the noise is going to be constant.”
But isn’t that the idea, Mr. Mayor? 
Those rumble strips only make noise when people are heading toward an accident.  If people drive better there’ll be no noise and maybe no accidents.  And the sound of crashing metal as vehicles collide isn’t exactly a lullaby.
As CDOT points out:  “In Connecticut, approximately 30 deaths and 2,000 injuries occur each year from head-on and sideswipe opposite direction crashes… when a vehicle crosses over the centerline and impacts a vehicle traveling in the opposite direction.” 
“Nationwide data shows 18% of non-intersection fatal crashes are caused by two vehicles colliding head-on and that 75% of these head-on crashes occur on undivided two-lane roads.”  And that’s not exactly quiet, right?
Still, CDOT has been through this before in 1999 at an undisclosed “high-crash location” when rumble strips proved too noisy and were ripped out.
But wait.  There may be a solution that warns wayward drivers without waking the neighbors from their slumber:  not rumble strips but “mumble strips.”


CDOT says they can now groove the centerline with sinusoidal designs (ripples rather than bumps) that are “formed by wave patterns in the pavement rather than grooves cut into it, making them quieter than earlier designs.”  Wavy instead of groovy, man.
Studies show the “mumble” pattern is up to 11 decibels quieter.   At its best, that roughly cuts the noise in half.
Total cost for the Vernon project:  just $5,000 in state funds, less than the cost of a single head-on crash, not even factoring in the human costs of injuries.
To their credit, CDOT will hold a virtual informational meeting on this plan on October 27, so residents will have a chance to be heard… possibly louder than the feared hum from Route 527.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Suspending the gas tax would be a shortsighted election year stunt
description: The state gas tax is the price we pay to ensure that we have safe and reliable ways to get where we need to go, with sufficient funding to build, operate, and maintain the essential transportation infrastructure we all depend upon.
text:
IT WAS Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., the Boston-born associate justice of the Supreme Court, who wrote in 1927 that “taxes are what we pay for civilized society.”   
When it comes to the state gas tax, this is the price we pay to ensure that we have safe and reliable ways to get where we need to go, with sufficient funding to build, operate, and maintain the essential transportation infrastructure we all depend upon.  
The current political environment, which has the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor proposing to leave at least $120 million (and probably more) on the table in order to gain political points, is a remarkable abdication of that principle and an example of how presumed short-term political gain will lead to long-term transportation pain. 
On Monday, Republican nominee Mike Minogue proposed suspending the gas tax any time the price of fuel exceeds $4 per gallon and working toward eliminating the levy altogether. Democratic incumbent Maura Healey, seemingly concerned about not keeping pace with her challenger amid a campaign season being defined, here and nationally, by “affordability,” has now proposed suspending the gas tax for two months.  Both candidates are doing the public a disservice. 
You can’t drive a car without heavy and continuous public investment in roads and bridges – building them, maintaining them, policing them, plowing them. The state’s 24-cent-per-gallon gas tax is an essential source of funding for those investments, though it does not come close to covering the full costs of driving in Massachusetts, including the public health costs associated with dangerous particulate emissions.   
The state relies on three main sources of funding for transportation needs: the sales tax on the purchase of vehicles, automobile registration and inspection fees, and the state gas tax. Over the last four years, so-called Fair Share, or millionaires tax, revenues have also supported transportation needs. Depending on the year, collections from the gas tax are either the largest or second-largest source of state-generated transportation revenue. 
The gas tax is a rough form of a user fee. It has, since the first days of the automobile era in the last century, been the foundation of how state transportation infrastructure gets built and maintained. States rely on gas tax revenues for both pay-as-you-go transportation projects as well as for the payment of principal and interest on transportation bonds issued for large capital projects.  
The state gas tax helps pay for the roads our ambulances and EMTs and firefighters use to save lives. It helps pay for the road system that enables fulfillment of our everyday needs, whether getting to school or work or a doctor’s appointment, or a visit to a friend. It pays, in short, for the very things that help establish and improve our quality of life. 
At a time when our transportation system is suffering from chronic and worsening traffic congestion, when the public transportation system is undergoing a massive and long overdue rehabilitation of its system, and when federal dollars for projects across the board are being held back or clawed back by the Trump administration, deliberately reducing state revenue by roughly $120 million (the Healey administration’s estimate) or more seems profoundly inadvisable and wrongheaded.  
The administration has proposed using “surplus” millionaires tax revenue to make up for the lost gas tax revenue, but this is a classic example of robbing Peter to pay Paul, as it means some other worthy public need will go unfunded.   
Suspending the state gas tax for two months might save the average driver about $25, barely enough to respond meaningfully to current gas prices and other inflationary pressures. The benefits would be miniscule; the downsides would be enormous.  
First, the actual loss might be in excess of $120 million. The gas tax is actually paid by wholesalers on a monthly basis (your payment at the pump reimburses them). Wholesalers are likely to load up on gasoline during any suspension period in order to benefit from more sales, and that could mean state revenue losses in excess of the projected $120 million.   
Second, this is sending the wrong message to Massachusetts drivers. By making the gas tax seem something that is optional or not critical to our transportation needs, both candidates are undermining the very foundation of state transportation funding, making it harder in the future to gain public trust for revenue initiatives of any type.   
Third, any Fair Share “surplus” is not net new money. It is money that should be used as it was intended, to pay for specific and growing transportation infrastructure needs.  Shifting money from one account to another is not finding a way to pay for this proposed suspension; it is a shell game.  
Finally, economists who have studied these types of gas tax suspension proposals estimate that drivers only receive about 72 percent of the benefit, with the rest going right back to the suppliers. So the actual benefit to drivers will be much less than most people probably expect.  
Massachusetts needs to invest in its residents, in order to promote the public good and public safety. That doesn’t happen at no cost. Tossing away $120 million in vital funding to score election year points is not the answer to rising gas prices.  
Losing $120 million (or more) is like losing almost the entire amount of money the MBTA has to pay every year for the RIDE paratransit services. It is close to the amount of money that the state uses to fund the regional transit authorities (about $97 million). It’s like losing roughly half of the money the state collects in tolls on the Metro Highway System.  
We should instead invest in policies that could help alleviate traffic congestion and improve access and improve air quality. Massachusetts should be making it easier for people to choose not to drive, or drive less, by spending more money on building a transformational regional rail system.  
Massachusetts should be making it easier for drivers to transition to electric vehicles, but we remain a laggard in making the investments that were facilitated by the Biden administration’s bipartisan infrastructure bill.  As reported in Commonwealth Beacon this June, despite receiving a $64 million federal grant four years ago, Massachusetts hasn’t built a single electric charging station in accordance with the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program.  
Over eight years since the Commission on the Future of Transportation said that we must “move more people in fewer vehicles,” Massachusetts is pushing more people to drive more, congesting roads more, polluting more. Political stunts like those being proposed by the two leading candidates for governor do nothing to address this trend and aren’t serving our best interests. Instead, they are undermining public understanding and support for investing in our common and shared futures. 
In the effort to navigate through the consequences of an ill-advised war in Iran, political leaders need to collectively rise to the occasion. The response to the pain at the pump shouldn’t cause more pain by reducing revenues necessary to keep investing in the infrastructure we all depend on.   
Political leaders of both parties should not be undermining the importance and value of the gas tax. Like any tax, it is unpopular, but it is one of the main engines fueling our transportation system and, through that, fueling our economy.   
It would be foolhardy and shortsighted to decide that the best way to help people who are feeling pain at the pump is to deliberately disinvest in the very systems they rely on for everyday necessities.   
James Aloisi is a former Massachusetts secretary of transportation.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Book Festival draws thousands to Jackson to celebrate the written word
authors: Anna Hu, Katherine Lin and Madeline Nguyen
description: Kate McKinnon, a former cast member of "Saturday Night Live," is introduced during the Mississippi Book Festival in Jackson on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026.
text:
Jubilee JiBol stood in line, clutching an oversized book for author Mychal Threets to sign. At 9 years old, she was already a veteran of the Mississippi Book Festival, which returned Saturday to the state Capitol.
“I’ve been coming since I was 1 years old, ever since I was a baby,” she said, as her mother, L.E. JiBol, nodded to confirm. Her brother Nile, 6, was a relative newcomer and has been working hard to improve his reading skills for future trips to the festival.
They joined thousands of other book lovers who swarmed the grounds of the Capitol and nearby Galloway United Methodist Church in Jackson, streaming through large white tents lined with tables stacked with books.
Jubilee JiBol, 9, and her brother Nile, 6, get help from a volunteer while waiting in line at the Mississippi Book Festival in Jackson on Sept. 26, 2026.  Credit: Bobby Caina Calvan/Mississippi Today / Mississippi Today
The annual festival, now in its 11th year, has become a gathering place for readers young and old to meet authors, discover books and celebrate Mississippi’s literary tradition.
Threets, better known as Mychal the Librarian, has been an evangelist for reading. His mission is to teach kids what libraries can offer and that they belong there.
‘Just let them read’
He is now host of the revival of “Reading Rainbow,” a television program aimed at encouraging children to read and develop a love of books. The reboot debuted last year and has been renewed for a second season.
“Just let them read and read because it’s so much fun. There’s so much joy in reading,” Threets said. “When I think about the future of libraries, that’s what I think of.” 
In the spirit of sharing that joy, Threets handed out free copies of his book, “I’m So Happy You’re Here: A Celebration of Library Joy.”
“A library is for every single person,” Threets said during a vulnerable, wide-ranging conversation in front of an audience at Galloway with author Margaret McMullan.
Their conversation touched on Threets’ struggles with mental health and his thoughts about Black teenager Emmett Till, who was kidnapped and killed by white men in Mississippi in 1955. Threets also encouraged kids to read and talked about taking his cat to the library as a child.
A long line of book-toting fans stretched for a block outside Galloway, which hosted some of the festival’s panels.
In the minutes before former “Saturday Night Live” cast member Kate McKinnon took the stage, parents corralled young children onto their laps. One uncle was already making plans to dash out to McKinnon’s 11 a.m. book signing.
Traveling through time
McKinnon first appeared as her alter ego, Dr. G. Edwina Candlestank, the eccentric narrator of McKinnon’s middle-grade series, “The Millicent Quibb School of Etiquette for Young Ladies of Mad Science.”
“I traveled throughout time,” Candlestank said, exaggerating each syllable, to the state of “Mye-sye-sye-pie.” She stalked onto the stage with a tuft of her short blond hair sticking up, wearing round black glasses and a lab coat.
As the crowd laughed, Candlestank ditched the lab coat for a black suit jacket to transform into McKinnon, now a New York Times bestselling author.
Audience members laugh as Kate McKinnon, a former cast member of “Saturday Night Live,” talks about her book, “The Millicent Quibb School of Etiquette for Young Ladies of Mad Science,” during the Mississippi Book Festival in Jackson on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“That’s the biggest round of applause I ever got in a Methodist church,” she quipped after the crowd settled down.
Her books follow three misfit sisters and their mentor, the mad scientist Millicent Quibb. The characters, McKinnon said, were built from the hair up. When inhabiting new roles on “Saturday Night Live,” her first questions were: What’s the hair? What’s the voice? She developed the characters in her books much the same way.
Asked about the inspiration for her books, McKinnon pointed to her love of the natural world. She talked about crawdads making their homes in the mud, skunks and snapping turtles she sees every day on her farm. To her, they are “more magical than anything any author could ever conjure in their head.”
McKinnon spent more time out of her seat than in it. She paced the stage as she recalled her childhood as a founding member of the “Honeysuckle Eaters Club” and slid through the church pews to ask young members of the audience what mad-scientist creatures they wished were real.
“A frog mixed with Godzilla,” one audience member replied.
“A chickibara,” said another, referring to a chicken mixed with a capybara – which McKinnon said happens to be her favorite animal.
From whimsical to weighty
The festival’s conversations went from the whimsical to the weighty, featuring writers whose work spans a multitude of genres. 
In the marbled chamber of Mississippi’s Old Supreme Court Chamber, five writers recounted what it was like to be on the other side of the bench, hearing a judge read out the sentences that would put them behind bars for years.
Cree Myles, left, and rapper and author Rick Ross discuss his new book, “Renaissance of a Boss: Notes from a Creative Reawakening,” during the Mississippi Book Festival in Jackson on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The paths that brought each of them to prison fill a chapter of the 2025 anthology, “Breaking Chains, Building Futures.” But at the center of the book is what came afterward: how education helped move them forward from their time behind bars, earn college degrees and lead organizations dedicated to helping others break the cycle of incarceration. 
Weaving their stories together is author Stanley Andrisse, a self-described former “career criminal” who would have spent life in prison for a drug trafficking conviction if the prosecutor had gotten her way.
Instead, Andrisse was sentenced to a decade behind bars. After his release, he went to college. He later earned a master’s degree, then a doctorate. He is now a tenured professor and scientist at Howard University.
“I clearly didn’t live up to those expectations that that prosecutor had on this young Black boy those many years ago,” Andrisse said.
Though his story took place around St. Louis, it deeply resonates in Mississippi, a state with one of the nation’s highest incarceration rates.
Mississippi’s past revisited
During another panel in the state Capitol, more of the past became the talk of the present, when another five authors shared stories drawn from Mississippi’s history – real-life tales spanning the state from the Delta to Hattiesburg.
W. Ralph Eubanks, from left, Eddie S. Glaude Jr., and Robert P. Jones speak during the Mississippi Book Festival in Jackson on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The stories took place during the civil rights era — an inflection point for Mississippi and the nation.
“They’re not just a Mississippi story,” said native Mississippian and novelist Steve Yarbrough. “All of these books, to one extent or another, they’re dealing with questions of race, inequity, inclusivity and basically, the question of whether or not some people are better or more qualified to live a good life than others.”
Through their words, the triumphs and traumas of pioneers both renowned and little known saw the light of day.
Among them was Clyde Kennard, the first Black person to apply to the University of Southern Mississippi. While his friend and fellow activist, Medgar Evers, is better known for challenging school segregation, Kennard’s story took center stage in the 2026 book “Mixing,” which chronicles his fight to desegregate USM and how officials framed and imprisoned him.
In veteran Delta newspaper editor Jim Abbott’s memoir, “Paper Man,” Mississippi’s civil-rights history is told by a man who witnessed it.
At the festival, the Greenwood native recounted how he went from a young, white Mississippian “angered” by the “negative publicity” that the civil rights movement brought his home state to a dogged newspaperman committed to exposing injustice and including Black voices in his stories.
Back outside, Jubilee mused about someday becoming a writer – maybe more stories about mad scientists. Something fictional, she said.
She knows the challenges of creating art. “Sometimes, I think about it,” she said. “But sometimes I’m just too tired and want to flop on the couch.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Independent reporters win investigative journalism prize for foster care series
description: Reporters Clara Bates and Anna Spoerre were awarded the A-Mark Prize for Investigative Journalism on Saturday by the Missouri Press Association for their reporting on problems in the state’s foster care. The award recognizes reporting that uncovers information not readily available to the public and requires “exceptional journalistic skill, determination and[...]
text:
West Humbert and Deon Henderson, leaders with Stand Up KC and Missouri Workers Center, lead chants to kick off a rally protesting recent actions by state lawmakers in May 2025. Annelise Hanshaw won first place for best news photograph and second place for best photo package for her work documenting the rally and Capitol protests (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Reporters Clara Bates and Anna Spoerre were awarded the A-Mark Prize for Investigative Journalism on Saturday by the Missouri Press Association for their reporting on problems in the state’s foster care.
The award recognizes reporting that uncovers information not readily available to the public and requires “exceptional journalistic skill, determination and effort.” It includes a $5,000 prize for the journalists and $2,500 for The Independent.
Bates and Spoerre’s reporting examined persistent problems in Missouri’s child welfare system, including children remaining in foster care longer than federal standards, uneven legal representation that can leave families and children stuck in the system and the experience of a teenager who spent nearly her entire life in foster care and later fought the state to keep her own baby.
Judges said the reporting combined “sharp focus on a specific subject with a sweeping indictment of statewide policy failures,” praising what they called an “almost Dickensian level of details” that made the stories both “heartbreaking and infuriating.”
The judges also cited the impact of the reporting, saying Bates and Spoerre’s work contributed to statewide improvements through legislative changes and helped prompt action on behalf of a young mother and her child.
The A-Mark Foundation, a nonpartisan nonprofit founded in 1997, partners with the Missouri Press Association to recognize investigative reporting by Missouri journalists.
The Independent’s coverage of the foster care system was also awarded third place for best news or feature series in the Missouri Press Association’s annual Better Newspaper Contest. The awards were presented Saturday during the association’s 160th annual convention in Columbia
In all, The Independent collected 14 awards in the Better Newspaper Contest on Saturday, including three first-place honors.
Editor-in-chief Jason Hancock won first place for best breaking news story for his coverage of Scott Faughn’s company taking over the Jefferson City News-Tribune, Fulton Sun and California Democrat.
Hancock also took first place for best election story for his profile of Bill Eigel examining the former state senator’s continued influence on Missouri Republican politics.<
Annelise Hanshaw won first place for best news photograph and second place for best photo package for her work covering protests at the Missouri Capitol.  She also won second place honors for best story about education and best information graphic.
Deputy Editor Rudi Keller and Bates won second place for best breaking news story for their coverage of Republicans turning to a rarely invoked procedural maneuvers to end a Democratic filibuster to pass an abortion ban and repeal a voter-approved paid sick leave law.  
The Independent staff took second place for best headline writing.
Bates also won third place for best breaking news story for her coverage of the death of a man in a Kansas City jail while waiting to be transferred to a state psychiatric hospital for court-ordered treatment.
Opinion columnist Janice Ellis took third place for best serious columnist, while Hanshaw earned third place for best photo package for coverage of the “No Kings” rally at the Missouri Capitol.
The Independent was also awarded third place for best online newspaper or website. Keller took third place for best reporting using the Sunshine Law for his examination of backlogs in public records requests across Missouri government.

name: Delaware
title: Salesianum Football Finishes Out-of-State Schedule with 2-1 Record
description: La Salle College High School defeated Salesianum, 28-10, on September 25, in Salesianum Football’s final game of the season against out-of-state competition.    WILMINGTON, DE — The La Salle College High School Explorers dealt Salesianum its first loss of the 2026 season, defeating the Sals, 28-10, Friday night.  La Salle entered the game ranked as one of th[...]
text:
Salesianum senior Tysir Jones evades a defender during his 78-yard reception in Salesianum Football’s matchup against La Salle College High School. Photo credit: Dave Reeder.
La Salle College High School defeated Salesianum, 28-10, on September 25, in Salesianum Football’s final game of the season against out-of-state competition. 
 
WILMINGTON, DE — The La Salle College High School Explorers dealt Salesianum its first loss of the 2026 season, defeating the Sals, 28-10, Friday night. 
La Salle entered the game ranked as one of the top 30 programs in the state of Pennsylvania, according to MaxPreps, and showed what makes them a formidable opponent.
Following a scoreless first quarter, the Explorers’ scored on their third drive of the game starting at their own 37 yard line. La Salle ran three plays before a pass from junior quarterback Luke Gordon to junior Bryce Hanton brought the Explorers to the Sallies eight yard line with a gain of 45-yards. The Sallesianum defense stopped the La Salle offense on their first three attempts near the goal-line, but on fourth and a yard to go, Gordon completed a pass to receiver Evan Pettine for the one-yard score.
Gordon’s passing touchdown put the Explorers ahead with 7:45 remaining in the first half. The lead held for a total of 34 seconds. 
Salesianum’s senior quarterback, Brady Nabb, led the Sallies offense out to the field at their own 20 yard line, following the Explorer scoring drive. Nabb caught the snap in the shotgun formation on the drive’s first play and delivered a five-yard strike to senior wide receiver Tysir Jones coming back toward the ball. Jones caught the pass and quickly turned his attention upfield. 
Jones side stepped the first La Salle tackler and used a stiff arm to intercept a second would-be tackler, before settling near the sideline. Jones took the reception 78-yards down the right sideline to the La Salle two yard line. Senior Jett Healy ran in a two-yard touchdown on the next play, tying the score with 7:11 to play in the second quarter.
La Salle scored a touchdown on its following possession via a five-yard run from Hanton and the Sals answered the score with a 28-yard field goal by junior Giuliano Villa before the end of the half. The Explorers led 14-10 at halftime in front of a packed Abessinio stadium crowd that included a fan favorite mascot.
Swoop, the Eagles’ mascot, was in attendance along with members of the Philadelphia Eagles cheerleading team as a part of their Friday Night Captains program, which helps celebrate and promote local high school football programs. Fans entering the stadium were given Eagles towels and Swoop made his way through the stands to take pictures and interact with the crowd before the game. As a part of the celebration, it was announced pregame the Eagles will make a donation to both football programs.
La Salle scored the last two touchdowns of the game in the third and fourth quarter, tallying a second score from Hanton on a 46-yard touchdown run in the third and a ten-yard touchdown catch from Pettine in the fourth. 
The Explorers defense only allowed the Sallies offense to cross the mid-field line twice and forced a pair of Sallies turnovers in the second half, holding Salesianum without a score in the frame. The Sallies offense finished the game with over 220 yards of total offense, the majority of which came through the air. Jones finished the game as the Sals’ leading receiver with five catches for 126 yards.
Salesianum will play its first road game of the season next week when they travel to Georgetown, Delaware, for a matchup against Sussex Central High School. The game will start at 7:00 p.m. on October 2. 
Sallies defeated Sussex Central, 31-7, last season at home.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Stone County re-entry program sees growing demand and waitlist
authors: JC Roberts, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center and McKenna Klamm, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center
description: Zachary Brady began the Pathway Home 5 program six months ago. Brady said mock interview exercises helped him gain confidence when applying for jobs after his release.
text:
STONE COUNTY — A re-entry program at the Stone County Correctional Facility has developed a waitlist as officials prepare to select participants for its next cohort. 
Twenty-two participants graduated from the Pathway Home 5 Re-entry Program last month. Warden John Moran said interest has grown as inmates have seen others complete the program and prepare for employment and life after incarceration.
“What I do see now is that we have a larger waiting list,” Moran said. “It’s obvious that the program’s working or that they’re getting something out of it because guys are wanting to sign up for it.” 
The program, administered by the South Mississippi Planning and Development District and funded through a U.S. Department of Labor grant, provides employment and re-entry training before participants leave incarceration and support for up to a year later. 
Participants learn resume writing, digital and financial literacy, employment readiness, personal development and interviewing. The program also helps address barriers after release, including transportation, work clothing, child care and finding employers willing to hire people with criminal records.
In the classroom, program participants learn resume writing, digital and financial literacy, employment readiness, personal development and interviewing. Warden John Moran says the facility eventually wants to expand to multiple cohorts. Credit: Bibhas Pantha/RHCJC
For graduate Zachary Brady, the program became more valuable than he initially expected. 
“It started out more or less like I might need to get this under my belt to go home,” Brady said. “I really didn’t know what the class had to offer, but once I got into it, I was very glad that I took it.” 
Brady said mock interviews helped him build confidence for finding work after his release. 
“We did mock interviews, so now whenever I get home, I won’t be nervous or not know how to speak to the people that I’m getting interviewed by,” Brady said. 
Chris Nixon, Pathway Home 5 program administrator, said the program’s work continues once participants leave the facility. 
Chris Nixon, administrator of Pathway Home 5, said the program’s goal is to continue helping formerly incarcerated people after their release. He said finding employers willing to hire people with criminal records can be difficult.  Credit: JC Roberts/RHCJC
“Once they get out is where we’ll pick up again and help them with their incentives and supportive service and employment and resources that we can provide for them,” Nixon said. 
Finding employment can be one of the biggest obstacles, Nixon said, particularly because participants need employers willing to hire people with criminal records. 
“There’s employers really needing people and they are willing to give them a second chance, and that’s really helpful,” Nixon said. “I’ve seen some really good careers come out of this for them, some high-paying jobs.” 
The program, which can work with participants for up to a year after graduation, is part of a broader effort at the correctional facility to prepare inmates for life after incarceration. Moran said more than 153 community volunteers also support inmates through programs and activities.
Brady said that community involvement has been meaningful as he prepares for release. 
“I’m grateful … to have people like that in our community that’s willing to step forward, to spend time with us and to help us rehabilitate ourselves for going home,” Brady said. 
According to Warden John Moran, the Stone County Correctional Facility currently holds 280 inmates, with a growing list of participants for the Pathway Home 5 program.  Credit: Bibhas Pantha/RHCJC
As the facility prepares to select its next Pathway Home 5 cohort, Moran said growing interest means some inmates will have to wait for a spot. The facility has previously tried running two cohorts simultaneously, he said, but maintaining multiple groups can be difficult. 
Brady said inmates who get the opportunity should take advantage of it. 
“If they want to take the program, take it, but take it and be serious when you take it,” Brady said. “You have to want it. You have to dedicate yourself and stay consistent and push through.”

name: VTDigger
title: ‘Mend it and keep it alive’: Inside Vermont’s growing repair culture
description:
New state program aims to increase opportunities to reuse and repair.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Mend it and keep it alive’: Inside Vermont’s growing repair culture.
text:
A sign outside the Old North End Repair Cafe. Photo by Simone Traynor/Community News Service

Simone Traynor is a reporter with the Community News Service, part of the University of Vermont’s Reporting & Documentary Storytelling program.
Every third Saturday in Burlington’s Old North End, volunteers come together to fix one another’s broken belongings, eat bagels and do something good for the environment. Everyone has a role.
At a recent session of the Old North End Repair Cafe, one volunteer greeted everyone, another sewed and repaired textiles and some dropped by just to enjoy the company. They came with the shared purpose of reducing unnecessary waste.
That’s a big challenge. Vermont generates about 912,180 tons of waste annually, with much of that total winding up in the landfill despite recycling programs, according to the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources 2024 Diversion and Disposal Report.
In an era of overconsumption, some Vermonters have taken to creating third spaces with the goal of repair. People passionate about the environment or simply looking to save money and reduce their waste have a growing interest in places where they can fix what’s broken and get to know other people in spaces like the repair cafe, which meets at 12-22 North Street.
“It’s a great community of people who are here to support each other and socialize,” said Ali Hamedani, a repair cafe volunteer. “It just seems like a wonderful community of friends with a shared goal of helping each other, helping random strangers, all for free, to repair and renew things and maintain connections with each other.”
A new state-funded program, ReuseVT, aims to connect Vermonters with opportunities to repair their broken belongings and reduce waste. The website’s directory lists repair cafes, including the one in Burlington’s Old North End. It also features Vermont businesses and nonprofits that provide repair services and libraries that loan items from cookie pans to snowshoes. 
When something breaks, the fastest, cheapest fix is usually to buy another one. Susan Alexander, director of ReuseVT, said that convenience has changed how people think. 
“There’s nothing more appealing to consumers than cheap and convenient,” she said. “The reality is, that toaster may have 99% working parts and just one little thing that needs to be fixed on it, but it’s really hard to find people with those skill sets.” 
Economically, repairing instead of repurchasing can be difficult for the average consumer.
“Sometimes repair is as expensive, if not more so, than replace,” Alexander said. “If I can buy a toaster online for $27, but my guy down the road (who can fix it) is going to charge me $35, that’s a hard barrier.”
However, there is a strong case for repairing and reusing items. It conserves resources, supports outlets for low-cost goods and promotes a local, circular economy. 
Repair keeps local dollars local, Alexander says.
“When I go to the thrift shop or when I went down the road and had my lamp repaired, I took the money that I’m earning on this job, I give it to the guy who’s fixing my lamp, then he goes down to the grocery store and buys his groceries,” she said.

Trav Fryer (green shirt) at the Old North End repair cafe. Photo by Simone Traynor/Community News Service

Trav Fryer, who runs the Old North End Repair Cafe, says the fixer-upper approach comes naturally to him. 
“It just feels very innate to me. Why would you throw it out? It’s so much more efficient,” he said.
He was inspired to start hosting repair cafes in Burlington after attending them regularly in Palo Alto, California.
Other regulars describe themselves as coming from “mend-it” families. 
“My mom grew up on a farm. The first move was always to try to mend it and keep it alive,” said Chrissy Bedard, a regular volunteer at the repair cafe. “Once you put your heart and soul into something, you want to keep it around as long as you can, so knowing how to fix it is a huge piece of that.”  
ReuseVT launched about a year and a half ago, funded through an Environmental Protection Agency grant awarded to the state’s Department of Environmental Conservation. Alexander wrote the original proposal, which is now in its second year. She said the funding filled a gap in how the state had long approached waste. 
“For years and years and years, people have put money into recycling,” she said. But reduction and reuse went underfunded. 
Many Vermonters are looking for ways to be more sustainable in their daily life. A source like ReuseVT simplifies the search with information including the website repair directory.
“The community has really been looking for a directory that’s specific to reuse and repair opportunities,” Alexander said.
Vermont’s reuse and repair culture goes beyond any one organization. Alexander noted that numerous organizations around Vermont are part of the reuse movement. ReSource Vermont, a statewide nonprofit with locations in Burlington, Williston, Barre and Morrisville, has a threefold mission. 
“One is to keep things out of the landfill, so it’s an environmental piece. It’s also poverty alleviation … and then their third thing, they also do a lot of repair training,” Alexander said.
Also in Burlington, Generator teaches skills like jewelry making or woodworking to anyone willing to learn — skills that can be applied to repair work as well as new products. 
“They basically create community around providing a space for people to either just come in and use it for a workspace, or they provide equipment and teach classes,” Alexander said.
She hopes to see the movement grow, and perhaps one day see an annual gathering and a vending event built entirely around reused and repaired goods. 
Meanwhile, repair cafes, such as the one in Burlington, are built around fixing things together. 
“We want it to be a learning experience and hands-on,” Fryer said.
Fryer sees something specific to Vermont’s rural and agricultural heritage in repair culture: scrappiness. 
“Farmers have to fix things themselves,” he said. “You’ve got to be able to fix the tractor to keep farming. You kind of just have to figure it out.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Mend it and keep it alive’: Inside Vermont’s growing repair culture.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan vets outline everyday impacts of Iran War, airing frustrations with GOP leadership
description: As gas prices surge to record levels amidst the ongoing war in Iran, military veterans led protestors outside a Lansing gas station Friday in opposition to the war alongside the rollout of an electronic records system they say is harming veteran healthcare. With the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks fresh in their minds, […]
text:
Duane Kleinhardt, a retired Army command sergeant major voices opposition to U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) during a protest on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)As gas prices surge to record levels amidst the ongoing war in Iran, military veterans led protestors outside a Lansing gas station Friday in opposition to the war alongside the rollout of an electronic records system they say is harming veteran healthcare.
With the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks fresh in their minds, veterans from multiple branches of the military shared concerns that the U.S. had embroiled itself in another war without a clear mission, asking what that will mean for those serving in the latest conflict abroad.
Steve Monti said he was 19 years old and fresh out of army training during 9/11, and that before he knew it, he was in Iraq.
“I was fighting for freedom, peace, democracy, oil – I couldn’t tell. I was too close in. I was too close to see the big picture,” Monti said. “Twenty-three years later, and I’m still not sure of what we accomplished, whose lives we made better. Certainly not the hundreds of thousands of people who lost theirs.”
Monti said the war in Iran is the same story playing out all over again, leaving a new generation to pay the toll. 
“And for what? Are we better off?” Monti asked “Is our gas cheaper? Do you feel more safe, more secure? What about your sons and daughters and their futures? All I see are the people like us, the workers of this country, being squeezed, being run dry. The working class is asked once again to tighten our belts so that we can pay for a war that none of us wanted and none of us asked for.”
Steve Monti, an Iraq War veteran, speaks out against the War in Iran during a protest on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
With the election on the horizon, rising inflation on everyday goods and increased gas prices have generated frustration among voters. Multiple speakers at Friday’s event, which was organized by the Ingham County Democratic Party and other groups opposed to President Donald Trump’s agenda like Common Defense, Indivisible Michigan’s 7th Congressional District chapter, laid their frustrations at the feet of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), the incumbent representing the highly competitive 7th Congressional District.
While Barrett has voted in favor of four resolutions asserting Congress’s war powers to limit and wind down military operations overseas, those measures have failed to gain support in the U.S. Senate, with the upper chamber voting down the most recent House Resolution on Thursday in a 49-50 vote.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
However, Barrett’s opponent, Lansing-area political organizer William Lawrence, and other critics have noted Barrett’s votes in opposition to war powers resolutions before the House in March and April.
“Tom Barrett initially voted against limiting Trump’s war powers,” said Duane Kleinhardt, a retired Army command sergeant major who served with Barrett in Guantanamo Bay. “He says now that he wants us to get out of Iran. Tommy, that is too little and too late.”
In an interview with Michigan Advance, Barrett said his initial votes against the war powers resolutions aligned with the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which requires the President to remove all troops after 60 days if Congress has not granted an extension.
“I take the issue of war very seriously. That’s reflective of my life experience. And one thing that I am not very flexible on is the issue of whether and how we send Americans into war,” said Barrett, who served in the U.S. Army for 22 years, including service during the Iraq War.
Lawrence’s campaign has also criticized Barrett for voting in support of a $95 billion budget framework which includes $60 billion for defense and $13 billion for intelligence.
Gas prices at a Speedway gas station in Lansing, Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
“Just a few months ago, the House needed just one vote to stop a bill that authorized tens of billions of dollars in funding for this war in Iran. It passed with Tom Barrett’s support,” Lawrence said during a campaign speech Tuesday. “In other words, he could have been the one vote that would have stopped it, and he allowed it to continue.”
Barrett said the resolution doesn’t mention Iran, and that the funding was for military and troop readiness.
“If William Lawrence thought that that bill was going to halt the war in Iran, then the obvious question is: since that bill has not passed the U.S. Senate, how is the war in Iran continuing today?” Barrett said.
Alongside frustrations over rising costs, veterans at Friday’s event also raised concerns about veterans healthcare.
Steven Friday, a member of the Stop the Rollout campaign, called for U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs officials to halt the implementation of an electronic health record system and for members of Congress to restrict funding to Oracle Health’s contract for the system citing issues with the system’s performance. 
“The Government Accountability Office reported this month that the VA has fully implemented only four of its 18 recommendations concerning the electronic health record program,” Friday said. “Fourteen are still not fully implemented.”
Protesters gather in opposition to the War in Iran and Republican leadership in Washington at a Lansing gas station on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Barrett, who serves on the House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs, noted that they had recently passed a resolution to subpoena the CEO of Oracle Health and Oracle Founder Larry Ellison over costly delays in implementing the new health record system.
Congress is doing the oversight work Barrett said, but stressed that veterans need to have portable record access, noting his father-in-law had issues receiving care at the VA in Battle Creek when he normally receives care in Tulsa, Okla.
Barrett said it is his “sincere intention and effort to make sure that we get to a point where every veteran has a health record system that is adequate in meeting their needs and allows them the portability of their healthcare.”
“We understand that where there are issues that need correction, we have to correct that. Where there are gaps that need to be filled, we need to fill that,” Barrett said. 
He pointed to the sheer number of records managed by the VA, noting that while this does not discount any issues or gaps in the system, the shift to an electronic records system is a significant overhaul that will require continuous oversight until it is fully implemented and operational.

The South Dakota Senate meets on Feb. 11, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/091726-Legislator-Pay-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
South Dakota lawmakers receive a salary of about $16,000, but the average payout per legislator was $26,813 during the last fiscal year after accounting for mileage, an allowance for living expenses, and out-of-state travel to conferences, according to data obtained by South Dakota Searchlight from the state’s Legislative Research Council.
During this year’s annual legislative session, which ran from January through March, lawmakers earned a salary of $15,970. The salary is adjusted each year by the state’s Board of Finance to 20% of the South Dakota median household income as reported by the U.S. Census Bureau, according to state law.
Lawmakers who reside more than 50 miles from the state Capitol receive additional payments of $178 per day to help cover their living expenses during the annual legislative sessions and during committee meetings held during the rest of the year. During sessions, lawmakers receive reimbursement for their first trip at a mileage rate of 5 cents per mile, according to the state constitution, then each trip after at 70 cents per mile.
Additionally, lawmakers can receive reimbursements for out-of-state conferences. That typically includes airfare, lodging, meals and registration costs.
To cover all payouts to lawmakers, the state spent about $2.8 million in fiscal year 2026, which ended in June.
Last month, a committee of state senators and representatives endorsed a budget increase that would help cover the cost of a salary increase. The anticipated salary for lawmakers during the upcoming session is $16,492, based on newly released median household income data.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri should take the time to get its next education commissioner right
description: Missouri education is entering a period of significant change. That makes the search for the state’s next Commissioner of Education more than a personnel decision. It is a decision about who will lead Missouri’s schools through some of the most consequential policy changes the state has undertaken in years. The Missouri State Board of Education […]
text:
The Missouri State Board of Education discusses a proposed change to the state's standardized test during its meeting on March 24 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri education is entering a period of significant change. That makes the search for the state’s next Commissioner of Education more than a personnel decision. It is a decision about who will lead Missouri’s schools through some of the most consequential policy changes the state has undertaken in years.
The Missouri State Board of Education should take the time necessary to get that decision right.
Fortunately, the board has something many organizations navigating a leadership transition do not: an experienced interim leader who understands the department, the policy landscape, and the people involved.
Stacey Preis was appointed interim commissioner in June following the retirement of Karla Eslinger. Preis brings extensive experience in education leadership and statewide policy, including previous service within the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education. She has also made clear that she does not intend to pursue the permanent position.
That gives Missouri an opportunity to resist the pressure to rush.
Rather than treating the interim period as a vacancy that must be filled as quickly as possible, the State Board can use it as a bridge, maintaining stability under a knowledgeable interim commissioner while conducting a thoughtful search for the leader Missouri will need for its next chapter.
And that next chapter will not be simple.
Missouri is simultaneously changing how it communicates school performance, reconsidering how it funds public education and confronting the urgent need to improve student achievement.
The State Board recently approved Missouri’s new A–F school and district grading framework, intended to give parents, policymakers and communities a clearer picture of school performance. Creating a system is one thing. Implementing it in a way that provides meaningful, understandable information and builds confidence in the results is another.
At the same time, Missouri is reconsidering something even more fundamental: how we fund our schools.
The School Funding Modernization Task Force is examining a funding system that has long raised questions about whether state dollars are distributed in ways that reflect the needs of today’s students and communities. Any significant changes that emerge from that work will affect students, districts, taxpayers and communities across Missouri.
And underlying both conversations is an even more important challenge: whether Missouri students are learning what they need to succeed.
Literacy must remain at the center of that work.
Reading is foundational to nearly every other outcome we expect from our education system. Students who struggle to read face greater challenges in every subject that follows. Improving literacy requires more than adopting a policy or purchasing a curriculum. It requires sustained attention to evidence-based instruction, educator preparation and professional development, assessment, implementation and accountability for results.
Taken together, these issues represent a significant period of transition for Missouri education.
The next commissioner must be prepared to lead through it.
Missouri should be looking for more than someone capable of managing a large state agency. The next commissioner must understand the connection between policy and implementation and know that passing a law or adopting a new system is only the beginning.
That leader will need to work effectively with the State Board, governor, legislature, educators, business leaders, and families, even when those groups disagree about the path forward. The commissioner must understand school finance and accountability while keeping student outcomes at the center of the conversation.
And importantly, the next commissioner will need credibility and experience to lead change.
That requires listening to educators responsible for implementing policy while maintaining high expectations for results. It requires explaining complicated issues clearly to parents and taxpayers. And it requires building an organization within DESE that can move major initiatives from policy documents to classrooms.
Those are significant expectations. They should be.
The State Board itself is relatively new to working together in its current configuration. Before choosing the next commissioner, board members have an opportunity to establish a shared understanding of what Missouri needs from the position over the next several years.
The question should not simply be: Who can do this job?
It should be: What does Missouri need this job to accomplish, and who has the experience, leadership ability, and commitment to student outcomes to get us there?
There will understandably be pressure to fill the position quickly. Leadership transitions create uncertainty, and permanent leadership provides clarity.
But speed and stability are not the same thing.
With Dr. Preis providing experienced leadership during this transition, Missouri has the breathing room to conduct a serious search, listen to stakeholders, establish clear expectations, and identify a commissioner equipped for the work ahead.
Missouri is making important decisions about accountability, school funding, and literacy. Each has the potential to shape education in this state for years.
The person leading DESE will sit at the intersection of all three.
Missouri does not need to decide quickly.
It needs to make it well.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lou Ann Linehan and Tom Briese: Resist efforts to roll back tax relief
description: We are writing in response to former state Sen. John  Stinner’s commentary of Sept. 19.  When we were sworn into the Legislature in January of 2017, the state was facing a budget crisis. The 17 new senators in our class were told repeatedly, “We are $1 billion short.”  In reaction to the forecasted shortfall, we […]
text:
The saying on the north side of the Nebraska State Capitol reads, "The Salvation of the State is Watchfulness in the Citizen." Feb. 28, 2026 (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)We are writing in response to former state Sen. John  Stinner’s commentary of Sept. 19. 
When we were sworn into the Legislature in January of 2017, the state was facing a budget crisis. The 17 new senators in our class were told repeatedly, “We are $1 billion short.”  In reaction to the forecasted shortfall, we reduced the minimum reserve from 3% to 2.5% and we reduced the school funding formula by increasing the local effort rate from $1 per $100 valuation to $1.03. The local effort rate change meant we were reducing state funding for public schools. In too many cases, that change resulted in local school boards having to raise property taxes to make up the difference. We supported the changes as we were told “we’re broke.” Turns out we were not broke;  the forecasts were far gloomier than the reality. This was the opposite of what had occurred two years earlier, when the forecasts were too rosy.  
Understanding how the budget process works in Nebraska is a laborious and time-consuming task. The crisis that many are pointing to today might happen. But one can make the case it is more likely it will not. As the Flatwater Free Press reported last week, Nebraska’s Forecasting Board “has on average, underestimated state revenues by 3% annually over the past 30 years. … But the forecast’s accuracy varies widely year to year. In 2020, the forecast came within .22% of actual revenues. A year later, the board undershot revenues by more than 19%, according to data from the Legislature’s Fiscal Office. The board has overestimated state revenues 17 times since 1984, including in each of the last two fiscal years, missing by an average of 4.6%.” 
Three or 4 percent does not sound like much of an error, but 4% of $6 billion is $240 million. Over two years, it can suggest a shortfall of $480 million. If one understands the inherent difficulty in accurately projecting revenue, facing a supposed $208 million shortfall by the end of 2027 fiscal year is hardly a crisis. Wringing one’s hands over a supposed shortfall at the end of 2029 would seem a significant waste of energy.  
So then why are so many politicians screaming “budgetary disaster”?  Answer: They do not support  the income tax cuts from a high of 7.8% of adjusted income to 3.99% implemented over the last few years. Every year there is an effort in the Legislature to roll those income tax cuts back. Stinner appears to agree with the naysayers that the income tax cuts were a mistake. He says as much in his commentary, “The effect of the income tax initiative has been a swift dismantling of the budget’s structural integrity.” We disagree. The effect of the tax cuts is leaving more money in the pockets of those that earned it. Due to the diligent work of Gov. Jim  Pillen and the current Legislature, especially of the Appropriations Chair Rob Clements and Revenue Chair Brad von Gillern, the structural integrity of Nebraska’s budget remains intact. 
Further, some politicians do not support the significant property tax relief implemented over the last few years starting with LB 1107’s passage in 2020. Again, as Stinner states, “Property tax relief, the costliest initiative … totaled $518 million, which included $310 million of property tax credits (in 2022-23). Fast forward to FY 2026-27, and transfers out now account for $1.76 billion, an increase of 239%. Less than $1 million of that money will go to something other than property taxes.” 
Stinner supported LB 1107, as did we. Property taxes were the No. 1 concern of Nebraskans when we were elected to the Legislature. Therefore in 2020, along with passage of LB 1107, we increased the property tax credit fund and continued to increase both it and the 1107 credit over the next four years. As Stinner writes, the state of Nebraska is now reducing property taxes statewide by $1.75 billion. But he seems to suggest that relief should be rolled back onto the backs of Nebraskans whose property tax bills were among the highest in the nation when we were elected. We disagree. We know there is still more work to do on property taxes, but we certainly do not agree that current property tax relief should be dismantled, therefore increasing property taxes by $1.75 billion.  
Stinner also suggests we are not focused on needs. As we said previously, the Legislature reduced school funding in the  2017 biennium budget. That was the last time the Legislature reduced school funding. The reality is Pillen and the Legislature increased public school funding by 34% in 2023, the largest increase since the state passed significant school funding in 1989. We increased special education funding from 40% of the schools’ costs to 80%, ensuring that all children are receiving the services they deserve. We removed community colleges’ general funding from the property tax rolls to state funding. We managed hundreds of millions of COVID cash according to rules laid out by the Biden administration.  And today, the state has over $840 million in cash reserves, a significant cushion for possible shortfalls. 
Anyone is free to disagree with the Nebraska Legislature’s efforts over the last decade to reduce Nebraskan’s tax burden and improve funding for our public schools.  But understand that all the hyperbole around the supposed “budget crisis” appears to be created in an effort to gain support to roll back your tax relief. We support Pillen’s and the Legislature’s — especially Chairs Clement’s and von Gillern’s — efforts to ensure that the tax relief implemented over the last decade remains in place.
