name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Supreme Court vacates decision to put Butte data center issue to voters
description: The Montana Supreme Court on Thursday vacated an earlier ruling that the Butte-Silver Bow elections office print a citizen’s initiative question on the ballots after learning the department had already mailed ballots to voters.  Thursday’s ruling overturned a Tuesday order that required an initiative seeking to regulate data center construction by requiring[...]
text:
A view of downtown Butte is seen through a car window on July 6, 2017 in Butte, Montana. (Photo by Janie Osborne/Getty Images)The Montana Supreme Court on Thursday vacated an earlier ruling that the Butte-Silver Bow elections office print a citizen’s initiative question on the ballots after learning the department had already mailed ballots to voters. 
Thursday’s ruling overturned a Tuesday order that required an initiative seeking to regulate data center construction by requiring voter approval to appear on the November ballots. 
But less than 48 hours later, the court reversed its ruling, stating it was unaware that voters had already received — and in some cases returned — absentee and mail ballots, according to the county. Sherman told the court that “absentee/mail ballots had been issued” but the Secretary of State’s Office maintains an Oct 9 timeline for general election ballots to be sent, with the exception for overseas ballots which go out Sept. 18.
The initiative was engaged in a legal battle after the organizers — Denise Kelly and citizens’ group 406 People First — submitted signatures to qualify for the ballot in early August. While Cynthia Sherman, the county’s clerk and recorder overseeing elections, initially accepted and certified the signatures — more than the 3,652 required — it later told the organizers that a new Montana law had bumped the deadline for turning in signatures by more than a week, invalidating the measure. 
The proponents of the measure took the issue to district court to prevent the elections office from using the new statutory deadline, and after the district court ruled against them, appealed directly to the Montana Supreme Court. 
In a five-page order, the high court said it stood by its reasoning in granting the injunction that would have required the initiative be printed. 
If the initiative were left off the ballot, and later found to have met legal requirements, there would be no remedy, the court had argued on Tuesday. But if it were included — and approved by voters — there would have been an avenue to revoke the initiative if found legally insufficient. 
Now, the court said there is “no remedy” under state law. 
After Tuesday’s ruling, the city-county filed a notice asking how it was expected to comply with the order with ballots already mailed to voters. 
State statute has provisions for correcting ballots if there are errors in some office, but does not spell out a method for correcting issues with ballot initiatives — including if they are left off. 
The city-county asked whether it should send out new, corrected ballots or send out supplemental ballots with the initiative question, and whether they should include all registered voters, including those who had already turned in ballots. 
“Montana’s ballot statutes do not contemplate this decision and we have no good answers for the city-county’s very good questions as to how Sherman can implement our order,” and comply with state law, the order states. 
The court also points out that the situation was “entirely avoidable,” if the city-county had filed a notice that ballots had already gone out while the court was deliberating, and if the proponents of the ballot measure had also indicated a timeline for printing. 
In addition, the court also said that due to a “clerical error” there was a multi-week delay before the court learned that an appeal had been filed, which also added to the issue. 
Representatives for 406 People First told the Daily Montanan Thursday night they are speaking with counsel and considering next possible steps. Lawyers for the group filed an additional emergency petition asking the court to reconsider the issue, determine the timeline for ballots being sent out, and ensure the county complied with a previous temporary restraining order.

title: Commission open to sculpture idea for Cameron, Nebraska’s ‘Capitol Cat’
description: LINCOLN — A commission expressed openness Friday to a revised proposal for a sculpture to honor the Nebraska State Capitol’s longtime unofficial feline mascot. Multiple members of the seven-person Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission said they might be able to support the scaled-back idea to honor 11-year-old Cameron the “Capitol Cat.” For nearly a decade, t[...]
text:
An AI-rendered image of what a proposed sculpture honoring Cameron the Capitol Cat outside the Nebraska State Capitol could look like is projected during a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Sept. 25, 2026. The artificial intelligence image is not the final design. The supporters and  sculptor Benjamin Victor would design the final work. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A commission expressed openness Friday to a revised proposal for a sculpture to honor the Nebraska State Capitol’s longtime unofficial feline mascot.
Multiple members of the seven-person Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission said they might be able to support the scaled-back idea to honor 11-year-old Cameron the “Capitol Cat.” For nearly a decade, the tabby regularly trotted to the Capitol, where he would greet legislators, staffers and the public. In May, Cameron and his owner, Dianna McGinnis, moved into assisted living.
The proposed location for a sculpture honoring Cameron the Capitol Cat outside the Nebraska State Capitol is projected during a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The revised proposal calls for a life-size bronze statue of Cameron on the south side of the Capitol atop a bench, the final materials of which — limestone, granite or otherwise — are still being ironed out. A final vote could come as soon as next month.
“In no way do we want to compete against the historical figures that are at the Capitol,” former state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln, a project leader, told the commission Friday. “Instead, we want to have just his presence there in a way that reflects the joy and the nonpartisanship that he brought to those who know him and to future people through the statue.”
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward is also assisting the project. Speaker John Arch of La Vista has also endorsed the idea.
‘I like this a lot better’
Commissioners generally thanked Wishart and her team for listening to commission feedback at an August meeting and scaling back what was originally a taller, more monumentlike proposal. The sculpture would move slightly closer to the state parking lot at the intersection of Goodhue Boulevard and H Street. It would also be lower to the ground, intended to be more interactive.
Commissioner Eileen Bergt at a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“I do like this site … and having it down lower and being able to sit next to it I think is great,” said Commissioner Eileen Bergt. “I think it’s more whimsical that way, rather than trying to elevate it more and more.”
“Generally, I like this a lot better than what we saw last month,” added Commissioner Andrea Gebhart. “I appreciate the feedback that you heard and actually incorporated into this.”
Among the additional feedback commissioners gave Friday was whether to add a plaza near the sculpture for students and visitors to relax in.
Bergt also suggested that when Cameron dies, his ashes could be incorporated into the area. Wishart said her team would talk with McGinnis and her family.
“Then his spirit lives on there,” Bergt said.
Commissioner Andrea Gebhart at a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Commission Chair Kile Johnson said he believes it would be good to have public art along Goodhue Boulevard, the street running south of the Capitol, if it’s “high quality.” A portion of Goodhue is included in the Capitol Environs District, which the commission oversees to preserve the impact and quality in the cardinal directions leading to the Capitol.
“And this, to me, is high quality,” Johnson said of the proposed Cameron sculpture.
Collin Christopher, a staff planner for the Lincoln-Lancaster County Planning Department, which assists the committee, said commission staff are generally comfortable with the idea and would recommend approval if it comes up for a final vote.
‘Be careful what you approve’
Benjamin Victor, an Idaho-based sculptor, is poised to sculpt Cameron’s bronze statue and pedestal, assuming enough private funds are raised. Johnson praised Victor’s past work, which is also displayed in the Capitol Environs District, including bronze statues for Ponca Chief Standing Bear and Dr. Susan La Flesche Picotte on Lincoln Mall north of the Capitol.
Victor has also sculpted four statues in Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol, including a Chief Standing Bear statue for Nebraska.
Former Nebraska State Capitol Administrator Bob Ripley during a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Bob Ripley, who was the State Capitol administrator from 1975 until 2023, again raised hesitation about the sculpture idea, as he did last month. He said he didn’t know how anyone could argue with the idea but worried what precedent it could set.
As an example, Ripley said he approved many activities on the north side of the Capitol in his former role, including rallies for the American Nazi Party. He said he didn’t support the event, but organizers had met requirements for hosting.
“I’m just saying: Be careful what you approve, because you may get someone coming along asking for approval that you may not want to stand up and make a campaign speech for,” Ripley said.
‘More than a charming story’
Courtney Wittstruck of Lincoln, a registered lobbyist at the Capitol, again testified in favor of the idea in her private capacity. She said honoring Cameron would be in line with the symbolism of the Capitol, similar to the Sower, bison and pioneer families found in and around the building.
She said Cameron is more than a “beloved cat” and proved people could “remember that the person on the other side of a political argument was still a neighbor and a fellow Nebraskan.”
“That is more than a charming story about a Capitol mascot,” Wittstruck said. “It is a simple, accessible expression of values this building was deliberately designed to teach.”
Courtney Wittstruck of Lincoln after speaking to the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission in support of a sculpture for Cameron the Capitol Cat on Sept. 25, 2026. She wears a shirt that bears a photo of Cameron. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Among the virtues of Nebraska which Cameron represents, Wittstruck said, she listed magnanimity, charity, temperance, justice and hope. Wittstruck said a child doesn’t need to understand constitutional theory to understand kindness.
“Cameron made those abstract ideals tangible and approachable by giving them four legs and a face people could recognize, and that I believe is why the fact that Cameron is a cat is not a weakness in this proposal,” Wittstruck said. “It may be precisely what makes this symbol work.”
Wishart told reporters after the meeting that her team has a “little more homework,” such as determining ongoing maintenance, selecting final materials and considering additional landscaping, but she hopes to be back next month seeking final approval. She said supporters are confident they’ll raise enough private funds and will take all feedback into account.
“We’re doing everything possible to make this a sculpture that everybody embraces,” Wishart said.
The next Capitol Environs Commission meeting is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. Oct. 23 in Lincoln.

title: Federal court upholds block on TN law making it a crime to aid minors seeking out-of-state abortions
description: A Tennessee law preventing adults from giving information to minors about legal out-of-state abortions will remain blocked, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit ruled Thursday. ​A three-judge panel agreed with a federal district judge that barring adults from giving out information about abortions violates the First Amendment. ​Senior United States[...]
text:
A three-judge panel U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit agreed with a federal district judge that barring adults from giving out information about abortions violates the First Amendment. Photo from a 2022 Nashville protest following the Dobbs v. Jackson ruling. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennnessee Lookout)
A Tennessee law preventing adults from giving information to minors about legal out-of-state abortions will remain blocked, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit ruled Thursday.
​A three-judge panel agreed with a federal district judge that barring adults from giving out information about abortions violates the First Amendment.
​Senior United States Judge Jane Stranch said in her ruling the Tennessee law had “no compelling interest in shielding its citizens from information about activities outside its borders.”
​Stranch added in the ruling, the state “criminalizes speech that encourages a minor to get an abortion yet is silent on speech encouraging a minor to carry a pregnancy to term with or without parental involvement.”
​Tennessee lawmakers passed the law in 2024, two years after the state’s near-total abortion ban went into effect following the Supreme Court decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization.
​State. Rep. Aftyn Behn, a Nashville Democrat, and attorney Rachel Welty filed a lawsuit against the law shortly after its passage, and a federal district judge prevented it from taking effect.
​Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti then appealed the ruling.
​The blocked law made it a misdemeanor for any adult who “recruits, harbors, or transports a pregnant un-emancipated minor” to obtain an abortion, including drug-induced abortion, without consent from the minor’s legal guardian.
​The law came in response to abortion advocates providing information and resources to those wanting the procedure in states where it remains legal.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: It’s time to act on fossil fuels
description: Pipeline and compressor expansion projects pose undeniable risks to our health and safety. It's time to speak out.
text:
In less that two weeks, the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection will host a public hearing about a methane gas compressor station in Oxford, Connecticut. This is the same station that had an accident earlier this summer and released a significant amount of pollution into local air. 
Enbridge must be held accountable, and this hearing is our opportunity to weigh in and make our voices heard.
Just over two months ago, on Sunday, July 12th around midnight, residents of Middlebury, Oxford, and Naugatuck were awoken by a loud, jet-engine-like noise, when a blowdown (a large release of methane gas into the air) occurred at this Enbridge-owned compressor station, a site where methane gas is pressurized to be transported along pipelines. These stations emit toxic pollutants, which are linked to a number of health conditions like asthma, heart disease, and certain cancers.
This blowdown, which took place at around midnight, was entirely unattended, with no Enbridge staff on site. When firefighters arrived, they had to wait for the arrival of an Enbridge technician to resolve the issue. Following the incident, residents were able to smell a considerable difference in the air quality.
Pollutants emitted by compressor stations and other fossil fuel infrastructure have long been pernicious, lingering in our communities and slowly but surely threatening public health and the environment. According to a 2023 paper, “An estimated 5.13 million…excess deaths per year globally are attributable to ambient air pollution from fossil fuel use and therefore could potentially be avoided by phasing out fossil fuels.” Research has also found that “Greater amounts of VOC emissions from natural gas pipeline compressor stations were associated with higher age-adjusted mortality rates.”
The Oxford compressor station is just one of the five compressor stations in Connecticut. Four of them are on the Enbridge pipeline that runs through Connecticut. Enbridge, one of the continent’s leading oil and gas transmission corporations, has an extensive history of noncompliance with environmental protection standards, including within Connecticut. 
In 2014 and 2016, their Cromwell site was found to have reported excess emissions of volatile organic compounds, which are known to be injurious to our health. Seven years after the company first started violating their emissions limit, Enbridge was forced to pay nearly $200,000 for noncompliance with emissions standards. 
These regulations and standards exist to protect the environment, but critically, us.

Syed Noorwez

Enbridge’s blatant disregard for regulations meant to keep us safe is emblematic of the fact that fossil fuel corporation interests are not in our best interest. The best explanation for this disregard is that Enbridge simply does not care about anything beyond its own profit.  A $200,000 fine, relative to Enbridge’s income of $5.8 billion in  2021 comes out to roughly 0.003%, a trivial amount.  To someone making $100,000 in a year (which is roughly twice the average household income in Hartford), that would be the same as $3. 
Despite the harm that Enbridge’s compressor stations and pipelines have caused, Enbridge shows no signs of stopping. The corporation’s Project R.A.R.E (Reliable Affordable Resilient Enhancement) is already underway, alongside plans to increase capacity at the Cromwell compressor station where they previously failed to meet regulatory requirements. On top of this, they have proposed Project Beacon, which will likely also expand compressor stations.
The information is all in front of us. Under the guise of increasing energy supply, these pipeline and compressor expansion projects pose undeniable risks to our health and safety. These risks are amplified when those in charge have little regard for anything beyond profit, least of all public health.
Study after study tells us that fossil fuel emissions cause irreparable damage to our health and our planet. Coupled with individuals in power who don’t care to look past financial incentive, fossil fuel usage has led us into a crisis that becomes increasingly difficult and costly to rectify. Stronger public health is in the interest of the public, while Enbridge’s interest is its own private profit. 
Fortunately, while the problem is clear, we possess the remedies. A transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources is long overdue. While this may not be profitable for energy companies like Enbridge, there is no greater profit to our communities than living happier, healthier, and longer lives. 
Please join me in making your voice heard and demanding stricter regulation and air monitoring of the Oxford Compressor Station.
Syed Noorwez is a student at Wesleyan University.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: Constitutional Amendment 4
description: While the top of the Nov. 3 ballot will bring new leadership to New Mexico, one of the constitutional amendments at the end of the ballot could transform the state Legislature by granting lawmakers salaries for the first time in the state’s history.
text:
The New Mexico general election ballot features Constitutional Amendment 4, which gives voters the choice about whether lawmakers can receive salaries. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)While the top of the Nov. 3 ballot will bring new leadership to New Mexico, one of the constitutional amendments at the end of the ballot could transform the state Legislature by granting lawmakers salaries for the first time in the state’s history.
Constitutional Amendment 4 asks voters whether they are for or against allowing New Mexico lawmakers to receive compensation equal to the state’s median household income, which is currently $67,800, according to U.S. Census figures. For 112 state lawmakers, the annual cost to taxpayers will be about $7.6 million.
New Mexico remains the only Legislature in the country that does not pay its lawmakers salaries, though they do receive per diem payments for costs associated with the annual legislative session and committee meetings in the interim. Lawmakers are also eligible to receive pensions after leaving office. 
The question’s arrival on the November ballot marks the final step in a years-long effort. The Legislature at the session earlier this year voted largely along party lines to approve House Joint Resolution 5, which puts the question of legislative salaries before voters.
If voters approve the measure, lawmakers would first receive salaries in 2029. 
Pro-salary advocates have said that paying lawmakers is necessary to attract high-quality candidates who might otherwise forgo running for office because they can’t afford it. 
Sylvia Ulloa, executive director of New Mexico CAFe, a southern New Mexico social justice organization that is part of a coalition pushing for Constitutional Amendment 4, told Source NM on Thursday she regularly encounters people who would make great lawmakers but opt out due to financial considerations.
“I’m thinking about a single mom with a disabled child in our Gadsden school district,” she said. “There is no way that she could ever serve in the Legislature, but what valuable life experience she could bring if she could actually do that.”
Ulloa, along with other organizations in the pro-salary coalition called Vote For Change, said paying lawmakers salaries could make lawmakers less beholden to well-financed lobbyists offering expensive meals or other perks. 
The coalition also sees paying salaries as a key step in a broader “modernization” push at the Legislature, along with reforms such as hiring paid district legislative aides, which state lawmakers began doing in 2024, and extending the legislative session beyond 30 days or 60 days. 
A pro-con guide from the Legislative Council Service for this year’s constitutional amendments also notes that one argument in favor of the amendment is that it may strengthen the legislative branch in relation to the judicial and executive branches.
The Vote For Change coalition has raised approximately $2 million as part of its campaign to convince voters to approve legislative salaries, according to recent filings. That includes a $1.2 million donation from Western Futures Fund, a Wyoming-based nonprofit that seeks to “promote responsible leadership in the Western United States,” according to the group’s website. 
A recent Albuquerque Journal poll released earlier this month found 39% of likely New Mexico voters plan to vote “yes” on Amendment 4, with 21% planning to vote “no.” Another 34% are undecided, and 6% said it “depends.”
The amendment also has critics. Paul Gessing, president of the conservative Rio Grande Foundation, said he is not opposed to salaries in theory, but said the one being offered to New Mexico lawmakers is too high and risks creating the wrong incentives. 
NM Legislature approves resolution for lawmaker pay, sending question to voters on November ballot

“I’ve just not seen any case made from anybody supporting us that we’re going to get a better-performing Legislature. We could see an expanded pool, if you will, of people who might serve and maybe there’s some benefit to that,” Gessing said. “But I think there’s also potential for people who get into it for more purely financial reasons at this point, and just kind of wait their time out to lock in the pension, and then ride off into the sunset after that.”
Gessing will debate New Mexico Forward Party Chair Bob Perls on the topic next month.
According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, a proposed New Mexico salary of $67,800 is higher than the national average salary for lawmakers in 2025 of $44,320. Lawmakers in New Mexico’s neighboring states of Texas, Colorado and Arizona also receive salaries of significantly less than New Mexico lawmakers would receive. 
The guide from the Legislative Council Service argues that offering sitting lawmakers salaries may put them at an unfair advantage over challengers who unlike incumbents have to forgo salaries to campaign and fundraise for office. It also raises the matter of the proposed New Mexico salaries being higher than those in other states.
Ulloa said tying the salary to median income ensures lawmakers earn the typical salaries of average New Mexicans, including experiencing a pay cut should that median income decrease. 
“That kind of built-in safeguard is something that New Mexicans really understand,” she said. “It can’t be swayed by political winds in any given legislature. It is tied in law and defined what that salary will be.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Drake University to contribute to Panama national AI strategy with academic programs
description: Drake University has been named by Panama's president as a partner in the country's national artificial intelligence strategy through its new degrees. (Photo courtesy of Drake University)
text:
Drake University had an economic impact totaling $424.1 million in 2025, according to a report released by the university. (Photo courtesy of Drake University) Drake University has been named a partner in the artificial intelligence strategy of Panama, a move the university president says builds on the pair’s relationship and expands its mission of meeting learners where they are.
The Des Moines private university, through its establishment of the only data analytics program in the Central American country, was acknowledged by Republic of Panama President José Raúl Mulino as an essential partner in developing talent to help implement its national AI strategy and grow the country’s technology and artificial intelligence economy.
Drake’s role in this work stems from its bachelor’s degree in data analytics and minor in artificial intelligence set to begin next fall at Ciudad del Saber, an education and entrepreneurship hub in Panama City. Drake University President Marty Martin said it was a “special moment” to hear Mulino acknowledge Drake on a national stage.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’re far removed from Panama, and yet we have worked so closely with them, and frankly, listened to what they needed, and what they needed aligned with our competency and mission, such that when we combine these partnerships that we have there with the strengths of Drake, our mission orientation, we’re able to find a pathway that’s really in service to that country and that region,” Martin said.
The data analytics and AI programs, announced in October 2025, provide two pathways for Panamanian students — a three-year and one-summer accelerated program where students earn both the bachelor’s degree and minor in Panama and a 2+2 program where students would come to Iowa to complete their last two years.
Martin said the university has worked closely with SENACYT, which when translated stands for National Secretariat of Science, Technology and Innovation, in developing the degrees, and Drake is a partner in the national strategy it crafted focused on AI, semiconductors and microelectronics.
With 17 applications already submitted to Drake, Martin said the university hopes to see a first cohort of 50 students next fall, most likely split evenly between the pathways that keep students in Panama or bring them to Iowa. Martin and other Drake officials will head to Panama next week to participate in a college recruiting fair, which the university sponsors, meeting the country’s minister of innovation and holding an alumni reception.
Ciudad del Saber in Panama City has partnered with Drake University to offer new degree pathways. (Photo courtesy of Drake University)
Drake officials are also in the process of identifying Drake faculty and hiring faculty in Panama, and Dean of Students Jerry Parker has already relocated to the area with his family to stay for the first year. While they haven’t made any decisions yet, Martin said they’re looking at other Drake degree programs to see which would work in Panama.
Panama is home to a “cadre of alumni” from Drake, Martin said, who hold “very prominent positions in the country.” He took his first visit there in 2017 to meet the alumni, who encouraged and supported the university’s efforts to put a presence in Panama, and to visit Ciudad del Saber.
“When you combine the alumni base we have with the wonderful entity that is Ciudad del Saber, it just became a natural place for us to think big,” Martin said.
After the Drake football team took an 11-day trip to Panama in 2024, Martin said he and others knew they had to “find a path” to establishing the university in the country, and visited Panama three times between May 2024 and May 2025 to develop and refine the ideas that led them to this level of partnership.
Drake is pursuing these kinds of programs, in Panama as well as programs with academic partnerships in Singapore and China, for two reasons, Martin said. The first is a driver in many university initiatives — growing enrollment.
As a university that has always been about meeting learners where they are, Martin said those efforts have included meeting students at their current “academic and social maturation,” as well as their geographical location through online programs. Now, he said, the university is “going to physical locations around the world to literally meet learners where they are.”
The second reason is the notion and practice of “civic diplomacy through education,” he said.
“We are much better when we know each other, when we understand each other, because out of that comes trust, and trust is the essential ingredient in this world getting along and progressing,” Martin said. “And so we’re making our own small contribution to that in China, we’ll make it in Singapore, we’ll make it in Panama and other places where we’ll have collaborations.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: USC’s Palmetto College will seek more money to continue enrolling high schoolers for dual credit
description: Without more funding, USC's Palmetto College may have to stop accepting high school students who want an early start on a college degree.
text:
The University of South Carolina’s Palmetto College may stop offering high school students dual enrollment to its two-year campuses due to a gap in funding. This photo was taken at USC's Horseshoe in Columbia, S.C. in October 2024. (Photo by Travis Bell/SIDELINE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Without additional taxpayer funding, the University of South Carolina’s Palmetto College may stop accepting South Carolina high school students who want to get an early start on a college degree.
Some 4,300 South Carolina high school juniors and seniors enroll in Palmetto College courses through what is known as dual enrollment, a program designed to help students save money on college and find work faster after graduating.
But while the program has grown in popularity, lottery-funded scholarship dollars to cover the cost at the state’s two-year technical colleges and universities have decreased.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In 2019, lottery-funded scholarships paid $110 per credit hour of dual enrollment costs for any student taking at least six credit hours. Since then, that amount has dropped 32% — to $75 per credit hour.
Meanwhile dual enrollment at Palmetto College increased 55% over the same time period and now makes up 65% of the student body, according to the state’s higher education agency.
About the college
Founded in 2013, Palmetto College is not a singular college campus. Rather, it’s a college network, giving enrollees access to USC’s four, two-year campuses, where they can complete an associate’s degree. And for those who wish to continue their education, turning their associate’s degree into a bachelor’s, the Palmetto College allows them to do so through one of 30 online degree programs offered by the college system no matter where they live.
“One of the goals of Palmetto College is accessibility,” Chancellor Craig Wilson told the SC Daily Gazette. “So, making sure that students, particularly these ambitious young students, have a place to actually learn in a great environment — it’s certainly something that we want to do.”
USC originally designed the college to cater to working adults who may have started but never completed a college degree. But it’s also offered dual enrollment credits to high school students from the start. Now it’s a large and growing part of what Palmetto College does.
The USC systems’ two-year campuses in Allendale, Lancaster, Sumter and Union serve as regional hubs where students attend in-person classes. Dual enrollment students can take some of these classes right in their high school, with no need to travel to campus.
“It’s very popular,” Wilson said. “That demand is not going to go away.”
One of Palmetto College’s top budget priorities for the legislative session come January is increasing the state’s $75 payment, he said. However, exactly how much the college will seek is undecided.
“We recognize that we’re running behind the eight ball on this, and sooner is always the best way to get this done,” Wilson said.
SC colleges have frozen tuition for several years. University presidents say that’s not sustainable.

The cost is the pain point.
Palmetto College typically charges $300 per credit hour for its classes, Wilson said. State funding only covers a quarter of that. Instead of charging students for the difference, the college absorbs it.
“It’s a matter of getting state support that would allow us to continue to do this job, and I would imagine that the other institutions who are providing higher education feel the same way,” Wilson said.
Other funding
South Carolina’s 16 technical colleges, which together teach 22,600 (or about 65%) of the state’s juniors and seniors dually enrolled in high school and college, also face gaps but have made up some of that lost funding through other state and local funding sources, according to a statement from the technical college system.
Palmetto College and the high schoolers it serves have been left behind, USC officials say.
For starters, technical college students studying for a wide variety of in-demand careers — healthcare, IT, manufacturing, construction, criminal justice, education, business, cybersecurity, welding, truck driving and more — are eligible for a secondary, $5,000 scholarship known as SC Workforce Industry Needs Scholarship.
More than 75% of the dual enrollment high school students who attend a technical college receive scholarships to cover the full cost of tuition, technical system President Tim Hardee previously told the SC Daily Gazette.
SC spending $3M more annually to grow dual high school and college enrollment

And in 2025, nearby K-12 school districts also chipped in funding to fill gaps not covered by scholarships at about half of the state’s technical colleges, Hardee said.
When it comes to the state’s public and private four-year schools, the colleges and their students receive no state scholarship support for dual enrollment at all. But they also have significantly fewer students participating in the program.
Eight of the 13 public four-years, including USC’s satellite campuses, offer dual enrollment, enrolling less than 2,000 total students combined. Eight of South Carolina’s 21 private colleges have programs, with less than 1,700 total high schoolers.
Some, such as Lander University and the USC system campuses in Aiken, Beaufort and Spartanburg, offer free or reduced tuition rates to dual enrollment students. The lower participation rates — less than 500 students enrolled in each school’s program, making up less than 10% of the student body — make it easier to absorb the lost tuition dollars.
Others, such as Francis Marion and Winthrop universities, have partnerships with a couple of local school districts that allow those districts’ students to enroll free of charge. Outside of those districts, however, participating high schoolers pay what any part-time college student would to attend classes.
Rural schools struggle
The Palmetto College looked at similar arrangements with school districts near its two-year campuses but ultimately backed away from the idea, given where those campuses are located.
“These are rural areas,” Wilson said. “Not all schools have the same economic base, the same tax base to pull from.”
“Whether it’s Lancaster or Allendale or Walterboro, all of the areas that we’re serving, those school districts aren’t really in a position to be able to add more,” Wilson added.
The same is true for rural technical colleges. So, in 2025, the technical system asked the Legislature for financial support.
Legislators responded with $3 million annually, divvied up across the 16-school system, that the more rural schools could use to fill the hole.
The Palmetto College wants taxpayers’ help too.
“Dual enrollment was set up for those who come from disadvantaged backgrounds, so the last thing we want to do is overburden them. Many of our students are first-generation students,” he said. “So, this this is vital in terms of affordability for our students.”

text:
The Ten Commandments on the Nebraska State Capitol. April 17, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — After an 18-month search to find a new director for Nebraska’s Public Employees Retirement System, the man selected for the position is resigning at the end of October.
NPERS legal counsel Tag Herbek confirmed in an email that Executive Director Thomas Pfeifle resigned effective Oct. 31. The Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Board officially approved Pfeifle’s employment on June 15.
Herbek said Pfeifle “expressed an interest to be closer to his family in Colorado” as the reason for his resignation. He said the board will hold a special meeting Sept. 30 to consider “leadership succession matters.”
Before selecting Pfeifle as executive director, NPERS went without a permanent director for more than a year and a half. The previous director, former State Treasurer John Murante, left in December 2024 after just over a year with the agency.
Through most of the search process, NPERS’ deputy director Tyler Cummings served as interim director. The board recommended Cummings to replace Murante, but Gov. Jim Pillen rejected his appointment.

title: Report predicts substantial hit to Maine’s economy if Trump’s immigration enforcement continues
description: President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement could result in the state losing anywhere from $395 million to $3.3 billion in annual economic output.  That’s according to a report commissioned by the Maine Office of New Americans, which assessed the contributions of more than 33,000 foreign-born workers in Maine and modeled how federal enforcement could le[...]
text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents search the passenger of a truck as they arrest both him and the driver during a February traffic stop in Robbinsdale, Minnesota. Minnesota faced a high rate of street arrests after Trump administration officials criticized the state’s sanctuary policies, but even states without such policies have seen street raids to round up immigrants. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement could result in the state losing anywhere from $395 million to $3.3 billion in annual economic output. 
That’s according to a report commissioned by the Maine Office of New Americans, which assessed the contributions of more than 33,000 foreign-born workers in Maine and modeled how federal enforcement could leave employers across various sectors critically short of workers. 
“This report is the first of its kind to examine what Maine’s economy could look like if immigrants continue to disappear from our workforce,” Gov. Janet Mills said in a statement. “President Trump’s cruel and dangerous immigration agenda is forcing us to contemplate this reality.” 
Maine’s immigrant workforce is relatively small but an increasingly important component of the state’s economy, concluded the report, which was prepared by Maine-based Wallace Economic Advisers using U.S. Census data.
An estimated 33,079 foreign-born workers directly generated about $177 million in state income tax revenue and $2.25 billion in personal income between 2020 and 2024, the report found. Factoring in broader economic activity that employment supports, the report estimates that immigrant employment helps sustain nearly 74,000 jobs and nearly $15 billion in total economic output.
When estimating the potential economic consequences of heightened enforcement in the state, the report looked beyond the number of arrests or removals, given that enforcement has ripple effects with not only immigrants but people of color generally fearful of going about their daily lives, causing disruptions to employers, reduced business-to-business purchases, and lower household spending. 
The analysis considered three scenarios: a low scenario assuming a relatively limited direct employment effect and modest withdrawal from activities, a middle scenario of more substantial and persistent enforcement, and a high scenario where direct enforcement is accompanied by a significant change in behavior among the noncitizen workforce. 
Applying these assumptions produced estimated labor force reductions of approximately 840 workers in the low scenario, 5,037 workers in the middle scenario, and 7,050 workers in the high scenario. 
This modeling has its limits, as the report caveats. The assumptions about how much enforcement would deter participation in daily life beyond immigrants directly detained involve a large amount of uncertainty, for example, so the analysis captures a range of potential labor market responses. 
The report does not estimate outcomes of actual enforcement that has occurred so far, so it is not meant to predict the future. 
Disruptions to Maine’s workforce have already been seen.  
After U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement’s large-scale operation in the state in January, the Maine State Chamber of Commerce, Portland Regional Chamber of Commerce and Lewiston Auburn Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce sent a letter to Maine’s congressional delegation detailing ways ICE’s presence was harming the state’s economy and calling for changes to enforcement. 
And after ICE fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in July, Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain told members of Congress that many of the immigrants in the community “retreated from public life,” skipping school and work. 
Several employers and workers provided testimony in the report, including Wyman’s of Maine, one of the world’s leading growers and marketers of frozen wild blueberries. About 38% of Wyman’s year-round, full-time employees are immigrants and the company has experienced considerable disruption in this talent pool in recent years. 
“The bottom line is that this is not a partisan issue,” the statement from Wyman’s read. “Sustaining agriculture in Maine truly does hinge on having enough employees who want to farm and process our wild blueberries. This is reality.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Not another Boston: How CT can find its place in the AI economy
description: For 37 years Connecticut has lacked a credible answer to its stagnation. But the AI revolution has flipped the odds in our favor.
text:
Connecticut’s economic condition is easy to misread. By the measures that make headlines, we look enviable: among the highest household incomes in the nation, and a state government in its strongest fiscal position in decades. The rainy-day fund is full, and the state has paid down more than $10 billion in pension liabilities.
But those headline rankings –and the tax revenues behind the state’s surpluses— are disproportionately the result of capital gains, dividends, interest, and rents flowing to a small number of wealthy households. Our high median income is real, and it is largely the legacy of high-wage jobs created decades ago. 
What the rankings do not show is a healthy, growing Connecticut economy underneath. The deeper numbers tell the truer story. Since 1989, the United States has expanded its employment by nearly 50 percent. Connecticut’s payroll growth over those 37 years is below 3 percent. We needed 18 years just to regain the employment peak set in March 2008, a peak virtually every state had passed, most a decade ago. And the quality of our jobs has been eroding alongside their quantity, with high-wage technical and corporate roles steadily replaced by positions paying far less. 
Recent quarters have brought genuine momentum, including stronger growth, new arrivals, a bond-rating upgrade. Most welcome, and, against a 37-year hole, a beginning rather than an arrival.
Ours is a state with a healthy balance sheet and a sick economy. The balance sheet will not stay healthy if the economy stays sick. The surpluses funding the pension paydown ride on volatile capital income generated outside the state; if our own growth does not return, the liabilities will.
This condition is structural, and it is old; it predates every current officeholder by a generation. And the essential first response has already been delivered: enforcing guardrails a bipartisan legislature built, Gov. Ned Lamont has restored the state’s fiscal foundation, faithfully, against every pressure to abandon the discipline. That foundation is the signal achievement of this era; it will pay dividends for decades. The question this essay takes up is what it now makes possible.
Why growth left
Let’s be honest about why Connecticut got left out. The modern data-driven economy rewards concentration: deep pools of talent, capital, and firms feeding on one another in a handful of giant metropolitan centers. Connecticut is a small state with no major metro, sitting between two of the most powerful metropolitan economies on earth. That is a structural fact, not a policy failure we can reverse with a marketing campaign. On conventional terms, whether hunting elephants, bidding for footloose tech firms, trying to out-Boston Boston, we cannot compete. We should stop pretending otherwise.
But economic history, including Connecticut’s own, teaches a critical lesson. Regions rarely win by imitating the leader. They win by differentiating, by driving deep into specialized capabilities the leaders do not have and cannot quickly acquire. Connecticut was never an economic power because of its size. It became the patent capital of 19th-century America through the precision manufacturing of the armory tradition. It made Hartford the insurance capital of the continent through accumulated expertise no rival could replicate. Specialized depth, not scale, is this state’s original playbook. Three words summarize three centuries of Connecticut economic success: differentiate, don’t imitate. The question before us was never how Connecticut becomes another Boston. It is how Connecticut becomes the world’s best Connecticut.
The layer Connecticut can win
Artificial intelligence hands us the chance to answer it. The AI economy has two layers. In the platform layer, the frontier models, massive compute, and elite research talent, every advantage concentrates: Connecticut will not win. New York’s $500 million Empire AI consortium and Massachusetts’ $100 million AI Hub target that platform layer. Matching them dollar-for-dollar would buy us an inferior copy of what our neighbors already have.
We do not need to build the AI brain. We need to become the best place in the world to apply it.
In the application layer, where AI is embedded in real industries, the scarce inputs flip. Value flows to proprietary data, deep domain knowledge, and physical assets. Those are precisely what Connecticut holds. 
The market is already pricing this logic: when Salesforce’s latest results confounded predictions that AI models would swallow the software incumbents, analysts led by Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld concluded that value in the AI economy is migrating to those who hold the scarce data intelligence cannot function without. AI underwriting is worth little without decades of claims data; this is the actuarial talent concentrated in Hartford. 
AI-augmented design and production of submarines and jet engines must happen where the factories, security clearances, and controlled processes physically sit. Groton, East Hartford, and Stratford cannot be relocated. Neither can the thousands of precision manufacturers that supply them. 
AI-driven genomic medicine requires sequencing capacity, clinical depth, and translational research at scale, precisely what the consortium of Yale, UConn, and the Jackson Laboratory was built to deliver, and an asset whose potential we have barely begun to realize. And these assets sit unusually close together: world-class universities, insurers, hospitals, defense plants, and the state government itself, all within an hour of one another. What Connecticut lacks in metropolitan scale it holds in convening proximity. Applied AI is, above all, a coordination problem among institutions.
What it looks like in practice: A state-brokered data commons, letting our insurers, hospitals, and manufacturers give vetted Connecticut startups secure, controlled access to the industry data they cannot get anywhere else —without that data ever leaving its owners’ hands— turning Connecticut’s institutional memory into its recruiting pitch; a compact among our anchor employers to open real operational problems, each year, to Connecticut startups and university teams. 
The scarcest assets in any startup ecosystem are not accelerators and mentors but hard problems and sophisticated first customers. Connecticut has both in abundance. For example, innovation vouchers that let a 60-person machine shop in Waterbury hire Connecticut talent to bring AI onto its shop floor.
And an AI extension service is an idea Connecticut invented. The nation’s first agricultural experiment station was established in this state in 1875, decades before the federal government followed. It was research at the Windsor station that developed shade-grown tobacco and built a world-leading Connecticut industry from public science carried onto private land. The AI extension service applies that same Connecticut invention to the factory floor and the claims office: practitioners who walk the floor and connect firms to Connecticut tools and training, not consultants who bill for slide decks.
These are not hypothetical needs. Under new federal cybersecurity certification rules now attached to the Navy’s latest submarine contracts, hundreds of small Connecticut defense suppliers must meet demanding security standards within the next year or watch decades-old work, and thousands of new hires, flow to better-prepared states. The vouchers, the extension service, and the training pipelines above have their first mission already waiting, with a hard deadline.
The workforce ambition should be equally sharp. Connecticut cannot out-produce Massachusetts or New York in generic AI engineers and should not try. The fastest-growing demand nationally is for AI fluency, for people who can work with, direct, and audit AI inside a domain they already master. That is our opening, because domain mastery is what Connecticut’s workforce already has. 
The aspiration: America’s most AI-fluent insurance workforce. America’s most AI-fluent aerospace and defense manufacturing workforce. One of America’s most AI-fluent biomedical workforces. Fluency compounds on expertise: our machinists, adjusters, and lab technicians can be elevated into directing the tools entering their trades. And the graduates our universities produce every year will finally see careers worth staying for, here rather than in Boston or New York.
Be clear-eyed about the alternative
Our insurers, manufacturers, and health systems will adopt AI regardless of what Hartford does. The projections are no longer abstract: a new Tufts University index puts expected AI-driven job displacement over the next two to five years at roughly 16 percent in finance and insurance and in professional and technical services, the sectors where Connecticut’s white-collar employment is most concentrated, in a state that has already lost some 25,000 insurance jobs. 
The strategic question is not adoption; it is where the value is captured. If the tools, the vendors, the startups, and the specialized workforce are built elsewhere, Connecticut absorbs the job losses, imports the productivity gains, and watches the domain knowledge that is currently our advantage migrate into other states’ firms. If they are built here, disruption converts into a new export industry. That window will not stay open long. Connecticut must act, and act now.
The quantum stakes
The stakes are no longer hypothetical. Last month Connecticut won one of just 12 NSF Regional Innovation Engine awards nationwide for QuantumCT. The first tranche is $15 million, with up to $160 million over a decade, if Connecticut delivers. That federal money must be earned, not banked: it is released in stages, only as quantum technologies demonstrably become embedded in defense, biotechnology, and financial services. 
Those are exactly the markets now being rebuilt around AI. Critically, AI software will design, optimize, validate, and carry quantum’s capabilities into use. If Connecticut sits out the AI economy, it will struggle to hit the milestones its quantum award requires and will likely watch the largest federal innovation investment in its history slip away. AI and quantum are not two initiatives. They are one strategy.
The rules are written; now build
Connecticut has, to its credit, already done something its neighbors have not: written the rules. The bipartisan AI legislation signed in June gives firms here what founders elsewhere still lack: regulatory certainty and a sandbox in which to build. For entrepreneurs creating AI for regulated, knowledge-intensive industries, specifically insurance, healthcare, aerospace and defense, bioscience, that is exactly the environment that matters most. But rules are not a strategy.
None of this asks Connecticut to abandon its fiscal discipline; it asks us to use what that discipline has built. Act one is complete. Act two is what foundations are for. A one-time, tightly capped investment of $100 to $150 million from the current surplus, less than 2 percent of what the guardrails have already delivered to the pension funds, deployed only alongside at least two private matching dollars for every public one, would mobilize $300 million or more for precisely the industries where Connecticut can actually win. 
These are investments in which the taxpayer shares the upside. And unlike the defensive $500 million the State has prudently set aside to buffer federal funding cuts, this is offense: an investment in growing the economy that ultimately secures the pension paydown itself, because only a broadening tax base keeps those liabilities funded through the next market correction.
Even the physical foundations favor us. Connecticut is a substantial exporter of electricity, with nearly half the power generated here serving customers beyond our borders. Where computing infrastructure is needed, Connecticut can host it selectively, on its own terms, with ratepayers protected rather than burdened.
In the coming weeks, the Connecticut Center for Economic Analysis will publish the full blueprint behind this argument, a granular policy brief with the specific programs, the financing, and the governance, along with a commitment to provide an annual public assessment of whether the initiatives are working. Connecticut has heard promises before; this strategy comes with a scorecard.
For 37 years Connecticut has lacked a credible answer to its stagnation. The AI revolution has flipped the odds: for the first time, the structure of an emerging technology aligns with the structure of our strengths. We will not get that alignment twice. The world’s best Connecticut is still ours to build.
Fred Carstensen is a Professor of Finance and Economics at the University of Connecticut and Director of the Connecticut Center for Economic Analysis.

name: Mississippi Today
title: US Rep. Trent Kelly running for top GOP spot on House Armed Services Committee
description: Rep. Trent Kelly, R-Miss., attends a House Armed Services Committee hearing in Rayburn Building titled the "Fiscal Year 2020 National Defense Budget Request from the Department of Defense," on Tuesday, March 26, 2019. (Photo By Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images)
text:
U.S. Rep. Trent Kelly, a Republican representing Mississippi’s 1st Congressional District in north Mississippi, hopes to become the highest-ranking GOP member on the House Armed Services Committee next year. 
Kelly, currently running for a seventh term, said in a statement to Mississippi Today that he’s focused on winning reelection in November. But if the district votes to send him back to Washington, he will run to be top Republican of the committee that has jurisdiction over the nation’s military.
“I have a long history of working on national defense strategy, and I believe I can make a meaningful difference for our men and women in uniform and for the defense of our great nation,” Kelly said. 
The current top Republican on the committee is U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers from Alabama. The Republican Conference’s internal rules limit members to a maximum of three years as the most senior person on a committee, but they can seek a waiver to be exempt from that rule. 
Republican committee chairs in the U.S. House are chosen through a process with the Republican Steering Committee and a vote by the full party conference.
Kelly is a former district attorney in northeast Mississippi and a 39-year Mississippi Army National Guard veteran who retired in 2025 as a major general. He serves on the House Armed Services Committee and is chairman of the Seapower Subcommittee.
Other GOP members running for the top spot are Rep. Rob Wittman of Virginia and Rep. Ronny Jackson of Texas, according to Punchbowl News.  
Kelly is running for reelection against Democratic nominee Cliff Johnson and Libertarian candidate Johnny Baucom, and the general election is Nov. 3.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Donald Trump to hold rally in Mobile amid Alabama GOP turnout concerns
description: President Donald Trump plans to hold a campaign rally in Mobile next week amid concerns among Alabama Republicans about turnout.  The rally will take place on Oct. 2 at the Mitchell Center.  According to polling by the Economist and YouGov updated weekly, Trump is broadly unpopular in Alabama despite winning the state with nearly 65% […]
text:
Former President Donald Trump speaks at a fundraiser for the Alabama Republican Party on Friday, Aug. 4, 2023 in Montgomery, Ala.  Trump plans to campaign ahead of the midterms in Mobile on Oct. 2 amid concerns of low voter turnout. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)President Donald Trump plans to hold a campaign rally in Mobile next week amid concerns among Alabama Republicans about turnout. 
The rally will take place on Oct. 2 at the Mitchell Center. 
According to polling by the Economist and YouGov updated weekly, Trump is broadly unpopular in Alabama despite winning the state with nearly 65% of votes in 2024. Among 2024 voters, the president remains popular, according to the polling. Alabama Republicans have in recent weeks expressed concerns about potential apathy among GOP voters, with whom Trump remains broadly popular.
Mobile is in the 1st Alabama Congressional District, which the Cook Political Report rates solidly Republican. It is adjacent to the 2nd Congressional District, where the race between incumbent U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, a Democrat, and Republican nominee Rhett Marques is considered more competitive, though leaning to the GOP after redistricting earlier this year. 
Trump held his first stadium-size rally for his 2016 presidential campaign in Mobile in August 2015.
Jerry Carl, a former congressman and the Republican nominee in the 1st Congressional District, wrote in a social media post Friday morning that it will be a “great honor” to have Trump in the district. 
“President Trump has been here a couple of times before but let’s make this the best trip yet! Come out to hear directly from our President and show our support!” Carl wrote.
Carl was elected in a special primary election in August over two other Republican candidates where each expressed concern of low voter turnout. Average voter turnout across all special primaries in four congressional districts for the special elections was about 5%. 
Carl will face Democratic nominee Clyde Jones, Jr., in November. Jones said in a phone interview Friday morning that he agrees that turnout is a concern, but Trump’s appearance likely will not help.
“This administration has, they have really done nothing to help the everyday person,” Jones said. “We all should be concerned about voter turnout. It’s been extremely low here in Alabama across the board.”
Jack Burns, a spokesman for the Carl campaign, wrote in a text message Friday morning that turnout will be higher in November than it was in August, and that Trump will “100% have a massive positive influence on voter turnout.”
“Trump is absolutely going to motivate voters to get out and vote. Trump loves Alabama and Alabama loves Trump,” Burns wrote. 
U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise, who Trump endorsed for the U.S. Senate and who appeared at the 2015 Mobile rally as a state legislator, said in a statement Friday that Trump will “energize conservatives” for the general election.
“Thanks to his administration, we are stopping the indoctrination of our children, standing strong on the world stage, and defeating the Radical Democrats. His rally will be the jet fuel we need to win big in Alabama,” Moore said.
A message seeking comment with U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, the party’s nominee for governor and another Trump-endorsed candidate, was left Friday morning.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: SNAP enrollment is down in CT since last year — but where?
description: In Connecticut, about 55,000 fewer people are enrolled in SNAP, including nearly 18,000 fewer residents under 18 receiving benefits.
text:
In Connecticut, the number of people enrolled in the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, fell by 15% from June 2025 to June 2026 — including nearly 18,000 fewer residents under 18 receiving benefits.
In total, 55,000 fewer people in Connecticut were on SNAP this June compared to last June, according to a report from DataHaven. Enrollment in the program decreased quickly under eligibility changes implemented through H.R. 1, which cut nearly $187 billion in federal program funding.
These findings follow a recent report from Connecticut Voices for Children, which found similar changes from July 2025 to July 2026.
All age groups, except for those 65 and older, saw enrollment fall. While residents 65 and older are not required to meet updated work requirements, the new rules require parents with dependents aged 14 to 17 to comply.
“People with dependents 14 to 17 are now subject to these work requirements,” Andrew Carr, a data analyst with DataHaven and co-author of the report said. “Increasing the population of those subject to work requirements, it creates new administrative burdens for people that may cause families to lose SNAP, which has consequences for children.”
The report used an adapted Program Access Index, which is the ratio of SNAP recipients to those who meet the federal income and age eligibility standards. While not a true participation rate, it is a good measure of program coverage, Carr said.
Based on this index, every town has seen a decrease. However, losses are slightly higher in urban areas like the Hartford and Waterbury areas.
“Losses spread across the state, but also that they’re a little more concentrated in cities,” Carr said. “The adapted program access index shows that some of the places where need for SNAP [is highest], at least according to the federal income and age criteria, are the areas where losses were greatest.”
Economic loss was also measured in the report. DataHaven found that some parts of the state lose more than $1 million in benefits each month, with Hartford losing an estimated $1.3 million monthly. 
In total, the state loses an estimated $11 million each month in benefits. 
While the impacts of eligibility changes are already seen in the state and the nation, not all changes have gone into effect. Penalties for states that exceed the error rate, or the percentage of SNAP benefits paid above or below what recipients should have received, have not gone into effect. 
“We’re in this period right now between these two sets of effects from H.R. 1 on SNAP,” Carr said. “We’ve already seen the effects of H.R. 1 on just increasing eligibility requirements for people, and that’s led to losses in SNAP … what’s important to to realize is that many of the effects that are relevant for SNAP haven’t even taken hold yet.”
Connecticut is currently over the error-rate threshold, sitting at around 9%, and may have to pay more $85 million to $89 million, according to the CT Voices for Children report. Penalties are effective October 2027.
While Connecticut has put some money aside to support those impacted by the eligibility requirements, this may not be enough with the implementation of additional changes.
“Government has taken measures to to help people that have lost coverage, but there are changes coming up the pike that are going to require a more like lasting response from government,” Carr said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Priest to death row inmates urges Mississippi to repeal nitrogen as form of execution
description: Death penalty opponents Sheila O'Flaherty, left, the Rev. Jeff Hood, center, and his son, Phillip Hood, participate in a vigil for Thomas Edwin Loden Jr. outside the Mississippi State Penitentiary in Parchman, Miss., Dec. 14, 2022.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You canread more about the section here.  

I have watched two men killed with nitrogen. Both still haunt me.
In late 2023, Kenneth Smith asked me to be his spiritual adviser. We spent weeks together before Alabama filled his lungs with nitrogen gas. Like any priest and parishioner, we prayed and read Scripture together. We talked about what was coming.
I was wrong about everything. The horror of forced suffocation went far beyond anything that I could have imagined.
When the nitrogen gas began to flow, all of the espoused theories of humaneness ended. Kenny’s muscles wildly seized. His chest heaved with great force. I still do not know how a strapped body could actually move a steel gurney. His head slapped the inside of the mask over and over. Everything was moving everywhere all at once.
We were told he would be unconscious in seconds. Yet his veins kept rising against the skin. Saliva, mucus and other fluids kept pooling. His eyes looked like they might explode. I took off my glasses. I sobbed. I had never felt further from God.
That was January 2024. It was the first execution by nitrogen hypoxia in the history of the world.
In Mississippi, the method had already been legal for seven years.
Upon the enactment of House Bill 638, nitrogen went in as a contingency method in 2017. If a court struck lethal injection or it became unavailable, the state first would move to gas, then to the chair and then to the firing squad.
The bill answered lawsuits over the state’s lethal injection drugs. Though nobody on earth had watched a nitrogen execution, Mississippi wrote the method into law anyway.
Then, Mississippi took the conditions out.
In 2022, House Bill 1479 rewrote Section 99-19-51. The statute now leaves the method of execution to the discretion of the Corrections commissioner, the deputy commissioner for Finance and Administration and the deputy commissioner for institutions of the Mississippi Department of Corrections.
The options include nitrogen hypoxia, electrocution, firing squad or lethal injection. Though the law names injection the preferred method as a matter of state policy, preference does not mean requirement.
Nitrogen is no longer Mississippi’s fallback. Nitrogen is one of Mississippi’s four choices.
Nothing has to fail first. No court has to rule. No supply has to run short. Three officials decide. The law gives the condemned man seven days of written notice to learn what they picked. That is the whole procedure. Seven days to find out which apparatus the state selected to kill you.
The Legislature made that decision in 2022. It made it two years before anyone alive had seen what nitrogen does. Nobody in the Legislature had seen what I have.
None of this is abstract. Mississippi is killing again.
Richard Jordan was executed at Parchman on June 25, 2025. He was 79 and had spent nearly 50 years on death row. The state used a three-drug protocol beginning with midazolam. Jordan was the lead plaintiff in a federal challenge arguing that midazolam leaves a man awake for the burning and the suffocation that follow. Mississippi killed him with the drug he was suing over.
Death Row at Unit 29, Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman.  Credit: Mississippi Department of Corrections
I was outside the fence that night. What stays with me is not the grief. It was the mood of the people running the thing. The staff seemed practically giddy. There was an air of celebration, the feeling a small town gets before the big football game. Now you want to hand those men a mask, a tank and the permission to suffocate people to death?
Thirty-five men remain on Mississippi’s death row.
Though Mississippi has recently chosen injection, nothing in the law requires it to choose injection again.
In 2017 and again in 2022, execution by nitrogen hypoxia existed only on paper – legislative reports, physiological assumptions and confident predictions about what a condemned man would feel. It was enough.
Eight men have now been killed with it. They are Kenneth Smith, Alan Miller, Carey Dale Grayson, Demetrius Frazier, Gregory Hunt, Geoffrey West, Anthony Boyd, all in Alabama, and Jessie Hoffman in Louisiana.
I was there for the first. I was there for the eighth.
Anthony Boyd also asked me to be his spiritual adviser. In the midst of deep prayer, we talked about God’s love.
Then the curtains opened, and the gas began. His chest heaved. His legs came off the gurney. He strained against the restraints. His breathing turned frantic and never stopped. By my count, Anthony was conscious and fighting for at least 19 minutes. He was pronounced dead at 6:33 pm. It was the longest nitrogen execution Alabama had carried out.
I called it the worst one yet. I still do.
The state has an answer for everything I just described. Convulsions become involuntary movement. Gasping becomes an expected physiological response. Terror becomes a reaction the man was not conscious enough to feel.
Each translation may be technically defensible. But not one of them tells you  any of what the executed knew. Whether they knew is the only question that matters, and the vocabulary was built so that such a question never gets asked.
The count is mine. The men are not. Eight of them are now on the public record. Mississippi can read that record without producing a body of its own.
In June 2026, the argument stopped belonging to me and a handful of other witnesses.
The U.S. 11th Circuit ruled that Alabama’s nitrogen protocol presents a substantial risk of serious harm over and above death itself.
Judge Emily Marks then entered an order permanently barring Alabama from using the protocol against Jeffery Lee. The Supreme Court did not clear the way for the execution to proceed.
The federal district court found that a man under the mask through the use of nitrogen experiences air hunger. Panic, dread, suffering the court described as capable of being worse than pain. It placed the duration as being too long in minutes.
Minutes were enough for the federal courts.
I watched Anthony Boyd fight for 19.
Those who celebrate the Lee ruling should first understand how he won. Under current Eighth Amendment doctrine, a condemned man cannot simply prove that the state’s method tortures him. He must also provide evidence of a better way to kill him. Lee did. He proposed the firing squad.
The court found the firing squad feasible, readily implemented and a significant reduction of the risk. That finding is why the injunction was issued.
One of the most consequential execution method rulings in modern American history was won by a man who had to volunteer to be shot to death.
Now put that beside Mississippi’s list – injection, gas, electrical current, bullets. Four ways to reach one result, kept on the shelf so that losing one method never stops the process. The state is not asking which method is right. The state is asking which method survives.
That is not lawmaking. That is inventory.
Mississippi should strike nitrogen from the list.
Let’s be honest about what that accomplishes. Strike nitrogen and three methods remain. The chair does not go anywhere. The firing squad does not go anywhere. Mississippi would have removed one instrument from a cabinet stocked precisely so that the loss of an instrument changes nothing.
Strike it anyway.
A law can remain on the books long after the world that produced it has disappeared. Mississippi has already demonstrated that. Mississippi rejected the 13th Amendment, banning slavery in December 1865. It did not ratify it until 1995, 130 years later. The federal government did not formally record that ratification until 2013. Nobody in 1995 believed they were defending slavery. The thing simply sat there.
There is no reason to let nitrogen become another piece of legal residue waiting for someone else to remove it.
Repeal nitrogen now.

The Rev. Jeff Hood is a nationally recognized priest, theologian and founder of the Execution Intervention Project. As a spiritual adviser to death row inmates nationwide, he has accompanied 13  men to their executions, including the first and eighth nitrogen hypoxia executions. Widely regarded as the leading spiritual voice on the death penalty, his work has been profiled in outlets ranging from the New York Times to the Rolling Stone documentary, “The Spiritual Advisor.”  For his service, he was nominated for the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize.

title: In reversal, Vermont Supreme Court allows Gov. Scott to enforce in-person work for state employees
description:
The order, a reversal of the state labor board’s decision, comes after a monthslong legal battle between Gov. Phil Scott’s administration and the Vermont State Employees’ Association.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  In reversal, Vermont Supreme Court allows Gov. Scott to enforce in-person work for state employees.
text:
Justice Nancy Waples speaks as the Vermont Supreme Court meets in Montpelier on Thursday, June 18, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
The Vermont Supreme Court sided with Gov. Phil Scott’s administration Friday, allowing the governor to order state employees to return to in-person work.
Friday’s unanimous decision reversed an April 1 order by the Vermont Labor Relations Board, which required the state to “rescind” a partial return-to-office mandate for state employees and repay staff for various costs associated with in-person work. Gov. Phil Scott quickly appealed the matter to the state’s highest court, issuing a scathing critique of the labor board itself, and the case saw oral arguments in June.
Last August, Scott’s administration announced employees would need to return to their worksites at least three days per week. The governor has argued that in-office work would improve collaboration between workers and make state government more accessible to constituents. 
Leaders in the Vermont State Employees’ Association have long said the return-to-office mandate would impose an inappropriate burden on its members, and that Scott’s administration has failed to bargain in good faith over the policy. Many state staff had begun working from home during the Covid-19 pandemic.
“The Governor’s assessment of the operating needs of his administration was reasonable, and it is not up to this Court to assess the wisdom of that decision,” said Friday’s order from the state Supreme Court.
This story will be updated.
