title: Vermont pick-your-own orchards’ success depends on the weather
description:
“We became marketers and entertainers,” a state apple expert said. “Pumpkin patch runners and corn maze makers.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont pick-your-own orchards’ success depends on the weather.
text:
Signs guiding the way through Chapin Orchard. Photo captured on Tuesday, Sep. 22, 2026. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger.
ESSEX JUNCTION — The Murdock family spends money on their apple trees all year long.
They have about eight days to earn it back.
At Chapin Orchard in Essex Junction, as at pick-your-own-apple orchards across Vermont, the year typically comes down to four weekends from late September into early October. When the sun is out, the parking lots fill.
When it isn’t, the apples wait, and sometimes they fall. 
“I can have the most beautiful crop,” Phil Murdock said. “But if people aren’t here to pick it, frankly, it’s going to end up on the ground.”
In the past two decades, pick-your-own apple orchards have blossomed across Vermont, where apples rank third in agricultural revenue behind the state’s more signature dairy and maple syrup industries. 
Still, these businesses operate at the mercy of New England’s fall weather. Even a few rainy days can tilt the balance, determining the success or failure of the entire year.
Though they’ve lost a few profitable days to rain, this year has been decent so far, Murdock said. But the season’s outcome is still uncertain.
Despite a frost that came at a critical point in April, Terry Bradshaw, chair of the Department of Agriculture, Landscape and Environment at University of Vermont, said the apple trees this season are in good shape.
“We’ve had just the right amount of moisture,” Bradshaw said. “If we had too much moisture, we end up with disease problems, and we aren’t really having a lot of that. So it’s just been a generally good year.”
Vermont pick-your-own orchards entered their peak season last weekend, which will last until mid-October. Murdock said his trees are primed for pick-your-own activities this year.
“This year we’re going to pick-your-own right through the end of October because hopefully it’s going to be 65 and sunny right through Halloween.”
An agritourism pivot
Vermont’s apple industry has always been a prominent agricultural moneymaker, Bradshaw said. The majority of apples grown in Vermont were shipped to other places 30 years ago, he said, but things started to shift at the turn of the century, leaving Vermont wholesale apples in the dust.
For one, the apple farming industry became more mechanized, Bradshaw said. Larger apple industries set up shop in places with different topography, since large-scale farming machinery is more difficult to operate on Vermont’s hilly terrain.
“When we started to lose our foothold in the national and even international market back in the mid ’90s, the capital wasn’t there for farmers to switch over to these new systems,” Bradshaw said.
It’s difficult to fight against economies of scale, Bradshaw said, so many apple farms began a pivot towards agritourism in the form of pick-your-own apple orchards. The pick-your-own orchards make their profits on apples that customers pick fresh from their trees. 

Phil Murdock stands in front of the Chapin Orchard barn on Tuesday, Sep. 22, 2026. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger.

Often, the orchards also offer apple cider, cider donuts and other local products for sale, as well as offering hay rides and other activities, as is the case at Chapin Orchard.
“We became marketers and entertainers,” Bradshaw said. “Pumpkin patch runners and corn maze makers.”
The transitioning to pick-your-own orchards, along with fresh orchards that sprung up in the past two decades, have created places for Vermonters to gather. Murdock sees multiple generations of the same families, and parents who came as children often bring their kids to his orchard decades later.
For Dan Bair, who owns Peck Farm Orchard in East Montpelier with his wife Leila, their pick-your-own orchard has become a “community resource.”
“Our unwritten rule [is] come here, turn your phone off, stay together,” Bair said. “So just create memories and enjoy yourself.” 
‘Not for the faint of heart’ 
The downside of the new business model is the temperamental nature of the weather, Murdock said. With such a short season, even the chance of rain can have a dramatic impact on business, Murdock said.
Murdock saw this phenomenon in action on a recent Sunday.
“It never rained,” Murdock said. “It was a decent day, but there was raindrops on the forecast. We did half the business on Sunday than we did on Saturday just because of the forecast.”
Luckily, Bair said, a loyal customer base can serve as a lifeline because some pickers come out despite the weather.
“At a certain point, people need to pick apples,” Bair said.

Dan Bair makes cider donuts inside his shop at Peck Farm Orchard on Wednesday, Sep. 23 2026.

All agricultural businesses deal with chance and loss, Bair said. Three years ago a huge frost swept over Bair’s orchard. He thought the entire apple crop would be lost, though he managed to salvage around 60%. 
Agriculture is “not for the faint of heart,” Bair said.
“There’s a farmer down the road, and I’ve seen him in the face of [a] barn fire, and he’s completely relaxed,” Bair added. “I didn’t understand it until you become a farmer and you experience a lot of loss. Once you do, you begin to just take it day by day.”
But there’s only so many losses a business can take when it makes its yearly income in eight days, Murdock said. The cost of growing apples — encompassing fuel costs for farm machinery, labor costs, and maintenance and repair costs of farm infrastructure and equipment — builds with each month of the year. The rising cost of fuel has a huge impact on farm operations, Murdock said, since they use it to power their mowers, tractors, cars and other machinery. 
Most of their prices have stayed steady, Murdock said, but higher operating costs mean the business brings in less revenue. There’s very little margin for error.
“We’re spending it all year round,” Murdock said, “but we stop bringing it in November 1.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont pick-your-own orchards’ success depends on the weather.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Tom Emmer is running cover for Don Jr.
description: On Wednesday, House Majority Whip Tom Emmer dismissed a proposed Senate investigation of the president’s eldest son. “Some senators want to waste time creating a new Russia hoax and attacking Don Jr.,” Emmer wrote. “Don Jr. is a private citizen and businessman so this unwarranted attack will go nowhere. This partisan distraction is NOT what […]
text:
U.S. House Majority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer (R-MN) speaks during a news conference on the results of the 2024 election outside of the U.S. Capitol Building on November 12, 2024 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)On Wednesday, House Majority Whip Tom Emmer dismissed a proposed Senate investigation of the president’s eldest son.
“Some senators want to waste time creating a new Russia hoax and attacking Don Jr.,” Emmer wrote. “Don Jr. is a private citizen and businessman so this unwarranted attack will go nowhere. This partisan distraction is NOT what the American people voted for!”
The request came from Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah. This week he asked Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, and ranking member Dick Durbin, D-Illinois, to investigate “the use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit.” 
Republican Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, both on the committee, said they would support an inquiry, and Durbin joined them in calling for an investigation. Grassley said he needed more facts.
Curtis asked for subpoenas of both Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden. Emmer’s post mentions only Trump Jr., even though he has frequently called for investigations into Hunter Biden.
What prompted it?
On Sept. 14, ProPublica reported that Umar Kremlev, a Russian businessman close to Russian President Vladimir Putin, paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward Trump Jr.’s May wedding celebrations in the Bahamas, including a private island rental and fireworks. Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, confirmed it and called it a gift from a friend. President Trump said his son had paid Kremlev back.
Curtis summed up his case on X: “A toaster is a wedding gift.”
Beyond the wedding
Kremlev’s payment isn’t the first Trump Jr. deal to draw scrutiny during his father’s second term.
Prediction markets. Curtis’ letter cites Trump Jr.’s ties to the country’s two largest prediction markets. Kalshi pays him as an adviser and gave him equity. 1789 Capital, the venture firm where he is a partner, committed $300 million to a recent funding round for Polymarket, where he is also an adviser. Both companies are ostensibly regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and the administration has sided with them in court as states — including Minnesota — try to shut them down as illegal gambling.
Defense contracts. Companies backed by 1789 won more than $735 million in federal contracts in 2025, according to the Financial Times. Rare-earth magnet maker Vulcan Elements got a $620 million Pentagon loan three months after 1789 invested. ProPublica reported that the push for the deal came directly from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro; 1789 said it played no role. Unusual Machines, a Florida drone-parts maker that made Trump Jr. an adviser and gave him shares, landed its largest Army order.
Other ventures. The family’s crypto company, World Liberty Financial, sold a 49% stake for $500 million to a firm backed by the United Arab Emirates’ national security adviser four days before the inauguration. And he and his brother Eric Trump bought into a company tied to a $1.6 billion, administration-backed tungsten mining project in Kazakhstan, though the Financial Times found no evidence they knew of the contract when they invested.
What Emmer said about the last president’s son
In November 2023, after Hunter Biden offered to participate in public testimony instead of a closed deposition, Emmer told Fox Business: “If you’ve done nothing wrong, you have nothing to hide.” He added: “And if the Biden family is exonerated, so be it.”
On Dec. 13, 2023, the day Hunter Biden skipped his subpoenaed deposition, Emmer posted: “Hunter Biden’s father may be able to control the DOJ investigation, but the Biden family won’t dictate the terms of Congress’ investigation.” Later that day he voted to formalize the impeachment inquiry into President Joe Biden.
On Jan. 17, 2024, Emmer said House Republicans would “hold Hunter Biden’s feet to the fire until we have his testimony.” NPR reported that he added: “No one, not even the president’s son, is above the law.”
In January 2024, Hunter Biden held no office. He was a private citizen and a businessman, much like Don Jr. is officially today.
How partisan is it?
A Republican senator made the request for the Trump Jr. investigation, backed by two Republicans and the ranking Democrat on the committee. A Republican chairman will decide.
“The country should not have to accept one standard for the family of a Republican president and another for the family of a Democratic president,” Curtis wrote.
Where there is a difference
The 2023-24 investigation was formally an impeachment inquiry into a sitting president. Hunter Biden was a witness in it, not its target. The question was whether Joe Biden took official action or benefited from his family’s foreign business, and in December 2023 Emmer said it was “very likely he benefited.” Hunter Biden also defied two subpoenas before sitting for a deposition on Feb. 28, 2024.
None of that applies to Trump Jr. so far. He has not been subpoenaed and no one has alleged that President Trump took official action on Kremlev’s behalf. Sens. Bernie Moreno and Jim Banks argue that Trump Jr. holds no administration role and that there is no evidence he sold access.
Why there is a difference
Most of that difference comes down to who holds power, not what actually happened.
Hunter Biden was a witness in an impeachment inquiry because the House majority in 2023 belonged to the Republican Party. That majority opened the inquiry and issued the subpoenas. Emmer voted for it.
Today, Republicans control the House, the Senate and every committee. Democrats cannot open an inquiry or issue a subpoena. In March, when Democrats on the House Natural Resources Committee moved to subpoena Trump Jr. over the Vulcan deal, Republicans voted to adjourn.
So “no one has subpoenaed him” and “no one has opened an inquiry” are the same fact. Evidence of wrongdoing cannot be found if no one is looking for it. Curtis’ letter asks Republicans to use their power and look. It doesn’t predetermine an outcome. Emmer’s post argues they shouldn’t even look, opposite arguments he’s made in the past, about Hunter Biden.
The same standard
Curtis wants the committee to examine “any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value.” That is essentially the question House Republicans asked about the Biden family in 2023.
Emmer, whose reelection opponent this year in the 6th District is Doug Chapin, has applied the “nothing to hide” standard well beyond the Bidens. He said the Clintons should be held in contempt over the Epstein subpoenas, and that Rep. Ilhan Omar’s husband “should be subpoenaed.” This year he has told three interviewers that if Minnesota had nothing to hide, it would hand its voter records to the federal government, even though the Justice Department has lost all 25 of its voter-roll lawsuits against states decided so far, Minnesota’s among them.
His broadcast transcripts and posts show him calling for subpoenas of private citizens. We found none in which he argued, before Wednesday, that a private citizen should be spared congressional scrutiny.
The question
In January 2024, Emmer said no one, not even the president’s son, is above the law. A Republican senator is now asking Congress to apply Emmer’s stated standard to both a Republican and Democratic president’s sons.
Does the majority whip still think it applies when it’s the son of the president of his own party or does it only apply to people across the aisle?

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky’s newest medical school aims to keep doctors in state
description: This story was first published in The Edge. Doctors who train in Kentucky will practice in Kentucky. That’s the thinking behind Eastern Kentucky University’s plan to build a medical school at its main campus in Richmond to help address a shortage of primary care and other physicians statewide. The first class of EKU-trained doctors is […]
text:
Eastern Kentucky University is starting a college of osteopathic medicine.(EKU photo)This story was first published in The Edge.
Doctors who train in Kentucky will practice in Kentucky.
That’s the thinking behind Eastern Kentucky University’s plan to build a medical school at its main campus in Richmond to help address a shortage of primary care and other physicians statewide. The first class of EKU-trained doctors is expected to graduate in the Fall of 2035.
“EKU doesn’t need a medical school to be a successful university,” EKU President David McFaddin told The Edge in an interview. “But adding a medical school to a successful institution with over 120 years of really outstanding educational outcomes — I think it is as sure of a thing as you can get, to say it’s going to make a positive difference in our communities and in our state.” 
Statewide physician shortage
There are 6,335 primary care physicians across the commonwealth, according to KFF, a health policy research nonprofit based in San Francisco, Calif., but nearly all of Kentucky’s 120 counties need more doctors.
“In real terms, that might as well be 100% [of counties],” Dustin Devers, DO, Chair of EKU’s proposed College of Osteopathic Medicine Advisory Committee, told The Edge in an interview. “They all feel it. Even the 6% [of counties] that may not fall into that category, they still feel it. It is an overburden to the physicians who are in those communities already. Everything suffers when there’s a lack of physicians.”
A report from state health and family services issued last year, claims that by 2030, Kentucky will need 3,000 more doctors, including specialists, to meet the state’s growing gap in care, driven in part by older physicians retiring, and also partly by shifts in population centers.
EKU President David McFaddin. (EKU photo)
To address the crisis, a new state law went into effect this summer, loosening regulations on licensure of foreign-trained physicians in the hopes of enticing them to practice in Kentucky, particularly in the most rural areas of the state where physician shortages are most keenly felt.
That’s against a backdrop of a coming nationwide shortage of primary care physicians. The shortage is expected to reach more than 86,000 just a decade from now, according to a report from the American Association of Medical Colleges.
Devers says he believes that doctors who train in Kentucky are more likely to stay here to pursue their careers. Survey data from the AAMC support Dever’s observation. That organization found that 55.7% of those who completed their residency from 2015 to 2024 stayed in the state where they trained. In Kentucky, it’s about half and half: during those same years, 50.8% of those who completed their residency in-state continued to practice here. That’s up from 42% in 2023.
Devers, originally from Alabama, is one of those doctors who stayed in the commonwealth after graduation. A family medicine physician with the Baptist Health Medical Group in Richmond, he received his degree from the Kentucky College of Osteopathic Medicine at the University of Pikeville in 2004.
EKU’s program will award a medical degree known as a DO–a Doctor of Osteopathy. Physicians with DOs are licensed the same way as physicians with an MD–Medical Doctor—degree. The difference between the two has narrowed over time, but is centered on differing philosophies. Those with DOs take a “whole-person” approach, while those with MDs are trained to think in terms of “specialties”. Both traditions are evidence-based.
“Regionally, [osteopathic medicine] probably makes more sense simply because most osteopathic schools have a heavy emphasis on primary care,” said Devers.
‘Only so many seats’
Another limiting factor on meeting the state’s need for primary care is that there are only so many available seats for up-and-coming physicians. This means EKU is poised to help expand the number of opportunities for doctors to train and stay in the commonwealth.
In 2024, the combined number of medical students that graduated in Kentucky was 464, according to KFF. The three medical training programs currently in the state include Devers’ alma mater at the University of Pikeville, the University of Kentucky College of Medicine, and the School of Medicine at the University of Louisville.
“EKU is doing a great job in educating a lot of healthcare professionals, but ‘physician’ is not [currently] one of those things,” McFaddin said in the interview.
At present, multiple health science degrees are available from EKU’s College of Health Sciences, including in nursing, environmental and public health, administration and medical sciences, occupational science/occupational therapy, and exercise and other sports sciences.
“We graduate a lot of healthcare professionals who leave here with undergraduate, graduate and doctoral degrees,” McFaddin said.
Having a fully accredited medical school on campus will tie together all of the many health science degree programs into one setting, similar to the real world where EKU graduates will eventually practice, he said.
Frankfort’s blessing
State lawmakers have already earmarked $50 million for EKU’s osteopathic medicine program, although $42 million is still in escrow, according to Brad Hall, EKU’s Chief Medical Strategic Partnership Officer.
“We’re really fortunate that they have leaned in with us on this project and appropriated those dollars,” said Hall. “Those will put us ahead of the game.” 
Hall said there are still some internal processes to go through with academic programs and approvals, including notifying accrediting agencies, including the Commission on Osteopathic College Accreditation and asking to be approved for national accreditation.
“We’ve gone through the Council of Postsecondary Education with an initial curriculum and the program approval,” said Hall. “Now we’re working on a building, facilities, whether that’s new or a remodel, we’re still assessing.” 
Hall said the next steps are to use the available $8 million in state funds to get the medical school accredited and to recruit a dean and associate dean. Meanwhile, combining all health science degree programs into one centralized so-called “health innovation center” is another top priority through 2028.
Leaders in Frankfort also have already amended the relevant state statute to allow EKU to offer the doctor of osteopathic medicine degree required for licensure.  
McFaddin said that although previously in his career he has worked with state policymakers, helping bring the medical school to fruition is the first time he has engaged Frankfort in something so “transformational”.
“The legislative support is so tremendous because it means that, one, they acknowledge what we’ve seen, and two, that they believe in what we’re doing and that they believe that we can do it,” McFaddin said.
Whitney McKnight contributed to this story.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Planned Parenthood files legal challenge to investigation, document demands by Tennessee AG
description: Planned Parenthood of Tennessee and North Mississippi petitioned a Nashville court on Wednesday to set aside a sweeping legal demand by Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti to turn over the organization’s donor details, healthcare provider information and the medical records of adult and minor patients. The legal petition, filed in Davidson County Ch[...]
text:
Planned Parenthood of Tennessee and North Mississippi clinic in Memphis. (Photo: courtesy of Planned Parenthood of Tennessee and North Mississippi.)Planned Parenthood of Tennessee and North Mississippi petitioned a Nashville court on Wednesday to set aside a sweeping legal demand by Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti to turn over the organization’s donor details, healthcare provider information and the medical records of adult and minor patients.
The legal petition, filed in Davidson County Chancery Court, makes public for the first time the existence of an ongoing and wide-ranging investigation into the nonprofit operator of four Tennessee clinics. Since the state’s 2022 abortion ban, the organization has ceased offering abortions as part of its healthcare service; instead, it offers information and referrals to pregnant patients seeking abortions outside of Tennessee. 
In a Sept. 3 demand letter, Skrmetti appeared to target those post-abortion-ban services. The letter said the state “ had reason to believe” the organization had engaged in multiple violations of state law. Among Skrmetti’s demands are for the Planned Parenthood affiliate to turn over all documents, emails, and communications connected to “any person you assisted, helped or are otherwise aware of” who obtained abortion pills in the mail or via telemedicine. 
Earlier this week, Abortion Care Tennessee revealed it is also the subject of a similar demand letter and investigation by the attorney general that seeks extensive internal documents regarding the delivery of medication abortion by mail. Abortion Care Tennessee provides information and funding to Tennessee patients seeking abortions.
Skrmetti’s demand letter to Planned Parenthood also seeks records of patients treated for gender dysphoria or gender identity disorders, including the records of more than a dozen individuals identified by name whose individual clinical records are being sought as part of the probe. The patient names are redacted in a copy of the demand letter entered into court records. 
The 17-page demand letter also seeks “all medical records and files for any minors for whom you provided, administered or offered to provide or administer any cross-sex hormones…puberty blockers or related drugs or treatments after July 1, 2023” — the date Tennessee’s ban on gender-affirming healthcare for minors took effect. 
Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti is demanding patient records, among other documents, from Planned Parenthood of Tennessee and Northern Mississippi. (Photo: John Partipilo)
Planned Parenthood has never offered gender-affirming to minors, its legal petition said. It has also never provided abortion care via telehealth, a practice outlawed by Tennessee lawmakers in 2022.
In its legal petition, lawyers for Planned Parenthood called Skrmetti’s demands “unlawful,” “intrusive,” and an attack on its free speech rights to offer accurate information about abortion. It described the demands as the newest iteration in years of “hostility” directed against the organization by state leaders, citing multiple policy decisions that eliminated portions of the affiliate’s funding and legislation that has impacted its service. 
It also quoted disparaging comments from senior state political leaders, including Gov. Bill Lee, who called Planned Parenthood a “radical political organization.” 
The petition characterized the attorney general’s demand for internal documents, emails, patient pamphlets, patient records, mental health evaluation letters, healthcare provider credentials, donor records and other records as both a direct assault on the organization’s free speech rights and a prospective one, intended to chill speech going forward. 
In a written statement on Friday, Planned Parenthood of Tennessee and North Mississippi CEO Ashley Coffield called Skrmetti’s investigation “politically motivated” and “deeply disturbing.”
“Attorney General Skrmetti is targeting Tennesseans across the state for seeking or getting essential health care services,” she said. 
“This is an obvious effort to further a political agenda to ban abortion, intimidate patients and providers, and shut down Planned Parenthood health centers, while violating the privacy of patients who have sought sexual and reproductive health care.”
A statement from Skrmetti on Friday said, “this office has the authority to request information when there may be a violation of state law that we enforce, and we routinely do so. A request for information lets us gather facts to determine whether further steps are necessary.”
The statement also said the attorney general would not comment on any “specific matter and will respond to any legal filings through the court.”
The demand letter 
Skrmetti’s demand letter begins by saying he has “reason to believe that Planned Parenthood is engaging in, has engaged in, or is about to engage in” multiple violations of state law. It cites the Consumer Protection Act, the Medicaid False Claims Act, the Tennessee Nonprofit Corporations Act and laws that bar gender-affirming care for minors and the prescribing and delivery of medication abortions through the mail. 
The letter cites legal penalties for noncompliance,  and instructs Planned Parenthood to provide 16 sets of documents and nine written statements, under oath, for the time period beginning Feb. 1, 2022 to the present, including:

“All documents and communications regarding any person you assisted, helped, or are otherwise aware of who obtained abortion pills via the mail, delivery service, express company, common carrier, or telemedicine, including but not limited to any handouts, pamphlets, emails or other documents intended to be given to patients, potential patients or other persons”
“All patient records and files for the persons listed in Appendix 2. Such records should include, but are not limited to, clinical records, medical reports, charge entry sheets, office notes, pre-authorization forms and documentation of care, and any “progress notes.’” The names of individuals listed in Appendix 2 are redacted in court filings.”
“All mental health letters prepared by mental health professionals that diagnose the persons listed in Appendix 2 with Gender Dysphoria or Gender Identity Disorder.”
“All documents referring to, describing, or relating to the scope of practice of the medical professionals described below.” The names of the medical professionals are redacted in court filings.
“All medical records and files for any minors for whom you provided, administered or offered to provide or administer any cross-sex hormones (including testosterone or estrogen), puberty blockers or related drugs or treatments after July 1, 2023.”
“Identify under oath all pregnant women or other persons whom you assisted in obtaining abortion pills via mail, delivery services, express company, common carrier or telemedicine that were intended to be or were actually used to terminate a pregnancy.”
“Identify your employees, officers, or agents who are responsible for the content of your website.”

The petition asks the Chancery Court to issue a protective order that sets aside the demands entirely or modifies the attorney general’s request.
“The First Amendment requires this court to set aside the (demands),” the petition said. It also cited patient privacy.
“Its demand that (Planned Parenthood) disclose its patients’ private health information contravenes (its) legal duties, basic medical ethics, and the privacy rights of patients. The court should set it aside.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New Haven alders advance proposal urging Yale to reject potential Trump deal
description: Alders on New Haven's Health & Human Services Committee endorsed a proposal calling on Yale not to strike a settlement with US Department of Justice.
text:
Three dozen Yale students, professors, and New Haven community members testified before the aldermanic Health & Human Services Committee Thursday evening — and called on Yale to uphold its institutional independence, contribute more to its host city, and reject a potential settlement with the Trump administration over the university’s admissions policies.
Ultimately, the committee alders — Kampton Singh, Frank Douglass, Theresa Morant, Frank Redente, Sarah Miller, and Elias Theodore — favorably endorsed a proposal calling on Yale not to strike such a settlement with the U.S. Department of Justice. The item now heads to the full Board of Alders for further review and a final vote.
The resolution — “Urging Yale University to Defend its Institutional Autonomy” — was authored by Theodore, who represents Downtown/Yale’s Ward 1.
The resolution is an “opportunity to say clearly that we are not about what’s happening in Washington, and we don’t support any effort to succumb to pressure here,” said Fair Haven Alder and Committee Vice Chair Sarah Miller.
“I’ve been really proud of New Haven standing up in very meaningful ways,” she said. The city is currently involved in six ongoing lawsuits against the Trump administration.  
A coalition of students, led by Theodore among others, have been campaigning against the potential settlement since June. Yale President Maurie McInnis confirmed in July that the university was in talks with the DOJ, but has not released any more information about the potential settlement since. 
“It is Yale’s longstanding practice not to discuss the specifics of any ongoing legal matter,” a Yale spokesperson told the Independent. “That said, Yale is committed to following the law and has continued to provide information to the DOJ regarding our admissions processes as required. Yale’s commitment to academic freedom is absolute and its admissions and hiring decisions will continue to be made independently and in accordance with the law.”
Although Theodore said he had invited both McInnis and Associate Vice President for New Haven Affairs and University Properties Alexandra Daum, no representatives from Yale attended Thursday’s hearing. 
In opening testimony, Theodore said that, “throughout this second Trump term, New Haven has protected our most vulnerable residents and our city’s values, even when doing so came with significant financial or political risks.”
He continued, “it is disappointing that Yale, an institution that should stand up with its host city and be a partner in this fight, is preparing to cut a deal with an administration whose actions have raised serious concerns among so many in our community.”
In their testimonies, under three minutes each, undergraduate students as well as students from the law and medical schools demanded that Yale uphold its values and institutional independence, while New Haven residents and local-labor representatives from New Haven Rising and Local 34 reprimanded the university for considering paying out a settlement when it could contribute more to the city.
“There is plenty of money,” said Local 34 Vice President and former Wooster Square Alder Ellen Cupo, saying Yale should “stop blaming the federal government for university austerity,” mentioning cuts to staff size and budget. Yale College Dean Pericles Lewis announced Thursday there would be no new cuts this year, according to reporting from the Yale Daily News. Yale increased its voluntary contribution to New Haven by $5 million per year in March.
“We know that settlements at other universities have come with enormous Treasury payments,” said Conor Webb, a Yale junior. “Brown paid $50 million. Northwestern, $75 million. Columbia, over $200 million dollars. It’s not hard to imagine a Yale settlement in this range. How big might our blank check be? I want that money to go to New Haven. I want it to be used to defend the community violence intervention programs this city relies on.”
Apart from the 37 people who testified in front of the committee on Thursday , another dozen professors, policymakers, and alders submitted written testimony via email. 
“Under the Trump administration, my immigrant friends fear to speak their minds lest they be targeted as other immigrant students have,” Yale junior Claire Newman wrote. 
“These fears, and the dampening effects they have on free expression, crucial research, and education will grow far, far worse if the University allows its policies to be dictated in any way by the Trump administration.”
Although they did not attend the hearing, U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro and U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal both submitted testimony to the committee on Thursday, redoubling their support of students and professors protesting the potential settlement. “Giving into a bully is not how you make them go away. It is exactly what empowers them. It invites them back for more,” DeLauro wrote in her statement. 
“Demonstrating that the governing body of Yale’s hometown will back them in their fight against USDOJ aggression—such as passage of this resolution—would send another powerful message to Yale’s leadership,” Blumenthal wrote. “Our opposition is based on our deep abiding respect and concern for Yale’s independence.”
This story was first published Sept. 25, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska childcare advocates press for major state investment, policy changes to fill growing gaps
description: Alaska childcare providers, families and employers are under intense strain with the lack of childcare availability and funding, according to advocates. They are calling for major state investment in the childcare industry and seeking policy changes under the next governor and Alaska State Legislature. Leaders with several non-profit groups held an online we[...]
text:
Preschoolers play in the snowmelt at Hillcrest Children's Center in Anchorage on April 18, 2024. (Photo by Claire Stremple/Alaska Beacon)Alaska childcare providers, families and employers are under intense strain with the lack of childcare availability and funding, according to advocates. They are calling for major state investment in the childcare industry and seeking policy changes under the next governor and Alaska State Legislature.
Leaders with several non-profit groups held an online webinar Wednesday focused on barriers and potential solutions to what they called “Alaska’s childcare desert,” which included advocates with the Alaska Children’s Trust, Southeast Childhood Collective and thread, an Anchorage-based resource and referral organization. 
Advocates described a patchwork funding system of federal, state and some local municipal grants for childcare providers, which has resulted in a lack of childcare spaces to meet demand, long waitlists, high costs for families and a lack of qualified childcare providers, who also work for low pay. 
“It’s a battle right now,” said Candice Vialpando, marketing and communications director with thread. “But every little bit helps, and every bucket of money that we are getting, we’re just putting out into the field to try and help, and keep programs open.”
Alaska has seen a wave of childcare centers close in recent years. Last year, one of Anchorage’s largest childcare facilities, Bright Beginnings Learning Center, closed due to rising costs and a shortage of workers, displacing 125 children and 35 staff. Since 2019, 25% of childcare facilities have closed, according to thread. 
The organization estimates 50% of Alaskan families cannot fully participate in the workforce because they lack access to childcare. They estimate the average cost Alaska parents pay is nearly $14,000 per year per child.  
Advocates are pushing legislators and state political candidates to make childcare a priority in this election. 
“Alaska is a childcare desert,” said Blue Shibler, executive director of the Southeast Childhood Collective, which provides resource, funding and workforce development support throughout Southeast Alaska. “The good news is, advocates like us on here have been working for years on this issue, and there is quite a bit of framework systems development that could turn all of that around pretty quickly.” 
She said that the state could make big changes quickly if a new executive branch and motivated legislators were open to their policy and funding ideas. 
Shibler said childcare providers are struggling to recruit childcare workers and pay liveable wages, which can result in long wait lists for care. 
“Childcare providers cannot charge families enough money to pay competitive wages in this labor market, and so they’re limited at how many kids they can take based on that,” she said. “So we’re working to improve that.”
This year, the Legislature approved $6.4 million to help boost pay and retain childcare workers, but Gov. Mike Dunleavy vetoed it. 
“That really hurt us,” Vialpando said.
Dunleavy also vetoed Legislature-approved increases of $355,000 to the family support program Parents as Teachers, a $3.7 million increase for Head Start programs and a $3 million increase for infant learning programs to support children with developmental delays or disabilities.  
A spokesperson for the Dunleavy administration, Jeff Turner, said by email Thursday that “substantial funding was provided,” for childcare. He pointed to the governor’s approvals in this year’s budget for $13 million in Head Start grants, $475,000 for Parents as Teachers and $12.3 million for early intervention and infant learning programs.
“Governor Dunleavy also proposed legislation for funding and opportunities to expand workforce training, unfortunately the legislature chose not to pass his legislation,” Turner said, referring to a bill that would have expanded the unemployment insurance trust fund.
State assistance grants, licensing and economic impacts
For state childcare assistance grants that are paid out to providers and families, Vialpando described issues with delayed payments, which can cause children to lose their spots. 
Vialpando said one issue is if families miss renewal dates, they have to reapply for assistance all over again. “It’s not just a quick renewal. It’s like a whole new application period, which takes a very long time,” she said. 
“And during that application period, they’re not getting assistance, so their childcare provider is not getting paid, so they don’t have care for their child during that time. And it’s like, does this person care for the kid without getting paid? Does the child stay home?” she said. “It’s a really bad effect that is happening, so I think that needs to be addressed: prompt payment.”
Officials with the Alaska Department of Health did not respond to a request for comment on state assistance delays on Thursday. 
Nonprofit groups are working to boost childcare worker support and professional development opportunities, including apprenticeship programs, and helping new providers with licensing and regulatory standards for new childcare programs. 
Shibler and others said providers continue to struggle with licensing issues and regulatory hurdles, and the Department of Health could do more to ease the strain.
“A lot of the licensing regulations are just really old and outdated. They just need a review,” she said. “To figure out how many of these are really important to maintain health, safety, and quality, and which ones are just sort of extra that we don’t need to be dealing with and putting on providers.”
With support from an Anchorage initiative directing marijuana tax revenue to the Anchorage Child Care and Early Education Fund, Vialpando said thread is able to provide some childcare providers with healthcare benefits. “Which is huge in a sector where people do not have healthcare,” she said. 
Teresa Wrobel, director of policy and advocacy, Alaska Children’s Trust noted childcare is becoming a priority issue for employers, as there’s a loss of hours as employees need to tend to childcare needs. She and others acknowledged lack of childcare is a major factor in some families leaving Alaska.  
Wrobel emphasized the Alaska Children’s Trust – which is focused on reducing child abuse and neglect — is advocating to address childcare issues to help alleviate stress on families. “Neglect happens with families when there is stress in the family, and we just know that childcare is one of those methods that can reduce stress on the family,” she said. 
Shibler and others expressed hope that future state leaders will address the state’s growing childcare gap. 
“So there’s all these little band-aids out there, you know, trying to fix the problem because nobody wants to take off the big bite, which is we really need to invest $50 million into a compensation system in Alaska,” Shibler said. 
“Childcare is a public good: it needs a public subsidy,” she said. “We subsidize public goods all the time. We’re just not doing it for childcare for some reason.”
