name: Kansas Reflector
title: Foster care official says Kansas should be ‘laser focused’ on Wichita’s placement crisis
description: TOPEKA — Kansas’s top foster care official said the state should be “laser focused” on Wichita to improve a youth placement measure that has consistently fallen short of court-ordered standards.  Foster care contractors in Sedgwick County, where Wichita is located, have continuously struggled to place children in housing instead of offices or unlicensed beds[...]
text:
Laura Howard, secretary of the Kansas Department for Children and Families, speaks at a June 10, 2025 hearing before the Senate Committee on Government Efficiency. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas’s top foster care official said the state should be “laser focused” on Wichita to improve a youth placement measure that has consistently fallen short of court-ordered standards. 
Foster care contractors in Sedgwick County, where Wichita is located, have continuously struggled to place children in housing instead of offices or unlicensed beds. Since 2024, numbers have deteriorated.
Laura Howard, secretary of the Kansas Department for Children and Families, told a legislative committee that in 2025 the “failure to place” metric worsened for the second year in a row in Sedgwick County. It appears on track to do the same in 2026. Failure to place refers to how often foster care contractors let kids sleep in an unlicensed environment.
She reviewed for the committee a recently released independent report that analyzed the entire state foster care system’s performance based on measures set by a court-mandated settlement agreement, which requires the state to seek better outcomes for foster children in 10 categories.
According to the report released Wednesday that analyzed 2025 data, 136 children spent a cumulative 870 nights without a proper place to stay in Kansas, and 94% of those were in Sedgwick County. In 2024, 100 children spent 316 nights without a placement. Again, most of those kids were in Wichita. In 2023, 57 children spent a total of 83 nights without a placement.
EmberHope Connections, the faith-based agency that took over as the state-contracted foster care organization in Sedgwick County in 2024, has struggled to make improvements, and it recently brought on a new president, Dee Nighswonger.
Numbers for 2026 show a worsening problem. Publicly available data reveal that as of Aug. 31, there have already been 1,163 nights when DCF has failed to place children. An estimated 96% of those instances were in Sedgwick County.
Howard said the state needs to be “laser focused” on Sedgwick County to address the issue, which she acknowledged is one that the state has discussed in recent years.
“I think it’s a larger issue than the case management provider and DCF,” she said.
Erica Case, an attorney for EmberHope, said Thursday that Kansas can improve its foster care system by limiting entry to children experiencing abuse, neglect or immediate safety concerns; prioritizing workforce retention; creating specialized family treatment courts for people in the criminal justice system for drug use; and expanding options for young adults with complex needs from intellectual and developmental disabilities.
The organization appears to be looking upstream, attempting to focus on solutions that can prevent children from entering foster care in the first place.
The number of kids entering care has increased in Sedgwick County almost every quarter since EmberHope took over, Case said.
“I understand that Sedgwick County is risk averse, and I’m fine with that,” Case said, “but we have to reimagine those prevention pathways to make sure that we truly are reserving out-of-home care for those that have been abused, neglected or are in immediate danger.”
The annual, court-mandated report of the state of Kansas’ foster care system showed some improvements, allowing it to be released from court supervision in four areas, pending a judge’s approval.
But Leecia Welch, chief legal counsel at Children’s Rights, said “the picture remains grim for far too many children in Kansas.”
“Defendants are failing to provide some children with even a safe place to sleep for the night, much less the stable, supportive homes they deserve,” Welch said. “In their own words, children describe ‘being treated like cattle.’

name: Mississippi Today
title: The governor awarded more than $104 million to improve rural healthcare in Mississippi. Where is the money going?
description: Gov. Tate Reeves talks about Mississippi's Rural Health Transformation Program plan during a press conference at the Walter Sillers Building in Jackson on Tuesday, Oct. 4, 2025.
text:
A handful of recipients accounted for a substantial share of the first round of federal awards to boost rural health in Mississippi, according to an analysis of funding conducted by Mississippi Today. 
Memorial Health System, based in Gulfport, received the largest share of funds — more than $15 million for 12 projects, while a consortium of hospitals in south central Mississippi received more than $13 million for seven projects. Together, the hospitals accounted for over a quarter of $104 million in grants announced by Gov. Tate Reeves on Sept. 14. 
Across all recipients, the grants will fund 167 projects to strengthen cybersecurity defenses, replace outdated computers and technology, expand access to diagnostic testing and health screenings, create new service lines and telehealth programs, implement AI-driven software and install back-up generators.
The first round represents more than half of the nearly $206 million allocated to Mississippi as a part of the initial year of the five-year, national $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. The initiative was designed to blunt the impact on struggling rural hospitals of federal spending cuts Congress passed and President Donald Trump signed into law in July 2025. 
Richard Roberson, president and CEO of the Mississippi Hospital Association, said though the initial awards spanned the state, disparities emerged in the areas and institutions allocated funding. 
There were never any targets for awards in certain counties or regions of the state, Reeves said.
“This was never going to be a top-down approach,” he said. “But rather, it is a bottom-up approach where every individual application that we received was judged on its own merit.”
An independent review panel scored proposals using a rubric that graded whether applicants’ planned to address a quantifiable need in rural healthcare and submitted a plan for implementation, budget and tracking outcomes. The panel’s recommendations were then vetted by the Mississippi State Department of Health. 
The review panel also considered how to distribute funds to ensure statewide impact and avoid duplication with other programs, according to funding notices.
Greg Flynn and Andrea Dilworth, spokespeople for the Health Department, did not respond to Mississippi Today’s questions about the application review process. Shelby Wilcher, a spokesperson for the governor, also did not respond to Mississippi’s questions.
Memorial Hospital in Gulfport, Miss., on Thursday, Sept. 18, 2025.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Awards made to Memorial Health System, a public nonprofit system, alone account for a seventh of the funds allocated for the entire state as a part of the initial three grant programs. The awards, totaling over $15 million, will fund projects that include a mobile MRI program, computer system upgrades for chemotherapy orders, new IT systems and expanded access to diagnostic testing and imaging services. It will also fund AI-enabled virtual primary, behavioral and chronic disease care services in Stone, George, Hancock, Jackson and Pearl River Counties. 
The health system operates three hospitals in Gulfport, Biloxi and Wiggins, and an array of clinics. It is jointly owned by Harrison County and the city of Gulfport.
President and CEO Kent Nicaud said in a written response to Mississippi Today that the organization made significant efforts to identify areas of need, including reviewing patient encounters to identify the services rural patients were often leaving their communities to receive, and submit thorough, actionable proposals for the grants. The health system enlisted the help of a national firm and a consultant to assist with the process. 
Kent Nicaud, president and CEO of Memorial Health System Credit: Courtesy photo
“This was never simply about pursuing grant dollars,” Nicaud said. “We were asking, ‘If we have an opportunity to rethink how care is delivered in rural South Mississippi, what can we do that will still make a difference five or 10 years from now?’”
Nicaud said that access to diagnostic testing and imaging are limited in Stone County, which has elevated rates of breast cancer and high mortality from heart disease, forcing many patients to travel outside of their communities for care. 
He added the health system’s proposals were designed to be scalable, and system administrators plan to share data and best practices learned from the initiatives with providers that want to implement similar projects in their communities. 
Nicaud serves as board chairman for the Mississippi Healthcare Collaborative, a statewide coalition of healthcare providers formed in 2024. He has contributed significantly to Reeves’ previous political campaigns, which he said did not impact how Memorial fared in the application process. 
“I did not discuss Memorial’s applications or funding requests with Governor Reeves, his office, or any state agency,” Nicaud said. 
A consortium of hospitals in south central Mississippi helmed by Gregg Gibbes also received a large portion of the initial grant awards — over $13 million for seven projects in Covington, Jones and Simpson counties. Gibbes is the CEO of South Central Regional Medical Center in Laurel, Covington County Hospital in Collins, Magee General Hospital and Simpson General Hospital in Mendenhall. Gibbes did not respond to Mississippi Today’s request for comment.
Delta Health Center, a Mound Bayou-based federally qualified health center with 17 locations, received over $5 million for five projects. The health center’s plans for the money include a 24/7 urgent and critical response center in Rosedale, patient monitoring and mobile community health workers and strengthening cybersecurity infrastructure. Robin Boyles, a spokesperson for the health center, did not respond to Mississippi Today’s request for comment. 
Baptist Memorial Health Care, which operates 14 hospitals in Mississippi, received one award worth about $1.5 million. Baptist Memorial Hospital-Calhoun, located in north central Mississippi, received the award to modernize critical IT infrastructure at Baptist hospitals in Kosciusko, Carthage, Yazoo City and a nursing home in Calhoun. 
The hospital system submitted six proposals, together worth $17.9 million, said Keith Norman, the vice president of government relations and chief community relations officer, in a written statement to Mississippi Today.
“Although we anticipated receiving a larger share of the $104.2 million available in the first funding round, the clearer criteria and lessons from the initial process should help us strengthen future proposals and expand services in communities that did not receive funding,” Norman said. “We value every community we serve, and our patients deserve equal access to modern facilities and enhancements across the state.”
Board of Health members’ organizations receive awards
Several healthcare organizations helmed by Mississippi Board of Health members received awards. The Board of Health oversees the operations of the Mississippi State Department of Health, the agency that oversaw the selection process.
Lampton Medical Associates, P.A., a Magnolia-based medical clinic led by Board of Health member Dr. Lucius Lampton, received over $2 million to modernize electronic medical records for 50 rural Mississippi healthcare practices. Lampton served as board chair until July, when Dr. James Chaney assumed the role. 
Lorie Till, the CEO of Northwest Mississippi Regional Medical Center, was appointed to the board by Reeves in July. She also serves as president of the Delta Health Transformation Council, a regional collaboration of hospitals and clinics. 
Both organizations received rural health awards. Northwest Mississippi Regional Medical Center received about $2 million for three projects to modernize IT infrastructure, support a maternal health initiative and create a cardiology imaging and reporting network. The Delta Health Transformation Council received $3 million to expand access to robotic-assisted surgery in the Delta. 
Flynn and Dilworth, spokespeople for the Health Department, Lampton and Till did not respond to questions from Mississippi Today about efforts made to prevent conflicts of interest during the application review process. 
Technology leads spending
Roberson said roughly two-thirds of the awards announced Sept. 14 will go to hospitals or affiliated clinics, according to his analysis. The remaining third includes federally qualified health centers, private clinics and urgent care centers, dental, vision and surgical specialists, pharmacies and assisted living facilities. 
Richard Roberson, Mississippi Hospital Association President and CEO, discusses the impact of the “Big Beautiful Bill” on health care in the state, Wednesday, July 9, 2025 at the Mississippi Hospital Association Conference Center in Madison. Credit: Mississippi Hospital Association President and CEO,
Roberson said while the proportion allocated to hospitals is substantial, it does not align with the funds’ original intention of supporting rural hospitals facing cuts. 
“The billions of dollars of cuts to hospital payments are going to have a dramatic impact, and it’s going to hit rural hospitals particularly hard,” he said. 
In Mississippi, federal cuts are expected to reduce provider payments by about $100 million annually beginning in July 2028, according to the Mississippi Division of Medicaid’s strategic plan published in July. 
Close to half of the funds awarded are for projects focused on technological improvements. A slightly smaller portion is set to fund infrastructure projects, and a much smaller amount is earmarked for telehealth initiatives. Officials will soon also announce awardees for several other grant programs, including $16.8 million for four grant programs aimed at addressing critical healthcare workforce shortages in rural communities and $14 million to create calm, therapeutic units at hospital emergency departments to improve crisis mental healthcare, Reeves said at a recent press conference.
Roberson said he would like to see more of the funds awarded to capital improvements, like helping rural hospitals struggling to replace equipment, add new services on-site or replace HVAC systems. These types of projects are likely to have a more lasting impact than technology investments — which can quickly become outdated — for small hospitals with slim margins, he said. He acknowledged that some of the allowed funding uses, like one that bars new construction, are dictated by federal guidelines. 
“I’m hoping that in the future, we can see more funds shifting to things like capital improvements because those are things that can make a bigger difference over time,” Roberson said. 
Khaylah Scott, a program manager at the Mississippi Health Advocacy Program, said she is grateful the funds are being deployed to improve healthcare in rural areas. But she noted that the federal funds will expire in five years, and they won’t expand health insurance to the thousands of Mississippians struggling to afford coverage. 
“It might mitigate or lessen the blow, but the blow is still coming,” Scott said.

name: Nevada Current
title: LVMPD attorney seeks to unseat judge in Clark County District Court race
description: Martina Bauhaus, an attorney for the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Dept. for almost two decades, is challenging Judge Jasmin Lilly-Spells, who is wrapping up her first term on the bench.  District Court Dept. 23 hears both criminal and civil cases, a docket that Lilly-Spells, a former public defender, acknowledges proved challenging at first.  “The law […]
text:
Martina Bauhaus, Jasmin Lilly-Spells. (Candidate photos)Martina Bauhaus, an attorney for the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Dept. for almost two decades, is challenging Judge Jasmin Lilly-Spells, who is wrapping up her first term on the bench. 
District Court Dept. 23 hears both criminal and civil cases, a docket that Lilly-Spells, a former public defender, acknowledges proved challenging at first. 
“The law is very vast. No matter what you do before you take the bench, it would be impossible to have practiced every type,” she said. “It did take some additional study and some time, but I’ve done well. I’ve done a number of civil trials. I am intimately familiar with the procedures and my appellate record for civil cases has gone well.” 
In civil appeals, Lilly-Spells has been affirmed in ten cases and reversed twice. In 33 criminal appeals, she’s been affirmed 27 times, according to Our Nevada Judges.
While Lilly-Spells’ error rate is low, so was her retention rate in the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s Judging the Judges 2025 evaluation, in which 57.3% of the roughly 200 attorneys responding said she should be retained. She calls the participant turnout “very low.” 
“I think that we should all be reflective and at all times. Constructive criticism is amazing because we should be aiming to get better and not be a stagnant judiciary,” she said, adding that shortly after taking the bench she put a locked “bright blue suggestion box” outside her courtroom.  
The solicitation, she says, has proved underwhelming. “We get maybe one comment every six months to a year.”
“When I have engaged with attorneys we’ve gotten feedback complimenting the things we’re doing in the courtroom,” Lilly-Spells notes. “So the scores didn’t add up with what I was hearing and seeing. Nonetheless, I think that they are important. They are to be considered.”
Lilly-Spells says she’s been most surprised during her first term by the volume of cases.  
“When I first ran, I promised to read every single page, and it’s not something that I have stopped doing,” she says, adding “I now rephrase that.”  She says reading exhibits, which can exceed 100 pages per motion, is not a valuable use of her time.
“People also said the job would be very isolating, and that wasn’t something that I really understood until I came into the role,” she observes. 
Lilly-Spells’ opponent, Bauhaus, “immigrated from Germany to the United States in 1994 after marrying an American soldier,” her website says.  
Bauhaus has an undergraduate degree in Political Science, which she says she found “to be pretty useless so I got a Masters Degree in Public Administration.”
She says she worked as a cocktail waitress to put herself through UNLV’s Boyd School of Law, where she anticipated practicing transactional law. “I never thought I’d be a litigator.” 
Bauhaus says the last time she engaged in trials was when she worked for the Nevada Attorney General’s office under Brian Sandoval, who served in that capacity from 2003 to 2005. She subsequently worked for AGs George Chanos and Catherine Cortez-Masto. 
Bauhaus says she began her career as a law clerk at Alverson and Taylor. “When I passed the bar I got handed 20 case files, and it was sink or swim.” 
During her 18 years at Metro, she served as litigation manager, assistant general counsel over litigation, and recently, over forfeitures. For the last five years she’s represented the jail. 
“A quarter of the inmates are mentally ill, and often refuse to take their medications,” Bauhaus asserts. “The jail cannot force them to take their medications. However, when they’d become a danger to themselves or others, I would go into court or and ask the judge to order they be medicated so they don’t harm themselves or others.” 
Bauhaus says she’s running because decisions she received from a local judge she declined to name “were not so much based in the law, but more in what the judge thought was right, and it became very frustrating.”
She says she initially intended to run against another judge but was persuaded to challenge Lilly-Spells, who was arrested in 2022 after an argument with her husband, whose video game console she allegedly attacked with a screwdriver. 
The judge entered a no contest plea to one misdemeanor count of domestic battery.
The two have since divorced, a decision Lilly-Spells says she made in the best interest of her four children. “I have accepted responsibility, and I am accountable.”
Bauhaus says her opponent’s arrest “erodes confidence in the bench. Judges should be held to a higher standard.” 
Lilly-Spells says the incident “illustrates that all of us are human” and has made her a better judge. 
“My judicial philosophy centers on four key components – compassion with an eye towards public safety, integrity, and accountability. Part of that is being accountable for who I am as a person, who I am as a judge,” she says. “It was a very private experience. The media portrayal lacks a lot of context, a lot of things that people will never know.” 
Lilly-Spells notes she and her husband shared 15 years of marriage and four children. She says that like their relationship, which was “not characterized by that one incident on Mothers Day,” neither should her work on the bench be “characterized by a snapshot that lacks context.”
As of July, Lilly-Spells had raised $209,000 and had roughly $163,000 in the bank. 
Her website and other sources indicate she is endorsed by dozens of unions and civic groups, including the Nevada Association of Public Safety Officers, SEIU Nevada, AFL-CIO, Professional Firefighters of Nevada,  National Organization for Women (NOW), Veterans in Politics, Nevada Veterans Council, Independent Black Voters, PLAN Action NV, Asian Chamber, Women’s Democratic Club, and Hispanics in Politics. 
Bauhaus is endorsed by Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill, District Attorney Steve Wolfson,  a variety of police officer associations throughout the state, and Teamsters Nevada. 
She had raised about $21,000 as of July and had about $13,000 on hand.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: How much leeway should officials have to deny gun licenses? SJC will decide.
description: Under the version of the state gun law in place at the time, as well as the sweeping 2024 gun law that retooled many of the state’s firearms laws, local licensing officials like police chiefs can consider a broad range of evidence to determine whether someone is suitable to be granted a license to carry.
text:
THE STATE’S GUN laws are not just under fire at the ballot box this fall. They are also in the crosshairs of a legal challenge before the state’s highest court, targeting the “suitability” part of the state’s prior licensing statue that gun rights advocates say allowed an unconstitutional level of discretion by licensing officials. 
In 2023, Holyoke Police Chief David Pratt denied Randy Westbrook’s application for a license to carry a firearm. Because of two sets of criminal charges more a decade prior — an assault and battery charge against his pregnant girlfriend and charges connected to a vehicle stop that discovered 17 baggies of powder and crack cocaine — Pratt determined that Westbrook was “unsuitable” for the license. 
Under the version of the state gun law in place at the time, as well as the sweeping 2024 gun law that retooled many of the state’s firearms laws, local licensing officials like police chiefs can consider a broad range of evidence to determine whether someone is suitable to be granted a license to carry. 
The law in place in 2023 prohibited issuing a license to carry firearms to an applicant determined to be unsuitable, “based on reliable, articulable and credible information” that the applicant exhibits or engaged in behavior that indicates they “may create a risk to public safety or a risk of danger to self or others” if given a license to carry.  
Westbrook challenged the decision, in a lawsuit funded by The Gun Owners Action League. 
His lawyers argue that the statute is “vague, overbroad” and violates due process protections because it does not offer clarity on what makes a person “unsuitable,” let alone how a person could remedy that issue.
Citing a recent landmark US Supreme Court ruling that established a new test for state gun laws, a Holyoke District Court judge declared the licensing statute’s suitability standard unconstitutional. A Hampden County Superior Court judge overturned the ruling on appeal from the police chief and attorney general’s office. The Supreme Judicial Court agreed to take up the case when it was appealed again, this time by Westbrook.
The case is set for oral arguments before the high court on October 7. Nearly identical suitability language exists under the new, more sweeping gun statute enacted in 2024, so a ruling that this level of subjective discretion is unconstitutional could deal a devastating blow to the Bay State’s licensing rules. 
The US Supreme Court decided New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen in 2022, invalidating licensing rules in states like New York and Massachusetts that let licensing officials refuse to issue a license unless the person offered a “good reason” for needing to carry. 
In the 6-3 decision along ideological lines, with conservative justices in the majority, the nation’s high court said these licensing rules were unconstitutional because they were inconsistent with Founding-era laws.
Then-Attorney General Maura Healey offered a scathing response but moved to obey the ruling, advising licensing authorities to stop working off the “good reason” standard. They should, however, keep enforcing the “prohibited person” and “suitability” provisions of the license-to-carry statute, she said. 
“These aspects of the statute are unaffected by Bruen,” declared the joint advisory from the attorney general’s office and the Executive Office of Public Safety and Security.
The District Court judge in Westbrook’s case concluded that there was no historical tradition supporting such “spongy terms” — like whether someone “may” be a risk to themselves or others — as a justification for limiting Second Amendment rights. But the Superior Court noted that the Bruen decision had approved licensing regimes with suitability requirements, like Massachusetts.
The reasoning, according to the nation’s high court, is that states are not allowed to grant or deny licenses based on whether there is a suitable need or purpose, but can based on whether the person’s character or temperament is suitable to carry a gun. 
According to the court record, Westbrook allegedly shook and punched his then-girlfriend, who was nine months pregnant, then chased her to her friend’s apartment where she had to hide in the bathroom. He admitted to sufficient facts for a finding of guilty on the aggravated assault and battery charge and controlled substances charges, in exchange for a continuance in his case and eventual dismissal. 
The police chief denied Westbrook’s license application “based on serious criminal charges to which he admitted to sufficient facts for guilty finding,” wrote the attorney general’s office in its brief. “These assault and drug offenses underlying these charges are themselves violent or create the possibility of violence. And although the charges date from 2010 and 2014, Westbrook submitted no evidence to Chief Pratt that he no longer posed a danger to public safety.” 
A group of Second Amendment advocacy groups submitted a brief in support of Westbrook. They acknowledged that recent US Supreme Court and Massachusetts SJC cases do allow for dangerous people to be kept from firearm licenses. 
But this case, they argue in a brief, is unconstitutional when it comes to Westbrook because it relies on cases for which there was no actual conviction. It is also, they wrote,  unconstitutional because it lets licensing officials use discretion to determine if someone is unsuitable through “non-objective criteria,” including whether they “may” create a risk to public safety. 
The current suite of gun laws was passed in 2024 explicitly as a response to Bruen. They expanded the reasons that licensing officials could reject license applications, and expanded the category of regulated firearms to include things like 3-D printed guns and unserialized ghost guns.  
That gun reform law is heading toward a repeal referendum on November 3. Even if voters opt against repealing the 2024 law, the court will have the last word on the question of local officials’ ability to deny a license to carry a firearm to someone they deem unsuitable.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Podcast: Pro and con voices on Amendment J, clarifying the citizenship requirement for voting
description: A question on the Nov. 3 general election ballot asks South Dakotans to add language in the state constitution specifying that people who are not U.S. citizens are disqualified from voting. The state constitution already includes citizenship as a voting eligibility requirement. Two years ago, state officials discovered 273 non-U.S. citizens had accidentall[...]
text:
State Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, left, supports an amendment to the state constitution to clarify the citizenship requirement for voting in South Dakota. Rep. Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls, opposes the change. (Photos by South Dakota Searchlight) 


Searchlight Report is a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight. Reporter and host Meghan O’Brien works with other Searchlight journalists to take listeners inside politics and policy in The Mount Rushmore State.			




 
A question on the Nov. 3 general election ballot asks South Dakotans to add language in the state constitution specifying that people who are not U.S. citizens are disqualified from voting. The state constitution already includes citizenship as a voting eligibility requirement.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Two years ago, state officials discovered 273 non-U.S. citizens had accidentally been registered to vote in South Dakota while their driver’s license forms were being processed. Noncitizens can obtain a driver’s license or state ID if they are lawful permanent residents or have temporary legal status, and there’s a part of the driver’s license form that allows an applicant to register to vote if they’re a citizen.
One of those 273 people voted, according to the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office. That was in 2016. All of the registrations were canceled after their discovery.
State Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, supports Amendment J. She said it would close a loophole in the constitution. Rep. Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls, opposes Amendment J. He said the state already has laws in place that criminalize noncitizens voting. They both explain their views in this episode of Searchlight Report.
A “yes” vote on the ballot question would add language to the state constitution specifying that noncitizens are disqualified from voting. A “no” vote would leave the constitution as is.
Click here to access a transcript for this episode.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Meet the Michigan climate candidate on Trump’s radar
description: Less than two months ago, William Lawrence was a relatively unknown progressive climate group co-founder and a dark-horse candidate for Congress running in a Trump district in the middle of Michigan.  But his August victory in the Lansing-area primary — where he capitalized when moderate Democrats split votes — has catapulted Lawrence firmly into the […]
text:
William Lawrence speaks about data centers and artificial intelligence in Mason, Mich., on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan Advance)Less than two months ago, William Lawrence was a relatively unknown progressive climate group co-founder and a dark-horse candidate for Congress running in a Trump district in the middle of Michigan. 
But his August victory in the Lansing-area primary — where he capitalized when moderate Democrats split votes — has catapulted Lawrence firmly into the national spotlight. The 36-year-old vying to represent Michigan’s 7th Congressional District is suddenly under heightened scrutiny from the Democratic Party, national news outlets and even President Donald Trump. 
The high-profile race, which pits Lawrence against incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), could tip the scales of power in Washington next year. It’s also a microcosm of some of the biggest debates playing out in national politics in the midterms that are likely to carry into the 2028 presidential race. The contest could offer lessons about voters’ opposition to data centers, their willingness to shrug off controversial social media posts and their appetite for left-leaning candidates promising drastic changes in the Trump era. 
Michigan’s 7th District is “one of the quintessential swing districts in the entire country,” said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics. It’s been historically competitive, voting narrowly for Joe Biden in 2020 and for Trump in 2024, Kondik said, and it’s “the kind of swing seat that Democrats probably should be winning in a year like this.” 
The left is hopeful Lawrence can capitalize on anti-Trump sentiment to win the race. Democrats’ congressional campaign arm recently added Lawrence to its “Red to Blue” program — signaling a boost in support from the national party. 
But Kondik and other political analysts still view the race as a toss-up, due in part to Lawrence’s past as an outspoken climate activist and progressive. 
“He’s the kind of candidate that I think Republicans are sort of dreaming of running against,” in part due to his track record of saying “a lot of pretty out-there things,” Kondik said. “But it’s also not obvious to me that he’s going to lose. I really think it is still a toss-up.” 
William Lawrence speaks to a voter at an “Ask me anything” event outside Lyon Township Hall on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan Advance)
Trump attacks
One complication for Lawrence: His controversial social media posts during his years as a progressive activist and climate organizer. 
Some of his now-deleted social media posts surfaced in a CNN report this month, including a post from 2021 in support of communal living. “Biggest W of my late 20s was finding a long-term stable co-op house. F*** isolation and the nuclear family domicile,” Lawrence wrote in one of the posts. In another post from 2022, Lawrence wrote that the “nuclear family home is an isolating, individualistic, violent way of organizing society.” 
For Republicans, Lawrence’s old posts and his activist record are political red meat. 
Days after those old posts resurfaced, Trump blasted Lawrence during a speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “One of the Democrats’ top congressional candidates is a self-described Marxist who says he hates family households, oh, that’s nice, and wants to destroy the American way of life,” Trump said. 
Lawrence told Michigan Advance that he learned about the president’s comments when the House Republicans’ campaign arm tagged him in a clip of the speech on social media. He welcomed the president’s attention. “I thought, ‘Hey, here we are. We’ve arrived,’” he said. 



Quotation







He’s smart and aggressive — I doubt he’s going to Congress just to have a job.


– Environmental activist and author Bill McKibben, who has known William Lawrence since his undergraduate days.


Barrett is also seizing on Lawrence’s old posts. “My wife and I live in a small town in this district and I’m raising a nuclear family — something that my opponent says is a violent way of organizing society,” Barrett told the Advance in a phone interview. 
Barrett, a U.S. Army veteran running for his second term representing the district, said Lawrence has been a “radical activist for his entire life as an adult. And you can’t then divorce yourself of that when you decide to run for office in a very, very competitive congressional district. You can’t just say, “Ah, well, don’t pay attention to anything I said.’” 
Lawrence addressed the resurfacing of his remarks in an interview earlier this month. 
“There’s things that I have said that … I stand by saying them at the time, even though I wouldn’t say them in the same way now,” Lawrence told the Michigan Advance in a parking lot where he sat next to a sign that said “Ask me anything” and took questions from locals.
There’s things that I probably disagreed with even at the time, and it was a moment of frustration. And there’s things that I … changed my mind in response to new information,” he said. 
Like others in his generation, Lawrence said, “I’ve just done a lot of time thinking out aloud on the internet. … And I think folks understand that.” He’s changed his approach since then, Lawrence said. “I’m in a different role now, and that requires me to hold myself to a higher standard.”
Lawrence specifically addressed his past comments about marriage during a recent news conference in Mason. “I’ve been happily married for four years,” he told reporters. 
William Lawrence speaks about data centers and artificial intelligence in Mason, Mich., on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan Advance)
Climate roots 
Before he was an aspiring congressman, Lawrence was a climate activist who helped launch the youth-led Sunrise Movement. 
He worked on a fossil fuel divestment campaign as an undergraduate at Swarthmore College and met up with other students around the country interested in cutting their universities’ ties with oil and gas companies. 
That eventually led to the creation of a national network of student divestment organizers and ultimately the co-founding of the youth-led Sunrise Movement in early 2017. That effort injected energy into the environmental movement as young activists staged a sit-in at then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office in 2018 and went on to prod the Biden administration on climate change. 
Lawrence’s links to the climate movement are still strong. Stevie O’Hanlon, another Sunrise co-founder and the group’s former communications director, is managing Lawrence’s campaign. 
Sunrise’s current executive director, Aru Shiney-Ajay, traveled to Michigan last Friday to train Michigan State University students and get them fired up for Lawrence’s election. 
She sees Lawrence’s political rise coinciding with a new era of climate politics. 
“I actually do see climate anxiety spiking among young people again” and data center and AI concerns are “a big part of that,” she said. “I think having Will in power would just be an incredible way to show how movements can go from taking the streets to the halls of Congress.”
Environmental activist and author Bill McKibben has known Lawrence since his undergraduate days. McKibben thinks Lawrence’s climate and activism background could help propel him to victory in the moderate district. 
“I think people are plenty ready for fighters — he showed in the primary that that was an asset,” McKibben said in an email. And he thinks Lawrence will be in prime position to shape the national debate on climate and data centers if he wins in November. “He’s smart and aggressive — I doubt he’s going to Congress just to have a job,” McKibben said. 
Data center drama
Lawrence’s allies say his roots as a climate activist and affordable housing organizer make him uniquely suited to harness opposition to data centers in his district. Those opponents include the younger university crowd worried about the centers’ climate impacts as well as moderate voters wary of the impacts on the environment, property values and utility costs. 
Lawrence is campaigning relentlessly on data centers, calling for a one-year federal moratorium on new construction. He appeared at a Lyon Township board of trustees meeting earlier this month to promote a moratorium to local officials. And he recently unveiled a plan to rein in data centers and artificial intelligence. 
A sign in Mason, Mich., near the site of a proposed data center on Sept. 17, 2026.(Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan Advance)
Barrett calls Lawrence’s stance on data centers an “absolutist” position. 
“I’m taking the approach that local residents ought to have the decision, and that data center developers — along with local elected officials — ought to make that case to the local residents and allow them to decide what’s right for their communities,” he said.  
Lawrence is slamming Barrett for voting for Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act that included tax breaks available to tech companies for data center construction. 
Barrett said the law included “broad tax reforms that certainly changed tax policy for all kinds of different things,” and didn’t single out data centers for support. 
Barrett touts his own past opposition to direct incentives for Michigan data center developers during his time in the state legislature. And in August, Barrett introduced legislation in Congress to ban the federal government from overriding local zoning decisions about data centers. 
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) at an event hosted by the America First Policy Institute in Charlotte, Mich. June 16, 2026. | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
“Local opposition to rapid data center expansion is emerging as a critical issue,” said Marty Jordan, an associate professor of political science at Michigan State University. 
Lawrence’s “consistent opposition to data center expansion” resonates strongly, Jordan said. “While Barrett has recently advocated for greater local control over these projects, his position is complicated by President Trump’s support for AI data center growth.” 
Ultimately, the candidates’ diverging views on data centers and other key policy issues may matter less in November than their party affiliations, said Erin Covey, House editor at The Cook Political Report. 
“For most House candidates, people are ultimately going to be voting for you based on the letter that is beside your name,” she said. “So even if they have disagreements with their own party’s nominee, we live in such a polarized era that keeping the other party out of power is always going to be the driving consideration for most people.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: A GOP power player and lobbyist is a key advisor to House Speaker Lisa Demuth
description: House Speaker Lisa Demuth has had several defining moments in her campaign for governor thus far. She lost the Minnesota Republican Party’s convention endorsement in May after 10 ballots, though her team successfully raised doubts about the tabulation process to dampen the endorsement of Kendall Qualls. Later, after missing out on what had been considered […[...]
text:
Lisa Demuth attends her campaign's watch party at Burger Moe’s in St. Paul on Tuesday, August 11, 2026. Demuth, center left, with Ben Golnik, center at computer, monitor results. (Photo by Tony Nelson/MinnPost)House Speaker Lisa Demuth has had several defining moments in her campaign for governor thus far. She lost the Minnesota Republican Party’s convention endorsement in May after 10 ballots, though her team successfully raised doubts about the tabulation process to dampen the endorsement of Kendall Qualls.
Later, after missing out on what had been considered a must-have endorsement of President Donald Trump, she went on to win the Republican primary for governor.
On the convention floor and on primary night as the returns came in, Demuth had at her side a GOP operative and lobbyist who is well known at the Minnesota Capitol, but less so to the general public: Ben Golnik.
Golnik is an advisor to Demuth’s campaign, armed with a vast network of GOP politicos, donors, delegates and operatives. He’s doing all of this work without receiving a paycheck from Demuth’s campaign, according to campaign finance reports.
But Golnik very much gets paid in his day job as a registered lobbyist who represents Big Pharma, the tobacco industry, a horse racing track and other clients.
Golnik didn’t respond to interview requests, but he told the Reformer in a text message that he volunteers for Demuth’s campaign like he has for campaigns in the past.
“I first met Speaker Demuth when she ran for the House in 2018. Speaker Demuth is a friend and I’m a volunteer on her campaign for governor,” Golnik said. “I’ve volunteered for dozens of campaigns over the years and enjoy being helpful.”
Lisa Demuth complained to Ben Golnik (left), about malfunctioning clickers amid voting irregularities at the Minnesota Republican Convention in Duluth, Saturday May 30, 2026. (Photo by Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)
Golnik is hardly alone. Many lobbyists raise money, drum up research, consult on ad copy and even knock on doors for candidates, which allows them to take the temperature of the electorate and maybe even get face time with the candidate. Democratic-Farmer-Labor lobbyists like Brian Rice and Larry Redmond are known to get deep in the weeds of campaigns. 
(U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the DFL nominee for governor, was once a registered lobbyist during her days in private law practice.)
Norman Ornstein, an emeritus scholar at the American Enterprise Institute, said many lobbyists volunteer and raise money for campaigns, but said a decision-making role for a lobbyist would be unusual.
The problem with the arrangement is whether Golnik’s free and apparently important work with the Demuth campaign would create an obligation to him or his clients if Demuth is successful in November.
“There is nothing illegal about this that I can point to, but a lobbyist for Big Tobacco and Big Pharma? Not a great look,” Ornstein said in an email.
Demuth at a Capitol press conference Thursday said her campaign has a number of volunteers and staff to help get their message out. Asked about Golnik’s responsibilities, Demuth declined to provide any details.
“We have volunteers that are on our campaign,” Demuth said.
Golnik is hardly the same as the legions of Minnesotans stuffing envelopes, however. He comes with a long resume of GOP political work and would be a candidate to be Demuth’s chief of staff, or some other key role, formal or not. 
As executive director for the Minnesota House Republican caucus, Golnik was former House Speaker Kurt Daudt’s right-hand man when the Crown lawmaker was among the state’s most prominent Republicans between 2014-2019 and was frequently discussed as a potential candidate for governor.
Daudt praised Golnik in a statement, noting that any candidate would be happy to have his assistance and that people in politics “wear different hats in campaigning, in public service, in advocacy and strategic advice-giving.”
“There are dozens of DFLers and Republicans who play such multiple roles. It is normal and legitimate for anyone involved in public life and cares about our communities to do so,” Daudt said.
Golnik founded the Minnesota Jobs Coalition after the Republicans’ 2012 debacle, which gave Democrats their first trifecta in recent memory.
Under Golnik’s leadership, the Jobs Coalition — which is still hammering Democrats today —  went on to help Republicans take the House majority in 2014 and then expand it in 2016.
When House Republicans lost the majority in a 2018 landslide, Golnik left the Legislature to take up lobbying.
His most prominent client is the Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk, which manufactures weight loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy. He also represents PMI U.S. Corporate Services — a subsidiary of the tobacco company Philip Morris — and the North Metro Harness Initiative, which does business as Running Aces.
Running Aces, which operates a casino, racetrack and restaurant in Columbus, Minnesota, donated $500,000 in June to the Restore Sanity political action committee, a super PAC supporting Demuth’s campaign for governor.
Running Aces President Taro Ito didn’t respond to the Reformer’s request for comment.
Golnik is friends with Tommy Merickel, an influential, behind-the-scenes business executive and fundraiser who succeeded Golnik at the Jobs Coalition. Merickel — who has worked closely with billionaire Glen Taylor for decades — is fundraising for the Restore Sanity PAC this election cycle.
The super PAC in recent weeks received a $10 million cash infusion, cutting into Klobuchar’s longtime financial advantage in the race.
According to a 2017 Star Tribune profile, Golnik is driven less by ideology than a competitive desire to win.
“When I’m playing chess with my kid, I don’t like to lose,” Golnik told the Star Tribune.

name: Nevada Current
title: Educator challenges incumbent for Nevada State controller
description: Republican Nevada State Controller Andy Matthews is seeking reelection this November as the state’s independent fiscal watchdog, while his challenger, Democrat Michael MacDougall, hopes a blue wave will help launch him to victory.  The state controller is responsible for administering the state’s accounting system, conducting state audits, settling claims ag[...]
text:
Michael MacDougal, Andy Matthews (Candidate photos)Republican Nevada State Controller Andy Matthews is seeking reelection this November as the state’s independent fiscal watchdog, while his challenger, Democrat Michael MacDougall, hopes a blue wave will help launch him to victory. 
The state controller is responsible for administering the state’s accounting system, conducting state audits, settling claims against the state, and collecting debts owed to the state. The controller also serves on the state’s transportation board and the executive branch committee, which oversees annual internal audits. The state controller is limited by the state constitution to two four-year terms and yearly compensation is around $100,000.
MacDougall said he hopes voters give more attention to down ballot races like his when they hit the polls – or send mail in ballots – this November. He pointed to recent polling showing Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford has a lead over Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo in the Nevada race for the governor’s seat.
“I think the national conversation will play a role in the local conversation here in Nevada, and I think that will help me. That’ll help up and down the ballot,” MacDougall said. 
Matthews, however, has the advantage as an incumbent with a strong fundraising arm. Matthews reported raising nearly $50,000 in campaign funds through July, compared to MacDougall’s nearly $24,000.
That fundraising also helped Matthews launch an advertisement in September highlighting his accomplishments in office. The 30-second ad, shows Matthews counting pennies as he touts the website his office launched that provides real-time information on state spending.
“Fundraising is only one part of running a successful campaign, MacDougall said. “I’m focused on meeting voters where they are, and being in the public eye, and being at events and meeting with people. I think that that has more of a sway than the dollar amount raised.”
Matthews did not respond to the Nevada Current’s request for an interview. 
Before being elected controller in 2022, Matthews served in the Nevada State Assembly. Prior to that he led the Nevada Policy, a conservative think tank.
On his campaign site, Matthews highlighted his work helping local governments create their own transparency websites. He also noted his work to modernize the state’s financial, human-resource and information-technology systems. 
Matthews also noted he enacted significant reforms to the state’s financial reporting. 
MacDougall criticized Matthews for delaying the release of the state mandated Nevada Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, a report that details the state’s financial position and is required by law. Matthews released the report more than two years after the fiscal year ended. 
Delays in audits erode trust in government, while timely audits demonstrate effective government and help build trust in the state, said MacDougall. 
“Citizens and businesses lose faith in government when audits are not conducted in a timely manner. Trust is crucial for effective governance, and delayed audits undermine this trust,” MacDougall said. 
On his campaign website, Matthews said if reelected he would prioritize the creation of a Nevada Office of Inspector General in his second term. 
During the 2025 Legislative Session, Matthews proposed the creation of a Nevada Office of Inspector General to independently audit recipients of state funds. Although the bill did not advance, Matthews promised to reintroduce it in 2027 and has submitted a bill draft request. 
MacDougall said he’s open to the creation of a Nevada Office of Inspector General, although he said he would have to examine the bill’s language.
“I think oversight is a good thing,” MacDougall said. “Any sort of oversight to ensure that people are behaving correctly is a good thing.”
If elected, MacDougall said his top priorities would be to conduct a state audit, support better access to public transportation, and recover millions in uncollected tax revenues.
MacDougall works as an educator teaching social studies at The Adelson School, a private Jewish community school in Las Vegas. He earned a bachelor’s degree in political science from Allegheny College in Pennsylvania, and a Master of Arts from the University of Iowa and one from the University of California, Los Angeles.
MacDougall said he views the role of the state controller as a referee that serves as a check on state finances, auditing every dollar in and out, including taxes and federal funds, said MacDougall. 
When it comes to recovering unpaid back taxes MacDougall said the office should explore targeted enforcement measures to improve tax collection, including punitive actions and streamlined services that could help bring in more revenue.
He said his campaign is focused on practical solutions to existing problems and forward thinking. He emphasized the importance of collaboration with other agencies and elected officials to find solutions.
One practical solution that could improve quality of life for Nevadans is expanding access to transportation. The state controller sits on the Nevada Department of Transportation board, influencing public and commercial transportation within Nevada.
MacDougall said he wants to make public transportation more accessible and affordable, including reduced or free fares for young people.
“It’s a service that is being provided and funded through tax dollars, so it behooves us to make sure we are making it the best we can,” MacDougall said.
MacDougall has been endorsed by SEIU Local 1107, the Nevada State Education Association, the Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, AFL-CIO, Teamsters Nevada, and Smart Local 88. 
Matthews has been endorsed by Lombardo, the Nevada Republican Party, Nevada Young Republicans, and the Keystone Corporation Nevada.

name: Nevada Current
title: Workforce development specialist, former state legislator face off in regent race
description: Five Nevada Board of Regents seats are on the ballot this year, but only one is an open seat not featuring an incumbent. That race, for District 5 in Southern Nevada, will bring to the board either a former state legislator or a current higher education professional with a background in workforce development programming. The […]
text:
Stephanie Molina, Mo Denis. (Candidate photos) Five Nevada Board of Regents seats are on the ballot this year, but only one is an open seat not featuring an incumbent. That race, for District 5 in Southern Nevada, will bring to the board either a former state legislator or a current higher education professional with a background in workforce development programming.
The Board of Regents oversees the Nevada System of Higher Education, which is composed of two research universities, a state university, four community colleges, and a research institute. NSHE enrolls more than 100,000 students, according to their website, and has a biennium budget of more than $2 billion dollars.
In 2023, the Nevada State Legislature passed a bill to reduce the number to regents from 13 to nine. They also shortened the term length of regents from six years to four years beginning with the 2028 election. To align with those changes, the winners of this year’s regents races will have truncated terms and have to run for re-election in 2028.
Regents run in nonpartisan races, but the board often features elected officials with experience in partisan politics.
District 5, which covers areas of North Las Vegas and Winchester, is currently represented by Patrick Boylan. Boylan, who was elected in 2020, has been the subject of much criticism for making racist, discriminatory and anti-transgender comments. He ran for re-election this year but came in fourth in a crowded six-person primary.
Former Nevada state legislator Mo Denis came in first in the primary, receiving 30% of votes. Stephanie Molina, a workforce development program coordinator at Nevada State University, came in second place with 20% support.
Now, Denis and Molina will face off on the general election ballot.
Denis, a Democrat, is no stranger to public office, having represented the area for 18 years in the Nevada State Legislature, including a stint as Senate majority leader. His legislative experience includes playing a major role in the 2019 revamping of the state’s K-12 education funding formula.
Denis told the Nevada Current earlier this year he hadn’t planned to run for another office after he termed out of the Legislature in 2022, but he felt compelled to run for regent because he felt the board was being “sidetracked” and “losing focus on students.”
Molina, also a registered Democrat, would be a newcomer to elected office, though she has previously served as president of the executive board president of UNLV’s Graduate and Professional Student Association and been a voting member of the Nevada Student Alliance. According to her campaign website, she wants to bring her experience with workforce and economic development programming to the board and “help build a higher education system that is more accessible, accountable, and responsive to the people it serves.”
“Having seen the system from multiple vantage points, as a student leader, a participant in faculty governance, and a higher education professional focused on workforce development, I am prepared to bring a thoughtful, data-informed, and service-driven perspective to the Board,” she wrote in a candidate survey for the Nevada Faculty Alliance.
In his survey responses, Denis wrote he views higher education as “central to Nevada’s economic diversification, workforce development, and community engagement. It creates pathways to opportunity, supports innovation, and strengthens communities across our state.”
The Nevada Faculty Alliance has endorsed Denis, as has the Culinary Union, Laborers, Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada, Clark County Education Association, and Nevada State Education Association.
According to her most recent campaign finance report, filed in mid-July, Molina did no fundraising during the first half of the year.
Denis raised nearly $39,000 during that period and spent most of it, entering July with $5,780 on hand. About a quarter of the amount raised was self funded. Other top contributors include the Clark County Education Association, Vegas Chamber, and Assemblymember Selena Torres-Fossett (D-Las Vegas).
The next campaign finance reports are due in mid-October.

name: Missouri Independent
title: The Fairness Project remains largest funder of effort to stop Missouri abortion ban
description: Since 2017, a D.C.-based nonprofit called the Fairness Project has poured more than $13 million into Missouri campaigns.  Every campaign it backed that has reached Missouri voters has won. And now it is making its biggest investment yet in the state. In 2024, The Fairness Project gave more than $4.5 million to a citizen-led ballot […]
text:
Abortion rights advocates gather for a canvassing kick-off event on Aug. 29 in St. Louis County (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).Since 2017, a D.C.-based nonprofit called the Fairness Project has poured more than $13 million into Missouri campaigns. 
Every campaign it backed that has reached Missouri voters has won. And now it is making its biggest investment yet in the state.
In 2024, The Fairness Project gave more than $4.5 million to a citizen-led ballot effort to overturn the state’s abortion ban. This year, it has donated $5.3 million to Stop the Ban, making it the largest donor to the campaign seeking to defeat Amendment 3.
The amendment, placed on the Nov. 3 ballot by Republican lawmakers, would repeal the abortion-rights measure Missouri voters approved two years ago and replace it with an abortion ban with limited exceptions. It would also place a constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors, which is currently banned in state statute. 
The Fairness Project’s prominent financial role — and the fact that, as a federally registered 501c4 nonprofit, it is not legally required to publicly disclose its donors — has also made it one of the main targets of conservative and anti-abortion leaders who argue that out-of-state interests wield too much influence over Missouri elections.
