title: State to tear down former governor’s residence
description: The Capitol Complex Advisory Council voted 8-1 during a meeting this week to tear down a former residence of Montana governors, located at 2 N. Carson Street in Helena. The building has been a topic of legislative and state discussion for years, as the residence, built in 1959, was in disrepair. It would have needed […]
text:
A postcard of the Montana's Governor Mansion which was built in 1959 and is located at 2 Carson Street in Helena. The Capitol Complex Advisory Council voted 8-1 during a meeting this week to tear down a former residence of Montana governors, located at 2 N. Carson Street in Helena.
The building has been a topic of legislative and state discussion for years, as the residence, built in 1959, was in disrepair. It would have needed nearly $4 million to repair when the issue was discussed during the 2025 Legislative session. That number was even higher, potentially more than $5 million. 
The building instead will be demolished, but the property will remain in state hands and become a greenspace, state officials said this week. Ralph Kuney, a member of the public on the Capitol Complex Advisory Council, was the lone vote against.
Annual maintenance on the building was around $100,000, Helena state Senator Mary Ann Dunwell said. Dunwell, a Democrat, used to represent part of Helena where the former governor’s mansion is and has been vocal on the issue.
“This has been going on for a long time, and I just appreciate everybody coming together and coming to a resolution, so we can move forward,” Dunwell said during the meeting. 
Steve Baiamonte, with the General Services Administration, said there remains a variety of issues with the property. 
“There’s asbestos abatement that needs to be done. There’s roofing repairs. There’s a complete replacement of the plumbing system, electrical system,” Baiamonte said. “It would be safer to say that honestly, what the house doesn’t need is a new foundation.”
In 2019 and 2021, the Montana Legislature appropriated a total $2.3 million for upgrades, but bids for repairs and upgrades to the building came in higher. There were suggestions of using it as extended office space, a session-long residence for legislators with families and a variety of other usages.
Dunwell said in an interview Thursday that some of the money will go toward razing the building and a portion will go to the park. Any leftover money will return to the general fund, she added.
As Montana grows, property near the capitol will be valuable.
“That piece of land could come in handy someday,” Dunwell said. 
Historically, there have been three residences used to house Montana’s governors. The first is now used as a museum and tourist attraction, showcasing the territorial and early days of the state. 
The second residence was the house built at 2 N. Carson St. And earlier this year, the state land board opted to accept a $5 million gift from the Gianfortes – a 12,000 square foot, historic mansion at 720 Madison Ave., which has been designated the governor’s residence in official documents, leaving the 1959 house in limbo.
The Montana Constitution requires the top five state officials, often referred to as “constitutional officers” live in Helena, but the state only provides a residence for the governor.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Mike Rogers claims he was an assembly line worker. The UAW said that is stretching the truth.
description: As Republican Mike Rogers makes his case to voters in Michigan’s high-stakes U.S. Senate race against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, he’s relied on his record as a federal law enforcement agent, his national intelligence expertise and his image as an every-day working man turned lawmaker. But one claim he’s made on the campaign doesn’t appear […]
text:
Former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-White Lake) after he filed signatures in Lansing in his bid for the Republican nomination for U.S. Senate. April 17, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan AdvanceAs Republican Mike Rogers makes his case to voters in Michigan’s high-stakes U.S. Senate race against Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, he’s relied on his record as a federal law enforcement agent, his national intelligence expertise and his image as an every-day working man turned lawmaker.
But one claim he’s made on the campaign doesn’t appear to hold water for the United Auto Workers — his insistence that he worked in an automotive factory during his stint at Adrian College between 1981 and 1982. The UAW formally endorsed El-Sayed in June.
In advertisements, campaign interviews and in messaging to voters, Rogers claimed several times that he either worked in a factory, an automotive shop or an assembly line where he built Chrysler LeBarons.
Research done by Michigan Advance and interviews with a member of the United Auto Workers shows that while Rogers never worked for one of the Big Three automakers during his college years, and that he never worked on an automotive assembly line building one of Chrysler’s most well known vehicles — the LeBaron — Rogers did work at Cars & Concepts in Brighton, Michigan, between 1981 and 1982. 
The Cars & Concepts facility, a large company in Brighton founded by former U.S. Rep. Dick Chrysler, did custom work on vehicles after they were already built on a Chrysler assembly line and shipped to Brighton for additional, after-market parts. 
The campaign also said that he worked for a period of time at Thermofil, in Fowlerville, where he was a line mixer. The campaign said he made materials that were used for dashboards, but did not indicate when he worked at Thermofil.
Although Cars & Concepts was not an assembly line owned by one of the Big Three automakers, it was known in the auto industry as a speciality engineering, design and aftermarket parts facility. According to historical photos and museum entries, Cars & Concepts was more akin to a mechanic or body shop, but Rogers’ team insisted, when asked by Michigan Advance, that the facility did have an assembly line type facility.
Cars & Concepts is no longer in operation.
1982 Chrysler LeBaron convertible at annual Tatamagouche Auto Show in Nova Scotia, Canada on August 3, 2019. This is the type of vehicle Mike Rogers claimed to have helped build in the early 1980s. (Getty Images)
The facility was not building the LeBaron, either, but rather modifying already-assembled vehicles into convertibles with removable sunroofs — a part that Cars & Concepts was known for and well suited to produce and add on.
In that way, the UAW said that Rogers was greatly inflating his experience as an assembly line worker on the campaign trail.
“He never claimed that he worked in an automotive factory when we were lobbying him at the beginning of the early 2000s,” said Art Reyes II, former president of UAW Local 651, serving Delphi plants in Flint, who was provided to the Advance for an interview when it asked UAW for a comment on this story. “He has tried to campaign as a champion of the auto worker when, in fact, he has no concept nor respect for the work that we do.” Reyes is president of the UAW Region 1-D Greater Flint Community Action Program (CAP) Council and also serves as a trustee for Mott Community College. 
The UAW, in a separate statement, also told the Advance that “the record for Mike Rogers that we are familiar with is his record in Congress, where he supported bad trade deals that cost Michigan autoworkers good union jobs.”
In response, Rogers’ campaign told the Advance that any claim the former congressman didn’t work on an assembly line because it wasn’t one of the Big Three plants, was “an insult to all of the hard-working men and women in our auto industry working for small, third-party manufacturers.”
“When Mike worked at Cars & Concepts, he worked on Chrysler LeBarons, where he drilled the left and right A-pillars to secure the molding. Then, while the car was still moving down the line, he riveted panels between the back seat and the trunk,” said Rogers spokesperson and Communications Director Alyssa Brouillet. “Of course the UAW — which is already biased in endorsing Abdul — wouldn’t count it because it’s not theirs. And if Democrat failures hadn’t shipped off so many of our auto jobs, frankly, we’d have more of these small manufacturers.”
What Cars & Concepts was, and what it was not
The Brighton facility where Rogers said he worked was founded in 1976 by businessman and Republican former U.S. Rep. Dick Chrysler, who represented what was then Michigan’s 8th Congressional District between 1995 to 1997. Rogers would later represent that same district during his seven terms in Congress from 2001 to 2015.
According to various sources — such as Automotive News, Hemmings and the Howell Carnegie Library archives — Cars & Concepts designed, built and installed aftermarket products on factory-built vehicles. What the design shop and facility was most known for was its removable sunroofs on convertibles for Chrysler and Plymouth vehicles.



Quotation







If you did not do time in the plant, that’s fine, but don’t act as if you had, and don’t talk to Michiganders about something which millions of us over the generations have experienced, have made careers of, have raised families on because of the collective bargaining power of the UAW.


– Art Reyes II, the former president of UAW Local 651


For Chrysler in the 1980s, the shop had a contract with the automaker to convert its K-Body type LeBarons into more luxury models, modifying pre-built vehicles into convertibles. 
According to Hemmings, a classic car marketplace, catalogue and media platform for enthusiasts, then-Chrysler CEO Lee Iacocca had visions of offering a new convertible because Chrysler had not offered one since 1970. A prototype was created and it attracted great interest, so Iacocca sought out the design expertise of Cars & Concepts to handle the conversions.
This contract was mainly focused on the 1982 LeBaron. Dick Chrysler sold the company in 1987.
By all accounts, Cars & Concepts was one of the premier aftermarket product shops in the nation, and that’s why Iacocca chose the company to help produce its LeBaron convertibles. The conversions were not necessarily easy, and did include a series of additional steps and some sheet metal work to ensure quality, Hemmings added.
Rogers’ campaign told the Advance that Cars & Concepts did have an assembly line-type process to do that work when he worked there in between 1981 and 1982.
Rogers’ claim that he “built” LeBarons at the facility is further refuted by the fact that the LeBaron, when it was being built in Michigan, was built at Detroit’s former Jefferson Avenue Assembly facility up until 1975, when the Imperial LeBaron was discontinued, and at the Hamtramck plant up until 1981, said a historian with Stellantis when the Advance asked about the LeBaron’s production history.  Stellantis is now the parent company of Chrysler.
Later year LeBaron production occurred in Delaware, Missouri, and other nations like Mexico and Venezuela, but the LeBaron GTS was produced at Sterling Heights Assembly in 1984.
Adrian College is in Lenawee County, and the UAW has no record of a Chrysler assembly plant building the vehicles in the county. Cars & Concepts is located in Livingston County, where Rogers’ campaign said he worked and grew up.
While what Cars & Concepts did was an important step toward creating the LeBaron convertible product for customers, Reyes told the Advance that it was a far cry from an assembly line, an auto-parts factory or a parts supplier that the Big Three work with to produce vehicles along the designated supply chain — nor would the companies be shipping partially-produced vehicles to those shops for vehicle completion.
“In an original equipment manufacturing sense, no,” Reyes said. “The likelihood is that would not have been the case. Aftermarket stuff, there were a lot of specialty shops that General Motors or any of the American Three would do, but they were not partially building the LeBaron in the plant, then sending it out to be finished.”
Art Reyes. Photo by Mike Huerta.
Rogers alleging automotive experience is new a feature in his recent campaigns
When Rogers was endorsed by “Autoworkers For Trump,” he mentioned in a news release that he had worked in two different auto factory facilities and understood the “blood, sweat and tears” of Michigan’s auto workers.
That appears to be a new aspect of his campaign pitch, starting during his 2024 U.S. Senate campaign against current U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin.
At a Michigan rally featuring President Donald Trump in September 2024, Rogers told the audience that he worked in a car factory — his first mention of the claim. But instead of building LeBarons, Rogers said he was building the Sebring Convertible, another Chrysler vehicle.
“My God, America works when Americans are working. Let’s give a round of applause to the people who are making the engine of America getting up and going. Thank you for letting us into your place. I hope some of you’re getting time and a half. That’s all I’m saying,” Rogers said. “I have to tell you why these jobs are  important. Certainly to me. I worked in a car factory — that Convertible Sebring. Remember those? Those are gems. Those jobs are important because they feed families. They nourish communities, and in the last four years, if you think about what the Democrats have done to us, I mean, my family has a saying, ‘you can’t drink yourself sober.’ You can’t spend yourself rich and you can’t regulate stupid.”
Of note, the Sebring replaced the LeBaron in the Chrysler line up as its manufacturer lineup — but not until 1995, according to J.D. Power. By then, Rogers was already a Michigan state Senator, well out of college and past his time as both a member of the U.S. Army and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While it’s possible that Rogers confused the two vehicles, the LeBaron wasn’t being built in any facility in Michigan other than the Jefferson Avenue Assembly plant and no longer in Michigan after 1975.
That same month, speaking to Republicans voters and donors, Rogers again said he worked in a car factory.
“We always had to work,” Rogers said. “Obviously I worked in a car factory, put myself through school. That was a deal, as well. They’d helped where they could, but with five boys, they’re not being able to write a check, but it was the best thing they ever gave me. So I worked in that car factory.”
His claim became a fixture in that campaign across a few more Trump rallies and interviews, like one Rogers did with The Tony Conley Show in July 2024. It also started appearing in campaign ads.
“I’m Mike Rogers. Slotkin’s for EV mandates,” Rogers said in an ad released in September 2024. “I’m for Michigan. I worked in a car factory. These jobs are important to our families.”
Rogers maintained that he was an automotive assembly line worker even into 2025, well after losing his race to Slotkin the year prior. 
In an interview with Breitbart News in 2025, Rogers again claimed that he worked on an auto factory floor making Sebring convertibles — which would have been impossible considering the Sebring wasn’t manufactured until well after Rogers had attended Adrian College, joined the military, worked in law enforcement and was a sitting member of the state Legislature.
Rogers again spoke of his “factory” experience during a September 2025 rally in Howell featuring Vice President JD Vance. Rogers told the audience that he specifically worked on an auto assembly line, and that those vehicles were Sebrings, not Lebarons.
“And when you think about my time on the assembly line, I worked in two  different assembly lines, one that built Chrysler, Sebring, convertibles,” Rogers told the crowd. “Those are great cars. And if  you got one that wasn’t, I didn’t build that one. I worked in a plant that made the materials to go that went into dashboards and parts. They were phenomenal jobs.”
Cars & Concepts did manufacture trim and additional fixtures, like shifters, to create more luxury looking vehicles, but that work in 1981 and 1982 was for the LeBaron.
The claim resurfaced during the 2026 campaign Rogers is currently waging.
Rogers said in an interview with Albanian TV of America that he “started out working on a car assembly line. I built Chrysler convertibles, the LeBaron.”
In July 2026, Rogers’ wife, Kristi, who has become a trusted campaign surrogate, said in a campaign ad that, “Mike worked in a factory. I worked at Burger King. Both our parents were teachers. It’s the middle class.”
When the Advance had asked Rogers what his experience was in the auto industry, the campaign at first said it was at Cars & Concepts. When fact checking this story, the campaign then said that he worked at a second facility. Before Michigan Advance published this piece, the Rogers campaign said he also worked at Thermofil, but did not provide dates for when he worked with the company, when asked a third time.
Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers (right) speaks at a rally on Saginaw Valley State University campus in Michigan alongside former President Donald Trump (left) on Oct. 3, 2024 ahead of the presidential election | Photo: Anna Liz Nichols
UAW says Rogers’ claims don’t square up with actual autowork experience
When asked, Rogers’ team asserted that his autowork experience came solely from Cars & Concepts. The assertion, and the company’s history, does not square up with what Reyes told the Advance he and other fellow autoworkers would consider actual automotive assembly line or parts manufacturing experience.
The UAW also told the Advance that there is no record of Rogers ever being a member — which in the 1980s would have been a must if he were a long-term automotive factory worker for one of the Big Three car producers.
Reyes, who also served in the military, said he doesn’t doubt that Rogers served in the military because he speaks about his experience in the U.S. Army in a way that only someone who served can. That was not the case in terms of automotive experience, Reyes added, and likened Rogers’ claims as “stolen valor” from the auto industry.
“It’s insulting to my brethren who have spent their lives chasing the chain, whether it’s an assembly plant or a parts plant, sequencing, packaging, whatever it is; the supply chain of the automotive industry,” he said. “If you did not do time in the plant, that’s fine, but don’t act as if you had, and don’t talk to Michiganders about something which millions of us over the generations have experienced, have made careers of, have raised families on because of the collective bargaining power of the UAW.”
Brouillet said, in light of the UAW having endorsed El-Sayed, that “Unlike Abdul, Mike actually had to pay his own way through college–he wasn’t bankrolled by Soros.” 
“If Abdul has ever worked a job where he had to get his hands dirty, we’re all ears,” Brouillet added.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI’s first inspector general could come from Washington, DC, or Florida
description: The director of investigations for the Palm Beach County, Florida’s inspector general’s office, the top watchdog for the U.S. Capitol Police and his investigations chief made Gov. Dan McKee’s list of potential nominees to become Rhode Island’s first inspector general. Over the course of three hours Thursday, the Inspector General Independent Advisory Commiss[...]
text:
David Harper, the U.S. Capitol Police inspector general and one of three candidates recommended to Gov. Dan McKee to become Rhode Island’s first inspector general, interviews before the Inspector General Independent Advisory Commission on Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) The director of investigations for the Palm Beach County, Florida’s inspector general’s office, the top watchdog for the U.S. Capitol Police and his investigations chief made Gov. Dan McKee’s list of potential nominees to become Rhode Island’s first inspector general.
Over the course of three hours Thursday, the Inspector General Independent Advisory Commission interviewed the five finalists for Rhode Island’s newest statewide position.
After another 20 minutes behind closed doors in a State House hearing room, the five-member panel selected David Harper, James Kirdar and Stuart Robinson as the top candidates to lead the new 12-person office, which will be tasked with rooting out fraud, waste, abuse and mismanagement by government agencies. Commissioners had through Sept. 28 to submit three names to McKee under the deadline set by the General Assembly when creating the position.
All three names are sent to the governor with a caveat: No final selection should be made until the candidates have undergone background checks by the Rhode Island State Police, a process Attorney General Peter Neronha, who is on the panel, said could take six to eight weeks.
“I understand the need for speed,” he said. “And I understand the need to try to meet a deadline set by the General Assembly — how well thought through, I don’t know.”
Watchdog groups and lawmakers from across the political spectrum spent more than two decades pushing for an inspector general, but failed to gain traction in the General Assembly until this year when new House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski, a Providence Democrat, made it his top legislative priority when crafting the state’s fiscal 2027 budget.
Legislation gave the nationwide search to a panel consisting of Neronha, General Treasurer James Diossa, Secretary of State Gregg Amore, Rhode Island Ethics Commission Executive Director Jason Gramitt and Will Fletcher, president of the Association of Inspectors General, who traveled from New York to attend each of the commission’s five meetings.
The job posting crafted by the commission following its July 29 meeting allowed interviews to be held in person or via video conference. 
Three candidates made the trip to Providence: Harper, Robinson and Steven Krueger, the first assistant inspector general for the city of New Orleans. Kirdar joined virtually, as did Thomas Whetstone, an analyst with the Louisville, Kentucky, Office of Inspector General.
The panel was initially scheduled to interview a sixth candidate: Mark Priebe, who has served as the acting inspector general for the U.S. Department of Education since December 2025. But Priebe withdrew his application Monday, confirmed Rhode Island Secretary of State office spokesperson Faith Chybowski.
Chybowski did not say why he withdrew, and Priebe did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
James Kirdar, assistant inspector general for investigations at the U.S. Capitol Police, attends the Inspector General Independent Advisory Commission’s interviews virtually on Sept. 24, 2026. In the background are General Treasurer James Diossa, left, and Secretary of State Gregg Amore. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
The finalists
Harper has been inspector general for the U.S. Capitol Police since February 2024. His resume notes that he expanded the office from 12 to 17 employees and oversaw tracking of 765 recommendations issued since the office’s inception — 694 of which had been implemented or closed as of March 31.
He told the panel he applied for the Rhode Island job because of a strong personal affinity for the region. Harper said he and his wife were married at Point Judith, his stepson and wife live across Rhode Island’s eastern border in Fall River, Massachusetts. His wife is a full-time caregiver in New Hampshire, and he previously worked as a federal agent in Massachusetts
“I love New England,” he said.
Robinson has been director of investigations for the Palm Beach County Office of Inspector General since November 2017. According to his resume, he has led more than 50 completed and publicly reported investigations involving a county with a $9.6 billion budget and 39 municipalities, including cases involving multimillion-dollar vendor overcharges and more than 36 grant and assistance fraud matters.
He also spent 25 years as an FBI agent and supervisor investigating public corruption, government fraud and financial crimes.
Robinson too has professional and personal roots in the region. He began his FBI career on the public corruption and fraud squads in Boston in 1990, and later served as a white-collar crimes and public corruption supervisor in Bridgeport, Connecticut.
Kirdar has been assistant inspector general for investigations for the U.S. Capitol Police since April 2025. Before that, he spent more than 16 years with the U.S. Department of Justice Office of Inspector General, where his resume states he directed a team of 24 field officers across eight locations and oversaw more than 625 criminal and administrative public-corruption investigations.
“Throughout my career, I’ve been guided by a fundamental belief: Public service is a responsibility, not a privilege to be taken for granted,” he told commissioners.
Kirdar also has a Rhode Island connection: He earned a bachelor’s degree in criminal science from Roger Williams University in Bristol.
The three candidates offered different approaches when commissioners asked how they would use the office’s subpoena power, which Neronha described as a “blank canvas” because state law alludes to subpoena power without making clear whether it applies only to records or also to witness testimony.
Harper said he would use subpoena power to obtain records from contractors and other outside entities and would also use it to compel witness testimony if permitted under Rhode Island law. He said he would favor giving the inspector general explicit authority to question witnesses under oath.
Robinson said his office in Palm Beach County rarely needs subpoenas because people generally cooperate with investigators. He said more than 75% of the subpoenas his office in Florida issued were to obtain bank records. If a government official refuses to cooperate, he would document that refusal in a public report.
“It paints the real picture when people walk out of interviews,” Robinson said.
Kirdar described subpoenas as an important tool for gathering documents from private entities but said he would be more cautious about using them to compel testimony from members of the public, coordinating with prosecutors before doing so.
The three finalists also differed on their definitions of success for the office.
Kirdar focused on building the office’s infrastructure and relationships during its first months while completing investigations within a 180-day target. Harper said the timeline should depend on the investigation, noting that major corporate or criminal fraud cases can take two to three years or more, while investigations into state agency mismanagement should take about a year. Robinson declined to commit to a timeline, saying inspectors general must prioritize accuracy above all else.
On transparency, Kirdar said he would generally publish shorter executive summaries rather than full investigative reports, while protecting names and other identifying information except when judicial or criminal action makes disclosure appropriate.
Harper and Robinson both said the office’s investigative findings should generally be made public, with exceptions for legal requirements, ongoing criminal cases and other sensitive information.
“We shine sunlight on the government,” Robinson said.
McKee now has 90 days to select his nominee, who will then go before the Rhode Island Senate for advice and consent. 
The inspector general may serve for five years and be eligible for reappointment for one term of the same duration. The annual salary range for the position is between $175,000 and $225,000.
Stuart Robinson, director of investigations for the Palm Beach County Office of Inspector General, sits in the audience during interviews for Rhode Island’s first inspector general on Sept. 24, 2026. At right is Steven Krueger, first assistant inspector general for the city of New Orleans. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)

title: Gov. Pillen announces 90-day pause on diesel taxes for Nebraska ag producers
description: LINCOLN — Gov. Jim Pillen signed a pair of executive orders Thursday aimed at easing cost burdens for Nebraska’s agricultural producers on the same day a like-minded initiative was announced for the 2028 election cycle. The first executive order suspends diesel taxes for vehicles transporting Nebraska seasonally produced products or livestock for the next 90[...]
text:
Gov. Jim Pillen announces a pair of executive orders aimed at easing cost burdens on Nebraska agriculture producers on Sept. 24, 2026. (Courtesy of the Governor's Office)LINCOLN — Gov. Jim Pillen signed a pair of executive orders Thursday aimed at easing cost burdens for Nebraska’s agricultural producers on the same day a like-minded initiative was announced for the 2028 election cycle.
The first executive order suspends diesel taxes for vehicles transporting Nebraska seasonally produced products or livestock for the next 90 days, effective immediately. Pillen said Nebraska ag workers can keep track of their fuel receipts and get refunds on their diesel taxes during this period.
According to a press release, the same executive order also allows highway-registered vehicles to hold, sell or use untaxed, dyed diesel fuel without facing state penalties.
The second executive order raises weight limits for vehicles transporting seasonal products and livestock, increasing the maximum up to 25% over the current limits without requiring extra permits or fees. Pillen said this will allow Nebraska farmers to fill their trailers as much as they need without worrying about state restrictions.
Pillen said both measures are intended to ease the energy burden on farmers during a period of higher fuel prices and continued impacts of historic wildfires in western Nebraska.
Wahoo farmer Doug Bartek said there is a lot of uncertainty in the state’s agricultural industry right now, primarily due to diesel and fertilizer prices. Though he said the executive orders aren’t a “silver bullet,” they will help.
“It just seems like all the way around, we’re kind of getting hit really hard, so this will come at a really good time,” Bartek said.
Sherry Vinton, director of Nebraska’s Department of Agriculture, repeatedly praised the timeliness of the executive orders at Thursday’s press conference. She said row crop farmers are dealing with “challenging profitability,” due to rising input costs.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Pillen’s executive order came on the same day that a new ballot initiative launched aimed for the 2028 ballot. The measure seeks to amend Nebraska law to establish an annual 61-day window Sept. 1-Oct. 31 suspending all state motor fuel taxes. Additionally, the initiative would cap motor fuel taxes at 35 cents per gallon and restore the full tax exemption on off-road agricultural dyed diesel.
Eric Underwood, who’s leading the charge on the initiative he’s called the “Harvest Fuel Tax Holiday Petition,” said he did not communicate with anyone from Pillen’s office ahead of announcing the initiative.
“My conversations with hundreds of Nebraskans over the last six months really became the spearhead for the policy amendment,” Underwood said.
Underwood leads the group Advocates for all Nebraskans, which attempted a citizen petition effort earlier this year to mandate employment of at least 450 police officers in Lincoln — an effort that did not make the 2026 ballot. The latest petition is under a new group: Make Nebraska Even Better.
In addition to his executive orders, Pillen announced that he was sending a letter to President Donald Trump expressing concerns about the Iran war’s impact on rising diesel prices. In the letter, Pillen asks Trump to enact a 90-day pause on diesel exports to foreign countries. He said the suspension would allow U.S. diesel reserves to rebuild and lower costs for American consumers.
“America’s farmers will thank you for putting them first as we work through these market disruptions in American families and see the effects of these lower prices in the grocery store,” Pillen read from the letter.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: US employers are relying more and more on ‘disposable’ workers
description: When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a […]
text:
Aerial view in worker hands installing bitumen roof shingles with air hammer and nailWhen I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a part-timer with no career prospects in that job.
When my best intentions to eat well are for naught and I gorge on Doritos, I remember that the tasters PepsiCo hires to test the chips’ addictiveness are contractors.
These are all examples of what I call “disposable jobs.” People who have them work at an employer’s site, but their employer makes no commitment to them regarding career prospects or job security. My research shows that employers treat more than 1 in 3 U.S. workers as disposable. That comes to just under 57 million full- or part-time workers out of the nation’s workforce of 162 million.
I am a labor economist. In my new book, “Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment,” I explain why this is happening, what forms it takes, how common it is, what the consequences are for people and for society, and what can be done about it.
 3 different varieties

To learn more, I commissioned a nationally representative survey of over 6,000 people in late 2022. I also interviewed nearly 100 workers, employers and policymakers.
I found that there are three categories of disposable workers.
1. Contractors who are employed by a staffing firm but work at a client’s site. Examples include temporary office workers, building cleaners and security guards. Many of these people are poorly paid, but some, such as travel nurses, are highly compensated. My survey shows that these contractors account for 13% of the workforce.
2. Freelancers who work for companies, organizations or agencies without being employees. Examples include Uber and Lyft drivers, food delivery drivers, computer programmers and freelance journalists. In my survey, organizational freelancers represent 5% of the workforce. I don’t include in this category freelancers who work for individual people, such as most dog-walkers and handymen, because my focus is on how employers treat their employees.
3. Marginal workers who are employed by companies, organizations or agencies. They lack career opportunities, and their jobs have high turnover built in. Marginal workers account for 17% of the workforce in my survey.
Marginal work is important due to its magnitude and because although those jobs look standard, they are designed to be disposable.
 Who are marginal workers?

Staff attorneys are quintessential marginal employees. They’re hired by law firms as employees, but the central feature of their jobs is that they are not on the promotion ladder to partner. Unlike their career-track counterparts, they have no job security. They are often hired to do the grunt work on a specific case, with the understanding that there is no commitment to keep them on if business lags or the project ends.
Adjunct professors are another good example. This group includes part-timers who teach a small number of courses and full-time contract faculty, but in both cases they lack job security and aren’t on track to obtain permanent, tenured, academic jobs.
In 1970 people with tenure or tenure-track jobs constituted 73% of those teaching at colleges and universities. By 2021 only 32% had that status, and the rest were adjunct instructors or contract faculty.
 Part-time marginal workers

Another example of marginal work is part-timers.
Employing part-time workers costs less than having full-timers on the payroll. Part-time jobs pay an hourly wage that is nearly 20% below what workers with full-time jobs earn after age, education, occupation and industry are taken into account. When benefits are considered, the gap rises by another 5%.
A second advantage of part-timers from the employer’s perspective is higher turnover, which provides an easy path to be able to adjust the size of the workforce and which enables them to avoid investing in career development.
When a team of researchers led by professor Susan Lambert interviewed 88 employers that pay low wages, they found that many use part-time work to make their workforces more “flexible.” One manager explained that high churn of part-timers gave the company so much flexibility that they didn’t need temp workers.
“Temp workers: We don’t need them,” he said. “Wait a day for turnover.”
Evidence that employers try to maximize the number of people working for them part time instead of full time and with benefits arose after the Affordable Care Act fully took effect in 2014.
The ACA requires that employers with 50 or more employees either provide them with health insurance or pay for them to buy it, but only for people who work 30 or more hours a week. Otherwise they pay, as of 2026, a penalty of US$3,340 per uninsured employee.
Another team of researchers compared trends in part-time work in three low-wage industries – retail, hotels and restaurants, before and after the ACA rolled out. They found that the use of part-timers increased by 500,000 in the years after the Affordable Care Act was implemented. This suggests that companies add to their part-time ranks to save on the health insurance costs of standard employment.
 Forces behind this trend

Why do employers want many of their workers to be disposable?
A primary motive is to save money. Employing freelancers and contractors means they can avoid mandatory benefits such as Social Security contributions and, for larger employers, contributing to the cost of health insurance.
Marginal workers, to be sure, do receive these benefits. But the high turnover built into their jobs means that their employers can invest less in their training and avoid the management costs otherwise associated with layoff severance and fair treatment on the job.
An additional motive for many employers is a lack of respect for what front-line employees can contribute. A 2023 report from the McKinsey consulting firm illustrated this tendency when it asserted that 5% of employees deliver 95% of “an organization’s value.”
This claim, which I believe is inaccurate, still speaks volumes about the attitude of McKinsey and the firms they interviewed regarding the other 95% of workers. They see those employees as disposable.
 Less pay and job satisfaction

My survey showed that contractors, freelancers who work for employers and marginal employees all earn less than regular workers do.
In addition, the survey found that contractors and marginal workers are notably less satisfied with their jobs compared with regular workers, whereas freelancers, due to their ability to choose where and when to work, are more satisfied.
The public also pays a price for the use of disposable workers. As examples, researchers have found that hospital infection rates rise when cleaners are contract workers and that the use of contractors leads to a higher rate of industrial accidents.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Audit acknowledges ‘significantly’ slower mail in South Dakota and recommends solutions
description: An audit report released Thursday recommends ways to improve mail service in South Dakota, and a member of the state’s congressional delegation said the report serves as “a reaffirmation that the mail service is worse than the Postal Service is suggesting.” Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds made a request in December for an audit by […]
text:
A view of the post office in Rapid City, South Dakota, on Sept. 22, 2026. A new audit report from the Postal Service Office of Inspector General diagnoses problems with slow mail service in South Dakota and recommends solutions. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)An audit report released Thursday recommends ways to improve mail service in South Dakota, and a member of the state’s congressional delegation said the report serves as “a reaffirmation that the mail service is worse than the Postal Service is suggesting.”
Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds made a request in December for an audit by the Postal Service’s Office of Inspector General. The OIG is an independent agency within the Postal Service answering to the Postal Service Board of Governors.
“We’re definitely making progress,” Rounds said Thursday after reviewing the report. “The OIG agrees with South Dakotans that mail service is as bad as we have been saying it is for the last two years.”

U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, speaks at the Dakotafest agricultural trade show in Mitchell, South Dakota, on Aug. 20, 2025. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Rounds has taken several other actions to pressure the Postal Service, including a hold on Senate confirmations of Board of Governors nominees. Rounds said Thursday he will keep the hold in place “until such time as I see results.”
One of the recommendations is determining the feasibility of bringing regional mail processing to the state. The Postal Service responded by saying it will upgrade a Sioux Falls processing plant to a regional processing and distribution center, which should keep most South Dakota mail in the state and reduce delivery time for some packages by one or two days. The service made that announcement Tuesday, two days before the report’s publication, and said the change will take effect in January.
The audit report is murkier on the timeline, saying the Postal Service expects to make the change “shortly after the turn of the calendar year,” but the plan’s “defined milestones, transportation schedules and operating changes” are being finalized with a target implementation date of June 30.
Problems caused by cost-saving measures
Problems in South Dakota are rooted in nationwide Postal Service actions undertaken several years ago to save money, according to the audit. Those actions have resulted in $755 million of transportation savings and have reduced other costs by about $2 billion, according to previous findings.
“However,” said the report, “network changes have significantly impacted the timeliness of mail delivery in South Dakota.”
One of the culprits is the consolidation of processing and distribution into 60 regional centers across the country, none of which was planned to be in South Dakota.
Meanwhile, a policy change dictates that mail originating in post offices farther than 50 miles from a regional center is no longer picked up the same afternoon. Instead, it’s picked up the next morning, “automatically adding an extra day before it is delivered,” the audit report said. Every post office in South Dakota is more than 50 miles from a regional center, because there is no regional center in the state, at least until the Sioux Falls plant’s upgrade is finalized.
Processing of some local mail has stayed within the state’s borders, but much of South Dakota’s mail began going elsewhere in early 2025 for processing at regional centers in Denver, Fargo and Omaha.
“As a result,” the report said, “intrastate mail that was previously processed within South Dakota must now travel hundreds of miles to up to seven states before re-entering the state.”

A map shows where mail in South Dakota has gone for out-of-state processing since the Postal Service consolidated regional processing and distribution centers. (Courtesy of Postal Service Office of Inspector General)

No communication of plans
The Postal Service failed to communicate about the impact to communities while moving more mail processing out of state in 2025, according to the audit.
The Office of the Inspector General for USPS recommended establishing “a required process to publicly communicate any impacts to mailers and residential customers, prior to implementation” when making changes to processing as significant as those that affected South Dakota. The Postal Service agreed with the recommendation and said it would implement it by August 2027, the report said.
Although South Dakotans were not informed of the changes that caused the problems in their state, they quickly began to notice and complain, especially about the delivery of medications and newspapers. The number of complaints reaching Rounds’ office numbered more than 1,000, he said.
The Office of Inspector General’s audit process included a public input opportunity that resulted in 509 comments.
“Public feedback confirmed widespread concerns,” the report said.
The office also conducted a data review, mailed 120 packages, and conducted observations and interviews at three processing facilities and 16 post offices.
Standards were watered down
Besides outlining the causes and effects of mail problems in South Dakota, the audit report explained that the Postal Service adjusted its self-imposed standards for mail delivery in the state to accommodate slower service. And yet, “even with additional days added to most service standards, the percent of mail delivered within those standards declined across all mail classes,” the audit report said.
The auditors recommended the Postal Service align its standards to appropriate delivery timeframes as mail is moved back in state for processing. The Postal Service agreed and is targeting June 30 for implementation.
All of the changes that negatively affected South Dakota were made, according to the audit, “without a state-level strategy.”
“Looking ahead,” the report said, “it will be essential for the Postal Service to evaluate modernization impacts not only at a national scale but in states — like South Dakota — where geography, distance and the absence of a centralized processing facility introduce operational risks.”
Rounds has some advice in the meantime for people voting by mail for the Nov. 3 general election in South Dakota, where advance voting started last week.
“Plan on getting it done a little ahead of time,” Rounds said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: ‘Better than before’: WA reopens historic Capitol campus building
description: More than two years of construction and $131 million later, a historic building on the Washington state Capitol campus is reopening.  A cadre of top state officials cut the ribbon and welcomed the public into the transformed Joel Pritchard Building on the south side of campus Thursday afternoon.  Lt. Gov. Denny Heck said the 77,000-square-foot […]
text:
The expanded Joel Pritchard Building on the Washington state Capitol campus after a ceremony on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)More than two years of construction and $131 million later, a historic building on the Washington state Capitol campus is reopening. 
A cadre of top state officials cut the ribbon and welcomed the public into the transformed Joel Pritchard Building on the south side of campus Thursday afternoon. 
Lt. Gov. Denny Heck said the 77,000-square-foot building wasn’t just expanded but built “better than before.” It faces the Capitol Dome with legislative office buildings on each side.
“It is truly magnificent,” Heck said.
This marks the latest step in the modernization of the Capitol campus, which has included the tear-down and rebuild of the Irving R. Newhouse Building, which houses Senate Republicans, and renovation of the John L. O’Brien Building, home to many state House members. The O’Brien Building work is set to wrap up in the coming months. The General Administration Building on the north side was demolished this summer, and skylights are coming back to the Capitol building.
The Pritchard Building, designed by architect Paul Thiry, joined the Capitol campus in 1958, the last addition to the Olmsted Brothers-designed grounds. It cost $1.3 million to build, at the time. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.
The north face of the Joel Pritchard Building is shown in this undated photograph. (Photo courtesy of the Washington State Archives)
For decades, the building served as the Washington State Library until the 2001 Nisqually Earthquake underscored seismic risks. The earthquake damaged the building, leading the state to relocate its library collection to a Tumwater facility. 
For years, most of the building served as an empty, windowless former book-storage facility. The massive renovation is meant to turn it into a bright legislative workspace.
There had been talks of demolishing the building, but instead it was restored and expanded.
“I think as we celebrate today, we made the right choice,” said Rep. Steve Tharinger, D-Port Townsend, who is chair of the House Capital Budget Committee.
Construction started in March 2024. The state appropriated over $131 million for the project.
The facade looks much the same, but the construction added a new wing with offices for some state House members. Staff from the state Office of the Code Reviser and Legislative Technology are getting new work spaces. Tenants will move into the building next month. There will also be a new cafe.
And the historic Washington Room was restored, including the 117-foot-long, somewhat abstract mural by artist Kenneth Callahan that adorned the walls when the building opened. The four-paneled, 360-degree mural depicts the arc of humanity, from its primitive start to modern day. It was transported to New York for refurbishment before returning to the Washington Room.
Two visitors take in the Kenneth Callahan mural in the Washington Room of the reopened Joel Pritchard Building. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)
The Du Pen Fountain outside will flow with water again soon. A James Fitzgerald mosaic and Mark Tobey painting remain inside.
The work also included stabilization of the steep hillside next to the building that leads down to the banks of Capitol Lake. This involved driving many concrete columns deep in the ground to support the building, Tharinger said.
The building is named for the state’s former two-term Republican lieutenant governor. Pritchard also served in Congress and the state Legislature, and is considered the “Father of Pickleball” for inventing the sport with friends in the 1960s. Gov. Bob Ferguson said his parents were active in Republican circles campaigning for Pritchard’s runs for elective office.
“The thing about Joel is, almost unfortunately, he’s better known as the inventor of pickleball,” Heck said, “which I think overshadows what a significant contribution he’s made to our state, what a magnificent public servant he was.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Advisory group suggests adding member of the public to South Dakota Open Meetings Commission
description: A member of the public could have a vote on South Dakota’s Open Meetings Commission if the state’s incoming attorney general, legislators and governor back a proposal recommended Thursday by an open meetings task force. The commission is a five-member board established in 2004 to hear complaints about alleged violations of open meetings laws and […]
text:
Attorney Sara Frankenstein speaks to members of the South Dakota Open Meetings Commission on Nov. 18, 2024, in Pierre. The commission's membership consists entirely of state's attorneys or assistant state's attorneys, but a task force has recommended legislation that would change the commission's makeup to include a member of the public. (Photo courtesy of SD Attorney General's Office)A member of the public could have a vote on South Dakota’s Open Meetings Commission if the state’s incoming attorney general, legislators and governor back a proposal recommended Thursday by an open meetings task force.
The commission is a five-member board established in 2004 to hear complaints about alleged violations of open meetings laws and issue censures to public bodies that have broken them.
Per state law, its five members have always been state’s attorneys or deputy state’s attorneys, all appointed by the attorney general. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The South Dakota Advisory Task Force on Open Meetings Laws, a 15-member group, was created by Attorney General Marty Jackley last year to consider updates to the state’s transparency statutes that apply to public meetings.
Every member of the group present for Thursday’s virtual meeting voted in favor of a proposed change that would expand the Open Meetings Commission to seven members and adjust its makeup to represent a wider range of voices.
If the proposal is adopted, the group would have four state’s attorneys or deputy state’s attorneys, two attorneys representing public bodies other than counties, and one member of the public. The attorney general would maintain the sole discretion to appoint members.
‘Defensibility’ with a public member
The idea of adding a member of the public to the commission came from Dave Bordewyk, the director of the South Dakota NewsMedia Association, which includes South Dakota Searchlight as a member. He was absent for Thursday’s meeting, but his proposal was backed by Steve Willard, president of the South Dakota Broadcasters Association.
Given that members of the public or media representatives arguing on their behalf are typically the ones who file complaints, Willard said, a layperson’s voice would add credibility.
City council and town board violated open meeting laws, commission finds

“For their purposes, I think there’s some comfort, and some defensibility on this particular group that it’s not so insular, that it includes a member of the public,” Willard said.
The proposal was one of four up for consideration on Thursday, including the one that was endorsed, which was modified to include seven members. 
Two other proposals would have added lawyers for public bodies other than counties, whose voices are represented by state’s attorneys, but not a member of the public. As written, all four kept the commission’s membership at five.
An informal survey of advisory group members found that most supported the idea of including at least one member of the public, but with reservations. Several expressed concerns about appointing a non-lawyer to a quasi-judicial role.
“I’m of the opinion that an attorney representing something other than a public body would be a good thing,” said Geoffrey Gray-Lobe, a Clay County commissioner.
Majority would remain prosecutors
Michael Smith is the state’s attorney for Clay County and a member of the Open Meetings Commission. Smith said he understands the value of a public voice, but also said the work of determining whether a public body broke the law is akin to prosecution. 
“There is a deep need to understand the law,” Smith said.
Open Meetings Commission finds two local boards violated South Dakota law

Austin Hoffman, who’s the McPherson County state’s attorney and also serves on the Open Meetings Commission, said he’d be comfortable with the idea of a layperson serving alongside him if the group’s makeup remained a majority of prosecutors.
Kellen Willert, the city attorney for Belle Fourche, agreed that a prosecutor-led group is ideal, but said the commission’s authority is limited. 
“The worst thing they can do is issue a censure,” Willert said. “I think it makes sense to have a member of the public on it. Nobody’s right to life or property is endangered.” 
Hoffman and the others who’d expressed reticence at the idea of a layperson interpreting the law coalesced around the seven-member, majority prosecutor proposal, in part because two extra people would make it easier to have a quorum and hold hearings if some members are absent.
Idea would need legislative, governor support
To take effect, the change would need to take the form of a bill in the next legislative session, which begins in January. That bill could be presented at the request of the attorney general or introduced by a lawmaker.
Jackley formed the advisory group, but won’t be around to pitch its proposal. He’s a candidate for South Dakota’s seat in the U.S. House of Representatives.
Fall River and Oglala Lakota County State’s Attorney Lance Russell is running unopposed for attorney general in the Nov. 3 election after securing the Republican Party’s nomination for the post. He will take over the job in January. 
He’s also currently a member of the Open Meetings Commission. In an email to South Dakota Searchlight, he said he’s a supporter of the group’s mission and its current five-member makeup, but has yet to talk to the task force members about their decision on Thursday.
“I am keeping an open mind on its recommendation and look forward to hearing the rationale for the proposal,” Russell said.

title: New Mexico education officials propose new budget with 2.9% increase
description: The New Mexico Public Education Department on Thursday laid out spending plans for a proposed $5.9 billion budget for the Fiscal Year 2028 budget, a 2.9% increase over FY27. PED requested, in the wake of the landmark Yazzie/Martinez case, $30 million for Indian education and $1.7 million for bilingual multicultural education, among other education initiative[...]
text:
New Mexico public education officials proposed a $5.9 billion budget request to a joint interim Legislative Finance and Education Study committees on Sept. 24, 2026, which included increased funding for school improvements. (Photo of Mayfield High School students in Las Cruces by Leah Romero for Source New Mexico)The New Mexico Public Education Department on Thursday laid out spending plans for a proposed $5.9 billion budget for the Fiscal Year 2028 budget, a 2.9% increase over FY27.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a joint presentation to the interim Legislative Finance and Education Study committees, PED officials detailed budget priorities, which include building on improvements with literacy rates and chronic absenteeism, and continuing to work to address lower-performing schools.
Specifically, the proposed budget includes $15.5 million for literacy and reading support; $16.6 million for literacy coaches; and $29 million for reading and mathematics intervention, among other items. 
In a statement issued Thursday, PED Secretary Mariana Padilla said the proposed budget “will help schools build” on the gains that have been made, while also addressing critical needs in mathematics, student engagement and educator recruitment. “These investments focus resources where they can make the greatest difference for students and give educators the support they need to succeed,” she said.
Another priority for PED in the proposed budget was student attendance and engagement — $35 million for career technical education; $10 million for summer internships; $60 million over three years for afterschool programs.
Padilla said that the department received a grant from the U.S. Department of Education that it plans to use for “career connected” education in middle schools throughout the state. She also highlighted summer programs served with the funding.
“Students build their job skills, their life skills, and are able to really develop some strong mentorship opportunities,” Padilla said.
PED requested, in the wake of the landmark Yazzie/Martinez case, $30 million for Indian education, $1.7 million for bilingual multicultural education, $1.5 million for Hispanic Education and $500,000 for Black Education.
Rep. Derrick Lente (D-Sandia Pueblo) acknowledged the funding priority, reminding the Legislature that before 2019, the Indian Education budget was $2 million. Student groups identified in the case saw the largest literacy and mathematics proficiency gains in grades three to eight from 2022 to 2026, according to PED statistics.
“We are not fighting over crumbs anymore,” Lente said. “We are seeing the capacity being built at a number of our pueblos, nations, and tribes — and seeing real results at this point.”

title: Douglas County sheriff plans to investigate county program for the poor
description: OMAHA — The Douglas County sheriff on Thursday announced that he will open an investigation into the practices of a county program designed to help the poor. Sheriff Aaron Hanson said his intent is to ensure that taxpayer dollars have not been criminally spent. The move comes on the heels of a report by the […]
text:
Douglas County Sheriff Aaron Hanson. Aug. 2, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — The Douglas County sheriff on Thursday announced that he will open an investigation into the practices of a county program designed to help the poor.
Sheriff Aaron Hanson said his intent is to ensure that taxpayer dollars have not been criminally spent. The move comes on the heels of a report by the State Auditor’s Office, which flagged alleged and potential improper distribution and use of gift cards intended for low-income county residents.
“We owe it, not only to every citizen in Douglas County, but especially to those this program is designed to assist, to ensure that hard earned property tax dollars are not being impermissibly or fraudulently misspent to the detriment of taxpayers and those who actually need the help this program is designed to provide,” Hanson wrote in a  media release.
Attached to Hanson’s media release was a letter addressed to Douglas County Board Chair Roger Garcia and Vice Chair Mike Friend. Referencing State Auditor Mike Foley’s findings, Hanson said he had consulted with Douglas County Attorney Don Kleine about the matter.
Nebraska auditor criticizes Douglas County’s ‘high’ cost to administer program for the poor

Both Hanson and Kleine are up for re-election in November. 
Hanson, in the letter, told Garcia and Friend that he had financial crime investigators in his office and would be “happy to assist” the county’s general assistance staff in vetting applications for potential fraud.
In addition to “problematic” distribution and use of Dollar General gift cards, Foley criticized the county’s general assistance office for high administrative costs, contending that for every $100 of financial aid to the poor in a three-year period, the county spent roughly $74 on administrative expenses. He said the top three salaries among 18 people ranged from $166,614 to $105,000.
Friend said county officials were analyzing Foley’s report. While he said he was concerned about the findings, he doesn’t think at this point that the matter merits a law enforcement investigation. 
Melissa Sewick, director of the county’s general assistance program, has defended her team’s efforts to “responsibly” administer public assistance, which she said includes a range from determining eligibility to helping clients connect with other resources. She said, however, that county officials recognize the importance of efficiency, have made some changes and continue to evaluate their processes in light of the auditor report.
Garcia was out of town and deferred to a statement by the county’s chief administrative officer. In that, Patrick Bloomingdale said: “I will discuss the proposed investigation with the County Board in executive session next Tuesday.”
Mike Friend, vice chair of Douglas County Board. (Courtesy of Douglas County)
Hanson thanked county officials in advance for their cooperation in the investigation, which he said was likely to be complex.
The sheriff previously had  sent a letter Jan. 7 to Garcia, Friend, Bloomingdale, Kleine, Commissioner PJ Morgan and County Finance Director Lori Pirsch.
That letter talked about a “worthwhile concept of renewing the working relationship” between the county’s office that handles general assistance and the Sheriff’s Office. 
Hanson said that in the past, the two offices had worked “proactively together” to investigate fraudulent applications that he said resulted in inappropriate disbursements to people. That “interplay” steadily declined over the decade, the sheriff wrote. 
According to Hanson, the general assistance office sent 14 referrals to the sheriff between November 2020 and May 2021. Since May 2021, there have been no referrals, he said, adding: “I suspect the drop-off was the result of personnel changes in that office.”
Hanson’s Jan. 7 letter included a memo from Chief Deputy William Niemack, who told the sheriff that he would like to “examine the current status of criminal fraud against Douglas County, specifically regarding general assistance.”
Niemack wrote that the sheriff’s criminal investigation division was not yet at full capacity at that time, but was increasing to 10 investigators. He asserted that a past proactive partnership led to efficient use of funds and violators being held accountable.

description: Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey is urging residents to check if they bought certain generic drugs, in which case they may be eligible for new settlement funds.  Maine and 47 other states and territories plan to use settlement funds from drug manufacturers to refund consumers that paid inflated prices for certain generic drugs from May […]
text:
(Photo by Mint Images/ Getty Images)Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey is urging residents to check if they bought certain generic drugs, in which case they may be eligible for new settlement funds. 
Maine and 47 other states and territories plan to use settlement funds from drug manufacturers to refund consumers that paid inflated prices for certain generic drugs from May 2009 and December 2019, according to a press release from the Office of the Maine Attorney General. 
The coalition filed a series of antitrust lawsuits against drug manufacturers, starting in 2016, arguing the companies conspired to raise the prices of generic drugs. The coalition has reached settlements with several manufacturers, totalling roughly $96.5 million. 
This month a federal judge gave initial approval to the coalition’s plan for the settlement funds.
Consumers can check the list of eligible drugs at https://aggenericdrugsclaims.com/, or call 1-866-290-0182 and email info@AGGenericDrugs.com. Consumers can then submit a claim for the drug purchase until March 8, 2027.
